- - - - - A MOUNTAIN STREAM. From the rim it trickles down Off the mountain's granite crown, Clear and cool; Keen and eager though it go Through your viens with lively flow, Yet it knoweth not to reign Through the chambers of the brain With misrule ; Where dark water-cresses grow You will traco its quiet fIJW, With mossy border yellow, So mild, and soft, and mellow, In its pouring. With no 2limy dregs to trouble The brightness of its bubble As it threads its silver way From the granite shoulders gray Of Ben Doraln. Then down the sloping side It will slip with glassy elide, Gently welling, Till it gather strength to leap With a light and foamy sweep To the corrie broad and deep, Proudly swelling; Than bends beneath the boulders 'Neath the shadow of the shoulders Of the Ben, Through a country rough and shaggy, Bo jaggy and so knaggy, Fall of hummocks and of hunches, Full of stumps and tufts and bunches, Fall of bushes and of rushes, In the glen, Through rich green solitudes, And wildly hanging woods, With blossom and with bell, In rich redundant swell, And the pride Of the mountain daisy there, And the f )rest everywhere With the dress and with the air . Ot a bride.

A Rouoa BEDFMLOW.—There is a good story going the round of the papers, told of a man in Edinburgh who had been drinking till a late hour at night, and then started for home in a state of sweet obliviousness. Upon reaching his own premises he was too far gone te dis- cover any door to the domicile he was about to inhabit, and therefore laid himself down in a shed which was a favourite rendezvous for the hogs. They happened to be out when the new-comer arrived, but soon returred to their bed. The weather being rather cold they, in the utmost kindness, and with the traest hospitality, gave their biped companion the middle of the bed, some lying on either side of him, and others acting the part of quilt. Their warmth prevented him from being injured by exposure. Towards morning he awoke. Finding himself comfortable, in blissful ignorance cf his wk lreabouts, he supposed himself enjoying the accom- modation of a tavern in company with other gentleman. He reached out his hand, and, catching hold of the bristles cf a hog, exclaimed—" Holloa, my good friend, you've got a strong beard! When did you shave last? NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c. A large consignment of dairy utensils has been despatched from Tarporley (Cheshire) to New Zealand, where they will be used in the first cheese factory established in that colony. The agricultural statistics of Victoria, Australia, for the past season show a falling off in the yield of wheat as com- pared with that of the previous year of over a million bushels, an average of about half a bushel to the acre. The agriculturists of Durham have before them a sug- gestion for a grand centenary exhibition in 1883, in com- memoration of the establishment of the first agricultural association in the county. The Agricultural Society for the county of Durham was established at Darlington on the 15th September, 1783. The _Buenos Ayres Stapdard says:—." The magnificence of this year's maize crop is proving too much for our railways. This is the first year that the River Plate could boast of what may be termed a decent crop of maize, and it is esti- hated that the crop available for export will reach 200,000 ne. Every steamer leaving port takes thousands of bags ief this new staple. and to new European markets." Mr. Thomas H. Easor, of Dorchester, a student at the College of Agriculture, Downton, has passed the examina- tions and obtained the diploma of the Highland and Agri- cultural Society of Scotland. Mr. Ensor has been elected a life member of the society, and authorised by the Council to use the distinction of Fellow of the Highland and Agricul- tural Society. Mr. Ensnr was the only Englishman who pissed. Ceresniraz CHEESE-MAXI:W.—Mr. Willard, America, when Rake his opinion of the Cheshire system of cheese-making, said, "I can describe it by a little incident which hap- pened on board the steamer. An Irish fiddler was playing a jig, which called the attention of a foreign musician, who asked him if he played by ear or from notes. "Neither," said he, "but by main force, be jabers." "Main force," said Mr. Willard, Is is the proper term for describing the Cheshire system." Lord Vernon has inaugurated a new era in dairy farming on his large estate in North Staffordshire and East Derby- shire, by the erection of a butter-making factory at Sud- bury, near Uttoxeter, which has just been set in operation for the exclusive use of his tenants. At present 300 lbs. of excellent butter per day are being made. His lordship has also commenced to erect a cheese factory on the American principle, near the butter factory, so that his tenants may find a near and profitable market for their milk. The United States Agricultural Department's July report on Indian corn shows that 2,500,000 acres have been planted; a 4 per cent. increase. The condition has been low, owing to late planting and the cold, wet weather, but it was im- proving throughout Jane, and promises a far better condi- tion in August should the season continue as favourable as now. The average is 85, against 90 last July. The yield I will be between 1,200 and 1,700 million bushels according to the meteorological condHone of the next 80 days. Winter what is 104, against 83 last July; spring wheat 100, against 90; oats 103, rye 101, barley 95. All cereals, except maize, promise a yisld per acre above the average. The Sydney papers give particulars of the sudden out- 1 bulk of a strange disease among horses, which appears to I be causing alarm in India, horses being commonly brought ' to Indian ports direct from Au.tralia. It broke out, it ap- pears, among draught horses in the district of Dubbo. For a time it was attributed to over-driving and want of water upon the long stages of the road from Dabbo to Caber; but the spread of the disease has shown clearly that its causes , IWdeeper. Latterly, indeed, it has attacked cab horses and Verses in stables in towns, and it appears to be of a highly contagious character. The main symptom seems to be a swelling in the hind legs' which developing, the animals after a while stagger and die. The Sydney Herald states that the town coalmen is littered with-stock dropped by travelers, and the air for miles round is putrid with decayed careless- STOPPING AND FERTILISING VEGETABLE MARROWS.— Unless the growths of the plants are trained thinly, so thet the leaves of one vine or growth do not overlap those of the other, the plants cannot be productive ; the first point, therefore, to secure is a thin disposal of the growths. As these advance they will show fruit. Souse of them may be stopped, that is, have the end pinched out one leaf beyond the fruit. This plant will then, if fertilised, swell rapidly, and afford early produce, and more room will at the same time he afforded for the extending growths. Let these extend until they nearly reach their allotted space, then pinch out the points. Side growths will then issue, and each of them probably will produce a female, which will be known by the embryo fruit supporting it, the male flowers being borne on simple, slender footsteik. All that is necessary for fertilisa- tion is for the pollen of the latter—the dusty particles that are produced by the stamens—to touch the pistil of the ,former. When the weather is dry the wind distributes the pollen grains, which adhere to the pistils, which is viscid ; or, the work is done by insects; but in unfavourable weather artificial manipulation becomes of great advantage. It is very simple. Choose a time in the forenoon preferably, when the flowers are dry •, take a male or staminate flower, and apply the pollen to the pistil of the fruit.bearing flower, and fertilisation will be effected. If the shoot is stopped at one leaf beyond the said flower the fruit will swell rapidly. THE "COST OF PROD lICTION."—At the next Chicago fat stock show a new feature will be introduced, namely, the awarding of prizes in classes for the purpose of ascertaining i the "cost of production" of the animals exhibited. Under this head detailed information is required as to the exact age, breeding, and weight, as well as market value of the several kinds of food consumed each year, from the date of ' birth to the date of exhibition. In pointing out the advan- tages to be gained from this novel competition, the National , Live Stock Journal (Chicago) says :—At the next show this information is to be verified, and not carelessly stated or guessed at, as the age has been in many cases heretofore. ' This comes quite up to the requirements of the case; and , when this information is fully received, this show will stand in advance of all others. It was often said by sceptical ,farmers of the old style, when their attention was celled to t•the gain of these early matured animals, and to their ex- cellent. market weight at two years old, "Well, that is only one gile of the case. If we knew the cost in food of grow- ing these wonderful animals, like hot-htmse plants, we i should then sae that they cost more than they come to." The cost aide of the problem is therefore a very important +one ; but however important it is seen to be, that side of the 'else has never yet been given at a fat stock show. The , prizes offered will pay for the trouble of keeping this ac- , count, and besides, this knowledge to the feeder himself ought to be worth much more than it costs. Why should' lnot the great industry of growing animals be reduced to I 'business principles? And what great mechanical or manu- facturing business could be carried on without knowing the cost of production? This advance :movement of the man- 1 agers of the fat stock show will attract much and deserved I attention abroad, and help Americen7farmers to hold the reputation of being eminently practical in their views of agricultural teaching. And when this clam shall be well filled at the Chicago fat stock show, fully complying with the requirements, it will teach a lesson of more importance to stock husbandry than any experiment yet brought out at any of our agricultural college farms or experiment stations. The problem of actual cost of growing a two-year-old, or even a pig, has never yet been worked out at any of our agricultural colleges or experiment stations—and yet these are exactly the places where such problems should be worked out, as they are in possession of farms, appliances, and ex- perimenters well adapted for such work.

CONCRETE HOUSES.—Perbaps the most novel 'application of concrete to constructional purposes is that invented by Mr. Lascelles. By the use of various ingenious devices he has made it possible to build a house, into the constructive parts of which, and even to a large extent into the decera• tire parts also, not one single atom of timber need enter. The method devised by Mr. Lascelles for forming a hollow wall that should be at once economical in materiel and iq space may beat be described as consisting of two thin skins of concrete fixed on either aide of a supporting framework. The framework, which may be of wood, iron, or iron ern- bedded in concrete, must, o I course, be of a sufficient strength to support the various floors and superstructure. The skins need be of sufficient thickness only to withstand the ordinary wear and tear likely to occur. Starting, then, with these conuitions, Mr. Lascelles erected a pair of cot- tages, the outer framework of which was composed of up. right wooden studs, 4 inches by 3 inches, 3 feet apart, and on this were fastened, with ordinary wood screws, slabs of concrete, composed of four parts of coke to one part of cement, with two rods of iron, one•eighth of an inch in diameter, placed diagonally in the centre of each slab. The inner faces of the slabs were finished with lime and sand, the wooden framework showing in the rooms. Two defects I made themselves known in these cottages. The first was that in damp weather, when the rooms were full of moist air, I on the lowering of the temperature outside, the moisture was depesited on the walls in the same way as it is under similar circumstances and from the same causes deposited on the window glass. The other fault was that the party wells proved to be no protection whatever in the matter of sound pawing from one side to the other. The remedy was found in each case to consist of doubling the concrete skin so as to form hollow walls. At the Same time it was foiled practicable to reduce the thickness of the slabs to one inch. —Our Homes, and How to Make Them Healthy. f RECENT PROGRESS IN TELEPHONY. - Some Impottant telephone reeults have been lately obtained by M. van Ryssel— berge, the Belgian meteoroloaist, whose very ingenious ' meteorograph was shown at the Park exhibition bet year. The house of a tenant farmer named Leddy, at Alumna, county Leitrim, was broken into on Sunday by Moonlighter., who beat Leddy in a fearful manner because of his kater- fering with a boycotted turf bank. During the celebration of mass at Kilcunning, KillorneY, on Sunday, 50 armed and disguised men visited the house of Lord Kenrnare's gamekeeper, named Moynahin, while the owner was absent at chapel, and took six guns and some pistols. They also decamped with a box containing some money. A meeting of the Land League section of the Irish mem- bers was held on Tuesday afternoOn,in the Conference-room, House of Commons, Mr. Justin 111‘Carthy presiding. A reso- lution was passed to the effect that the party desire to express their sense of the national loss sustained by the death of Miss Fanny Parnell, and to tender their sympathy to Mr. Parnell and his family. A correspondent at Balls telegraphs that the crops in that district have been badly injured by the continued wet weather. The potato blight has appeared in several places. and it is feared the crop generally will not be a good one. Oats look promising, and turnips look well, but haymaking has received a severe check. New meadows in some places have been cut, and the hay lying on the ground for several weeks. Fuel turf is in a very bad state in consequence of the heavy rains. The police have received important information from a pumpsiriher named Michael Jones in connection with the blowing tip of the residence of Mr. John Ross Mahon, agent to Lord Clonbreck. Jones states that he supplied the dynamite with which the outrage was perpetrated, and gave the names of three men who purchased it. They have been arrested, and Jones has been taken to Dublin. His wife has been threatened, and is under protection. On Sunday night a large party were surprised by a police patrol whilst engaged drilling on Mushera Mountain, be- tween Milletreet and Macroom. The police, having heard words of command given, lay in ambush, and witnessed for a short time the manceuvres of a large number of men. They then surprised them, called on them in the Queen's name to surrender, and threatened to fire if they refused. The whole party fled; but on the police preparing to tire, five of them stood; and these were taken into custody. O'Connell, the informer, states that he is in a position to identify them all.

TIIE IRISH LAND ComatissroN.—A numerical return of appeals from decisions of sub-commissions heard before the Irish Land Commissioners up to June 30, 1882, and a similar return of appeals from decisions from civil bill courts, are published as a Parliamentary paper. The total numbec of appeals in the first-named category was 638, of which 51 were in Belfast, 127 in Dublin, 69 in Limerick, 37 in Killarney, 52 in Cork, 43 in Waterford, 14 in Galway, 62 in Castlebar, and 183 in Londonderry. Of the appeals from civil bill courts, 1 was heard in Belfast, 2 in Limerick, 1 in Killarney, 8 in Waterford, 21 in Castlebar, and 1 in London- derry. In this return are included such cases as,after having been listed for hearing, were (1) heard 14 the court, (2) stated by the parties to be settled, or (3) finally with- drawn by leave of the court. It is noted that since the 6th July, and consequently since the date up to which the fore- going returns were compiled, Mr. Justice O'Hagan and Mr. Commissioner Vernon have been engaged in hearing appeals in Belfast, and have dispesed of about 135 cases. AN ALARMING PICTIIRE,—In his speech at Mal•low, on Sunday, Mr. John Dillon, M.P., drew an alarming picture of what we may expect to see ire the House of Commons if the Crimes Bill is put vigorously into operation. The Par- liamentary representation of Ireland, which was formerly a curse, was, he said, now one of the greatest blessings that could be conferred upon the people, because it was "a weapon with which they could defeat the tyranny of the stranger." If the Irish people would give Mr. Parnell a clear majority of the Irish representatives—" not traitors or ruffians N.,ho backed up the Government "—then "for every man that was arrested in Ireland they would waste a day or two in the House of Commons," and prevent that House from doing any business. Having supplied the Government with another excellent reason for pressing on the procedure rules, Mr. Dillon referred to the Land Corporation, and plainly stated that "it would be the duty of the Irish party, when the right time came, to advise the Irish people t'? devise a machinery, which they might call by some new name, for the purpose of defeating that Corporation." He and his friends hoped to be able to defeat the new Coercion Act, as they had defeated the former one. AffeOTHER IRISH OUTRAGE: ATTEMPT TO SHOOT
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED ] THE PRISON LIFE OF MICHAEL DAVITT.
BY THE AUTHOR OF "SKETCHES OF CONVICT LIFE," ETC.

CHAPTER IL—DARTMOOR. To such a man as Davitt, full of energy and apparently fond of excitement, the.monotony of his many months con- finement at Millbank must have been terribly depressing. As a political prisoner, and under the strictest surveillance, he was not allowed to do any of the little odd jobs outside the cell, which alleviate in some measure the solitariness of life in separate confinement. It was not because of his physical infirmity, for other one-armed men were let out to dust the walls, 'Esc., and so long'as they took care to watch for the coming of any of the principal warders, chief warders, or deputy governor, the warder usually took no notice of such men when a little surreptitious conversation was going on.

llivitt—was anything but a favourite among the officers. There was so much fuss made about his safety that the warder who had him in charge had anything but an easy time of it. The visits of the higher authorities of the pri son to that particular ward were far more frequent than tei Any other, and hence the warder ba4 0 b() Continually on tie alert, aLid !t2(.1. !!`:!t. '.lninent to Spare to t aVe a 4ulCt read of the paper or even a short snooze after dinner. Some "old lag" well versed in all the dodges of the principal and chief warders to catch unwary officers was almost invariably appointed ward orderly. It was his duty to see that "the screw" got into no trouble through a breach of the thousand-and-one ußwritten rules which officers of con- vict prisons are supposed to be fully acquainted with. For instance, the orderly took care that the full number of art'cles of dirty clothing were returned on Saturday after the convicts had changed their linen. He assisted the officer in serving out the meals, and had the privilege of eating up all the spare bread, am The office of orderly was therefore one much coveted, its holder having an amount of power and authority which the authorities of the prison Hever dreamt of.

Another reason why Davitt was disliked by the officers was his reticence with regard to his past history. Most convicts, especially those who have led a criminal life, are prone to tell stories of their past history and what got them into trouble, but Davitt was, on the contrary, not disposed to talk to the officers ; and to the schoolmasters, if they showed any inclination to enter into conversation with him on school days, he would only complain of the exceptional character of his treatment.

The chaplains of "separate " convict prisons usually visit each convict in his cell about once a month, althoughl it must not be supposed that the " visit " is of any length. The warder unlocks the door, the chaplain walks in, asks the convict how he is getting on, if he has any complaints to make of the schoolmaster, expresses a hope that his punish- ment may be blest to his future temporal and spiritual benefit, and takes his leave. That is a fair sample of the chaplain's visit, unless the convict has been "somebody " before his conviction, in which case the chaplain will usually unbend from his official dignity, and converse freely enough. For rank, position, or wealth is regarded, even in a convict prison. As a Roman Catholic, Davitt should been visited by the priest, but it would never have done for his reverence to show any partiality to such a notorious Fenian as Michael Devitt. So his reverence ignored the presence of Davitt in the prison, and only visited him when he was sent for—four or five times during the time he was at Millbank. Dartmoor, to which prison Davitt was sent from Mill- bank, is, in some respects, one of the worst prisons a con- vict cm be located in. It is situated in the wilds of Dart- moor, on the slope of a high hill, and is about 1,000 feet above the sea level. The prison was originally built during the French war of 80 years ago, and hundreds of Frenchmen were confined—and died—there. If the English Govern- ment had any desire to get rid of the troublesome prisoners, they could not have done better than send them to such a terrible climate as that of Dartmoor. The winters there are exceptionally long andasevere, the cold being intense; whilst in summer the rains are so frequent that often for days together the convicts cannot go out to work. Fogs, too, are of frequent occurrence, so that, taken altogether, Dartmoor is a terrible place for a convict. The French soldiers and sailors died by scores, aye, by hundreds, during their imprisonment, and, in reclaiming the bog land, the convicts have often dug up their skeletons, with buttons, medals, &c., showing that they were buried in their uniform. Yet, not- withstanding that the climate of Dal tmoor is so severe, it is one of the prisons to which invalids are sent. There is, of course, very little chance for a consumptive convict sent to Dartmoor, and it is seldom he is again removed until he is past hope, and then perhaps he will be sent to Woking prison—to die. The work at Dartmoor is turf-making, turf being re- quired for the prison gas-house, for the use of the officers, I the prison co.* house, the officers' quarters, &c. As the I area for cultivated land round the prison increases, the bog I land whence turf is obtained becomes further away, and hence enly the best conducted men, with comparatively short sentences, or who are within a year or so of being en- titled to a ticket of leave, are sent to work on the bogs. The turf is cut into large blocks, about 18 inches in length, by ten in breadth and thickuess. These are carried by the convicts to the drying ground, cut into slices about 21 inches thick, and laid on the ground to dry. If the sun is hot they are turned next day, then • set up in two's on their edges, and finally stacked in stacks about five feet high. After lying in the stack a week or two they are carried in bags up the hill to the tram lines and taken in wagons into the prison to the turf house, a building capable of contain- ing many hundreds of tons. When the turf has been taken off the land to such a depth as to be near the gravel sub- soil, the ground is turned over to the foundation, then drained, and sown with turnips as a first crop. Bone manure and ashes are used as fertilisers, and everything done that is possible with such land to obtain good crops. But, although the land pays for the cultivation, it is only because the cost is small. Meadow grass, barley, oats, carrots, parsnips, and potatoes are also grown; but the latter are very small and watery, causing bitter complaints among the convicts, who have to eat them. Quarrying the grey granite stone of Dartmoor is a kind of work scarcely suited to invalids, but it is done for the requirements of the prison, which has recently been greatly enlarged. I The old-fashioned cells in what are called "public works" convict prisons—in contra-distinction to the " separate " ' prisons—are constructed of corrugated iron, about eight feet high, seven long, by four wide. They are only intended for sleeping purposes, but during the many days in which, on account of wet or fog, the convicts are not allowed to go out to work, they are usuadly kept in those cells. At flrst, after his arrival at Dartmoor, Davitt was located in the punish- ment cells—for greater security. They have this advantage over the iron cells, that they are larger and better ventilated; but the noise created by men under punishment, who often sing and shout at the top of their voices, especially at night, precluded the possibility of sleeping, and Davitt asked to be removed to the iron cells. These cells at Dartmoor are con- structed back to back, the door and window lookine, into the hall, therefore there is no open ventilation to the outside. They are also very dark; sodark, indeed, that Davitt often I bad to lie at full length on the floor, and put his book partly under the iron door of his cell, between which and the floor there is a space of about three inches.

There was one alleviation for Mr. Davitt at Dartmoor—a capital library. Old convicts who have in turn been located at all the English convict prisons, say that the library at Dartmoor is the best of them all; and Davitt had access to works which such a man would doubtless read with the greatest avidity. Such works as Macaulay's, Johnson's, Alison's, Prescott's, Gibbon'.%, and other standing math gs are there to be had, and Davitt's confinement at Dartmoor was thus greatly alleviated.

The work Davitt was put to at Dartmoor showed the utter callousness of convict prison authorities. For a few days after his arrival from Millbank be was set to atone-breaking, and of course, having only one hand, it soon became blistered from using the hammer. Then he was put into what is called a "cart party," and along with seven others, with halters or collars round their necks, he was employed in supplying the prison with cods from the coal store, hauling rubbish and stone; that being the only party out in all weathers, wet and dry. After being about a month in this party, one day the collar which Davitt wore across his breast caught the remnant of his right arm, and almost forced the bone through the skin. He went and saw the doctor on the following morning, who, on examining the stainp, excused him from Hos; cart labour. Davitt was then put back to stone-braiking, and was so employed for some months. Next he was attached to a building party, engaged on the new prison, assisting in making mortar, carrying tubs of water, and though he bad only one hand, using a large rake to stir up the mortar. Then he was put in a crank, and with three others had to wind up large stones. Here he was expected to turn as much as a man with two hands, or he would be making the other men's task harder. Then Davitt was employed in breaking putrid bones, and pounding them up, for manure, in a small shed near the prison. He was kept at that work during a whole summer, and he complained bitterly of its unhealthy character, the smell being very offensive on account )f the heat of the weather.

When we bear in. mind that Mr. Davitt is a tall man, of . good physique, we can easily understand that he found the food at Dartmoor insufficient, especially in winter. It was fai inferior to the food at Millbank or Portsmouth; the worst in quality, and the filthiest, as compared with the food at any prison in which ho was confined. The potatoes, especi- ally, being grown on the bon, were very bad; and he could not eat them. When the potato season was near its close' and before the now ones were large enough—the season being ; very backward at Dartmoor—twelve ounces of dirty horse carrots, such as are given by the farmers to their cattle, were substituted for the potatoes. In. addition to the faod being of bad quality, it was prepared in such a horribly dirty fashion as to '4 turn the stomachs" of any prismer used to the ordinary delicacies of civilized life. Black- beetles, horse hair, pieces of old brooms with which the bakehouse and cookhouse were swept out, were found 'in the bread, in the soup, and the puddings. Pieces of coalc_z•rating in the teeth, and small stones occasionally varied the con- vict's experience of prison food. Many convicts, probably the majority, were not over fastidious o.la the subject, and took things as they came, with a degree of sti:,-ieal philo- sophy bred by familiarity with prison life; but to. Mr. Davitt the cleanliness of Ids food was of the utmost consideration'. There are about 1,000 convicts at Dartmoor, and three men have to wash that number of food tins in two or three hours. One cannot wonder,. therefore, that the dinner tins were often in a beastly state. I have stated some of tY,e discomforts to NV bich Mr. Davitt had to su,lemit at Dartm,,or ; in my next chapter something far wor.to hea to bt recorded. To be continued: :7071.-i. m*e4l.

div.head: BEAUFORTS.
div.p: THE BEAUFORTS.

The Spectator, in noticing the reprint of the first series of "Oar Old Nobility," expressed a doubt whether this kind of writing could be productive of useful results. The editor of the Spectator, at the time of the first Reform agitation, was of exactly the opposite opinion, for he devoted special sucplements to information of a somewhat kindred character, from which, however, I have derived hardly any assistance. I venture to hope that, as the work of the Spectator proved useful in regard to electoral reform, my own will not be altogether ineffective when the subject of Land Tenure Reform comes to the front. I believe, too, that more recently the Spectator published a series of articles on " The Great Governing Families of England," which have furnished me witii several useful hints, although the great houses were therein treated far too tenderly. This very phrase, "Great Governing Families," used as recently as 1865, and equally applicable now, expresses a most disagreeable truth. Believing, as I do, in government by the people and not by a few great houses, I humbly venture to hope that I may assist in tearing off the mask of a gigantic imposture, and lead some tenants of the great houses to understand that they are under no obligation to those who receive their rents, and especially that they are under no obligation to sacrifice their political convictions to please the owners of the soil they till or the houses which they inhabit.
Let us take, for instance, his Grace the Duke of Beaufort, who owns in— Gloucestershire 16,610 acres. Monmouth Brecon Wilts Glamorgan
Total M,02„ with a rental of .e 56,209.

The Gloucestershire estates were partly acquired by pur- chase. The far-famed seat at Badminton, which has a park ten miles in circumference, was purchased of the Botelers in 1608 by a younger son of the head of the house of Somerset, and was bequeathed by his only daughter to the Somerset who was afterwards created the first Duke of Beaufort, by whom the mansion was erected in 1082. Other manors in Gloucestershire appear to have been acquired by purchase , still more recently. But it is in the counties on the Welsh border that lam more particularly interested. Monmouth- shire returns two Conservatives; one of whom is a son of the Duke. That the overwhelming majority of county electors in South Wales are Liberals, I presume that no one who knows anything of the district would doubt for a moment. Nowhere is Nonconformity more staunchly Liberal than in South Wales. and nowhere does Nonconformity appear in such strength. It is the territorial tradition alone that makes the return of a Conservative in either of these counties possible. That evil tradition has been recently broken in Brecon for which the Liberal candidate, who, in 1874, was defeated by a majority of 558, now sits as member. That which is possible in Brecon is possible in Monmouth; but the tenantry of the Duke of Beaufort and other territorial magnates have yet to learn that when they have paid their rents they have discharged their obligations in full. The Somersets are Plantagenets'' • and the Herberts, from whom they derived most of their Welsh property, were Normans. They represented the power of the sword, he forcible dis- possession of the weak by the strong. Time has consecrated the conquest, and I have no desire to disturb it, though my fathers dwelt in Wales long before the first of their ancestors set foot upon its soil. But so long as Welshmen who culti- vate their lands sacrifice their convictions at the polling- booth, and vote as their landlord or his agents order them, so long they wear the shameful badge of conquest. The ballot was brought into use to protect their liberties ; those who do not make use of the advantageare slaves. The Duke of Beaufort may lord it over the soil, but when he tries to lord it over our consciences every true-hearted Welshman should cry—Hands off !

"Old John of Gaunt, time-honoured Lancaster," third son of Edward 111.. had a family by his first wife, his eldest son being Henry IV.; by his mistress, Catherine Swinford, whom he afterwards married, he had three sons and a daughter, who took the name of Beaufort from a castle in France, where they were born. The second of these sons was the Cardinal Beaufort of Shakespeare, the eldest was created Marquis of Somerset and Dorset. The son of the latter was created Duke of Somerset, and had an only daughter, who ' was married to Edmond Tudor, Earl of Richmond, and be- came mother of Henry VII. He also left an illegitimate son, Charles, who took his father's title as a patronymic. Charles Somerset was therefore the half-brother of the mother of Henry VII., and, as was to be expected, he shared in the spoils of the final victory of the House of Lancaster. He obtained a number of employments from Henry, but, what was of far greater importance to the fortunes of his descendants, he became a great lord of the soil by his mar riage with the daughter and heiress of William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke and Huntingdon, through whom he acquired the larger part of that nobleman's estates. He was Lord Chamberlain to Henry VII. and Henry VIII.; it the reign of the former monarch he was known in right of his wife's possessions as Baron Herbert; by the latter monarch he was created Earl of Worcester. We must now turn to the Herberts, whose early history is somewhat obscure. It is not quite clear who the original Herbert was. According to one account he was the bastard son of Henry I.—the bar-sinister frequently appears when dealing with the Somersets. According to another account, he was Lord Chamberlain to that King, whose mistress he married. We need not fro into the troubled history of South Wales in those times' but pass on to William Herbert, first Earl of Pembroke. As a simple Knight, he distinguished I himself in the French campaigns of Henry V., but his for- I tune was made by espousing the Yorkist cause. The strength of the Lancastrian cause had -lain chiefly in the I North and West; the bloody fight at Towton was followed by enormous confiscations, and one of the chief gainers thereby was Herbert, who obtained immense grants of lands , in South Wales. For instance, I fired in Jones's "History

div.head: RECORDER OF DUBLIN.
div.p: THE RECORDER OF DUBLIN.

An attempt was made upon the life of the Recorder of Dublin while sitting in his Court at five o'clock on Thurs- day evening. He had just dismissed an action brought by a litigations and excitable person named John Fitzpatrick, an elementary teacher, who claimed a sum of £l7 from a Mr. Gardiner as tuition fees, at the same time remarking upon ; the frivolousness and frequency of Fitzpatrick's cases. Fitzpatrick, who had been very excited during the hearing, approached the traverser's bar, immediately facing the bench, and drawing a revolver from his pocket, pointed it at the Recorder, exclaiming at the same time, "By Heavens,. vou won't give me justice; then I will have your life." He Pulled the trigger,. but there was no explosion. The utmost excitement instantaneously arose. The Recorder put up his hands to his face, policemen in the .galferies leaped down, rushing towards Fitzpatrick, and women fainted, while a gentleman who was nearest to the madman, springing at him, brought him to the ground. Ha tried to transter the revolver to his left hand, but a constable wrenched it from him, and he was secured and carried to the cells below the court, and afterwards to Green-street Police Station, where he was formally charged with the offence. On examination of the revolver it was found to be loaded, and it had oily been prevented from going off when the trigger was pulled by the obstruction of a ramrod. Fitz- patrick declared that he had not intended to kill the Recorder, but only to make a protest against injustice. He is7well known in Dutlin as a person of small and flighty intellect, of childish excitability, and extraordinary views of his personal importance..

The last three wickets fell without any addition to the score, the innings closing for 213. Tne home team com- menced their second innings with Molyneux and Swain and scored 56. but had all the chances been taken it is questionable if thoy would have scored half that number. CARNARVON called attention to the Singular letter purpoit- ing to come from Ourabi Pasha a:dcl addressed to the Prime Ministers remarking that it Wl?..s clear that it wee drawn an English rather than an 'Egyptian hand. He wished to know how the letter was addressed, how it readked the Prctnier, and whether It formed the whole or only part of a correspondence,—Earl GRANVILLE relied that the letter in question was the only communication the Prime Minister had received from Ourabi, and he was not able to say who brought it, The Prime Minister had not Bent any answer. THE BILLS OF EXCHANGE BILL.—The 116 RD CHANCELLOR moved that the Bills of Exchange Bill be referred to a Select Committee for the purpose of considering the nume- rous criticisms and suggested alterations received by the Government.--The motion was agreed to. Irmate TROOPS FOR EGYPT.—Lord ENFIELD then moved the consent of the House to the revenues of India being applied to defray the expenses of the military operations which may be carried out by our Indian forces beyond the external frontiers of Her Majesty's Indian possessions. He believed that the number of men would not exceed 6,000, with a small reserve at Aden. At the sitting of the Indian Council that day the provisional arrangements had been accepted and passed without dissent.—Lord CRANBROOX remarked that none of their Lordships would oppose the motion bearing in mind the special interest possessed in it in India, and that the object of the expedition was to secure peace in Egypt, and a free passage through the Suez Canal.—Lord STANLEY of ALDERLEY objected to the charge being placed upon the Indian revenues, as the expenditure would be mainly for the Egyptian bondbolders.—Earl GRANVILLE denied that a contest was being entered upon on behalf of the bendholders.—The Marquis of SALISBURY was glad to hear this, as he should be opposed to imposing any burdens not only on the Indian but upon the English people in the interests of the bondholders.—The motion was then agreed to. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.

THE RESERVES.—The PRIME MINISTER brought up a message from Her Majesty announcing that as there was a state of emergency within the meaning of the Acts of Par- liament she is about to call out her reserved forces, or such portion of them as she thinks necessary, for permanent' service.—lt was agreed that the message should be taken into consideration on Wednesday. THE VOTE OF CREDIT.—On the motion of Mr. Gladstone that the House go into Committee on 'the Vote of Credit, Lord Er.cno moved an amendment to the effect that while the House was ready to vote such sum as was necessary for the protection of the Khedive and the security of the Suez Canal, it was not prepared to enter upon a war for the restoration of the authority of the Khedive, unless in con- junction with the forces of the Sultan.—Mr. GLADSTONE deprecated the submission of such a resolution at the present moment, and asked the House to come to an immediate decision upon it.—The amendment having been put and negatived without a division, the House went into Committee, and Mr. GLA.DSTONE moved the vote of £2,300;000.—Colonel STANLEY asked the Government to be -sure of the objects for which they went to war, and to take care that no false impression was created in the minds of the Mahometans of Egypt.—Sir LA.WSON contended that upon the evidence before them there was no reason for what was going on, and expressed his satisfaction that Mr. Bright had by retiring from office shown that he thought this war unjust and immoral. The hon. baronet insisted that it was neither more nor less than a war for the bondholders, and was a great crime against humanity.—Sir C. DILICE in reply asserted that it was the belief of the Govern.ment that the anarchy in Egypt was caused by military tyranny, and that there was reason to ' believe that calm would follow the suppression of the tyranny The Khedive had support of the most reasonable and sensible of the Mahometan population,and it was the desire of the Government in redeeming Egypt from the military party to leave the people to manage their own affairs. The only aim the Government had was the prosperity of the country. They had no objection to the birth and growth of the national movement in Egypt until it became military. 'lt was impossible to tolerate the continuance of anarchy in Egypt, and the dominance of a purely military party in that country would place our communications with India in permanent jeopardy. The primary object with which they went to Egypt was to protect their own subjects, and our fleet being there for an undoubtedly legitimate purpose it was surely necessary to protect it, for the Government had no right to expose their men to daily increasing dangers. He saw nothing contrary to either Liberal or Radical prin- ciples in striking hard when British representatives were threatened.—Sir J. HAY, in the course of a lengthy criticism, said he thought sufficient force ought to have 'been sent to enable the Admiral to effect a landing—Sir J. TEASE doubted whether the Government policy from its beginning to its end commended itself to the moral sense of the nation. He. however, felt that he could rot vote against the proposal of the Government.—Sir S. NORTH- COTE attributed much of our difficulties to the French alliance, and pleaded for a little more consideration for Ottoman feeling. The discussion of the vote was con- tinned by a snfall number until the sitting was suspended at I seven o'clock.

TURKISH INTERVENTION.—Before the House adjourned, Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked whether there was any truth in the statement that Turkey had conscnted to send troops to Egypt.—Sir C. DILKE said the Porte had not accepted the Identic Note, but had accepted the essence of the Note, which was to send troops to Egypt, but it was entirely open to them to discuss the three conditions of the Note at the sitting of the Conference on Wednesday. ' IlaE VOTE OF CREDIT.—The debate on the Vote of Credit was again resumed at the evening sitting, when Mr. RICHARD spoke against war generally, and the intervention in Egypt in particular. Amid much laughter he said he had some- times thought of bringing forward a resolution proposing that ivhen proposals for war were brought forward and carried in the HOuse of Commons the majority should be forthwith incorporated in one of the regiments and sent out to receive the first fire of the enemy. If that were done Mr. Richard thought there would be fewer wars.—Mr. GORST, by the cid of a Blue-book and newspaper correspondence, presentzd a terrible indictment against the Government. He admitted that it was no use attempting to bring upon Ministers the censure of the majority of the House of Com- mons, "but," he solemnly declared, "they will not escape the censure of the civilized worId."—Mr.CILUIBERLAIN followed and took the trouble to answer point by point the speech of the honourable and laarned gentleman. Discussing British interests in Egypt, Mr. Cham- berlain said that certainly not the primary interest was that of the bondholders. He was not inclined to run down these persons as usurers, but it was clear, that any engaging in speculations of tbat kind must take the risks of hie speculation. There were, however, other inter- ests. There was the Suez Canal, with respect to which the right bon. gentleman read some interesting figures, showing that one-seventh of the whole foreign trade of Great Britain passed through the canal, while four-fiftbs of its traffic is by British ships. There were also the private commercial interests, the possessors of which have a right to look to their Government for reasonable protection. These great inter- ests he declared amid loud and general cheering, were not to be sacrificed to the ambition of a military adventurer, nor could he imagine anything more disastrous to the influence of England in the East than that it should go abroad that we had been set at defiance with impunity by Arabi Bey.— Sir RICHARD Civass continued the debate in an almost empty House, and at one o'clock it was, on the motion of Mr. SHIELD, adjourned.
HOUSE OF COMMONS-WEDNESDAY.

EGYPT: THE VOTE OF CREDIT. Scarcely anything 'besides Egypt was talked about in the House. The Prime Minister early in the sitting was called upon to give an ,assurance that in the steps contemplated for the protection of the Suez Canal the only object in view was the security of the Canal and the freedom of the passage through it, and that there was nuquestion respecting the administration of the Canal, its position as a commercial undertaking, or its international character.—On the motion of Mr. GLAD- seconded by Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, an address was agreed to thanking Her Majesty for her message com- municating her intention to call out the reserve forces.— Sir 11: WOLFF wished ts be informed if the Conference would decide who was to condact the war operations in Egypt, and whether the chief command would be in British or Turkish hands. Mr. GLADSTONE: thought the question • premature, but he hoped his not answering it would not be taken as giving the smallest countenance to the supposition that the disposition of the Eritish force was to be under the control,of a Turkish commander.—Lord COLON CAMPBELL entered-into an elaborate criticism of the Egyptian policy of the Government. He contended that the message from the Crown had been too long deferred, that the contingencies which had occurred might have been perceived, and that if we had made earlier preparations we should have had a better chance of seeing an early-surrender on the part of the Egyptian troops, and have saved Egypt much misery and this country a large amount of cost.—The debate on the Vote of Credit was resumed by Mr. SILIELD.—He was followed by Sir H. Wow, who wished to know with what allies we were going to undertake hostilities.—Mr. CAMPBELL- BANNERMAN, dealing specially with the conduct of the navy, complimented the Admiral, the seamen, and the marines on the admirable manner in which they had dis- charged their duties and restored order in Alexandria.—Mr. RATiosoNE urged-that it was a fallacy to suppose that our commercial prosperity was dependent on the maintenance of the Suez Canal.—Mr. GOSCHEN gave a history of his own mission to Egypt and the establishment of the European Control in that country. He contended that the Control had been productive of beneficent results, as it had lightened kaxation and relieved the country of abuses. These good I,usults had excited enmity in certain quarters, and the action of France at Tunis, following on the acquisition of -Cyprus by England, lead the Egyptian mind to the conclu- sion that the English meant to take Egypt next. As a con- sequence attempts were made to stir up fanatic- ism Against the Europeans. He trusted that the Oovernment would make it clear that they were proceeding, not as the champions of the Cross against ' the Crescent, butas the champions of order and good govern- meat. lie believed it was the general opinion of those who ' had studied the subject that it would be best for England to !Act alone, ,but that we should have the goodwill and the moral support of the other Powers.—Mr. Bourke was addressing the House when the time arrived for suspending I the debate.

ALLEGED LCOTING BY BRITISR TROOPS.—Before the House adjourned, Mr. CHILDERS stated that General Sir A. Alison had telegraphed that he had inquired into the re- ported looting by British soldiers in the Xhedive's Palace at ;,,crileh, and found that there was no foundation for it.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIESDair. Tie RESTRVES...— The Lords' address thanking Her Majesty tem her message relative to the calling out of the reserve force,s was formally moved by Earl GRAN-VILE.— The proposal rile critioiged by the Earl Of PAAPABIrOIf,

who suggested that as the wives ami `children of the men to be called out would be unprovidcd for, it would be well t grant them some portion of their pay in advance —The Earl of MORLEY recognised the importance of the subject, but hoped the difficulty would be reduced to the lowest possible peint by taking in the first instance those who had last joined the reserve, and who therefore would be the youngest men.—The address was agreed to. TEE ARREARS BILL.—Lord CARLINGFORD moved the second reading of the Arrears of Rent (Ireland) Bill, ex- plaining at length its provisions, and remarking that it was introduced for the benefit alike of landlords and tenants, and that it was hardly likely that it would involve any heavy demand upon the Consolidated Fund.—The Marquis of SALISBURY urged that if the Government were sinc.?.re in their profession of a desire not to invade landlords' rights, they ought to make the bill optional to the landlord as well as to the tenant. If the bill passed in its present form, so far from healing the sores of Ireland, it would only occasion new and extravagant expectations, enforced by more atrocious means, and leading to new and more dangerous concessions. Whilst he was not willing to propose the rejection of the bill, containing as it did some valuable provisions, he did not wish to be understood as consenting to the more dangerous principles it embodied, and could not undertake to join at some future time in passing the bill into law unless those principles were removed.—The Marquis of LANSDOWNE felt that some settlement of the arrears question was indispensable, and that on the whole the settlement proposed by the Govern- ment was the only one likely to.be effectual.—The Marquis of WATERFORD denounced the measure, but thought their Lordships should not take the responsibility of rejecting it on the second reading, but that they should insist upon the introduction of reasonable amendments.—Earl COWPER looked upon the measure as a wise one, and Lord BURY' objected to it as unfair to the English taxpayer.—After some remarks from the Duke of Abercorn, the Earl of Dunraven, the Earl of Donoughmore, Lord 'entry, and Lord Denman, the bill was read a second time, and the Com- mittee was fixed for Monday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAT.

THE ARREARS BILL.-Mr. THEYELYIN, in reply to questions, stated that if the Arrears Bill became law, the Lord-Lieutenant would certainly consider the offer of the Canadian Government to grant 160 acres of land to Irish settlers who might be sent out under suitable circumstances.

TICE POLICE SUPERANNUATION BILL AND THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—Sir W. HA.RCOURT declined to take the responsibility of withdrawing the Police Superannuation Bill, and also declined very peremptorily to give any in- formation as to the arrest at Puerto Cabello in connection with the Phcenix Park assassinations.—Mr. GLADSTONE had to confess that it was now hopeless to attempt to pass the Corrupt Practices Bill. He further declined to take it in the autumn session, which would be devoted to the rules of procedure. IRISH PRISONERS.—By way cf, again illustrating the necessity for the new rules, Mr. Healy -shortly afterwards moved the adjournment of the House, in order that he might lodge a complaint respecting the detention of about seventy, prisoners in Cork, and in the course of his observations, re- marked that the Attorney-General for Ireland was "simply humbugging them."—The SPEAKER ruled this expression unparliamentary, and Mr. Healy withdrew it.—The ATTORNEY-GENER AL then explained that he had directed the trial of the prisoners to be taken at the present assizes, and they might, for anything he knew to the contrary, be now in progress.—Several Irish members continued the debate, after which Mr. Healy withdrew his motion. AnAitt "PASHA'S LETTER.—Mr. GLADSTONE informed Mr. Labouchere that the letter purporting to be from Arabi Pasha came to him under cover of a letter from Mr. Blunt, whose connection with the Egyptian Question was doubt- less understood. :

THE -,VOTE OF CREMT. - The debate on the Vote of Credit was resumed by Mr. BOURKE who insisted that the Government had failed, in ignoring the authority of the Sultan, in offending the religious feeling of the Mahometan population, and in being ready to alter their policy to suit the .circumstances of another Power. He trusted that the Government would not hold their hand until they had -carried through the work, that they would rely on British power, moral and physical alone, and call forth all the powers of the nation, and of our Indian possessions if neces- sary.—Mr. • Cutre,nns remarked that the object of the Government had been to carry out the joint political in- fluence of France and England in Egypt which had"-been established by their predecessors. Europe was now satisfied that we had no selfish object in -view. 'He hoped that Egypt would cease to be a mili- tary 'Power, except with respect to such a force as it was necessary to maintain for protection against her neighbours in the South, and if we took part in her future settlement by 'force of arms we should be in a position to make her cease to be a military power. The right .hon. gentleman stated that niral 'Seymour had been asked by telegraph if Major Tulloch had warded him against bombardment without land- ing troops, and the reply was "No, certainly not." Mr. Childers having dealt with the charges of stupidity and imbecility on the part of the military administration,- stated that altogether 10,000 men of the army reserve had been called out, of which 3,000 were intended for service in the Mediteranean, the remainder being drafted into regiments at home so as to strengthen the force in the mother country. Taking into account the Indian force that would he Bent to Egypt, we should be able to send out an army of 40,000 men without in any way dis- turbing the arrangements at home. The vote had been taken for three months' service, and if unfortunately the campaign should continue beyond that time it would be necessary to apply to Parliament for a further vote.—Lord could not understand why it was intended to send out so large a. force, unless it was intended to occupy the country afterwards. He held it to be the duty of the Opposition to support the Government in this great emergency, reselling the right to criticise the means by which we had been brought into "this great mess."—The debate was continued by 11r. 'Villiers-Stuart, Mr. Justin M`Carthy, Mr. Labou- chere, Sir G. Elliot, and other hon. members.— Shortly after midnight, Sir S. NORTHCOTE addressed the House. The right hon. gentleman thought the issue put forward by the Prime Minister was far too narrow, being based upon special pleas. The theory of self-defence was, he held, an insult, to common sense, and was a sort of attempt to make war upon peace principles. On the other hand, the arguments .of the Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs formed the foundation of a policy which was capable :of being-taken up as a national policy. He was prepared to support the Government on the ground of national duty, but he was unable.to overlook their mismanagement in dealing with the diffaculties, which he had admitted had been very great. He hoped the spirit of the country would 'e re- speeded to and done justice to by the spirit of the Ministry, I'for the vote would undoubtedly represent the feeling of the great majority of the people.—Mr. Gladstone having replied, the House divided, and the numbers were : For the ,Vote of Credit 275 Against
Majority. 2se
