The twenty-third annual meeting of Riflemen at w imble- don closed on Saturday, when the Duchess of Albany pre- sented (he prizes. To-day (Saturday) Lord Penzance will hear an applica- tion at the House of Lards to deprive Mr. Mackonochie of the living of St. Alban's. At a court-martial held at Devonport on Monday, Assistant Paymaster Preston, of Her Majesty's ship Belleisle, was condemned to lose three years seniority and be dis- missed his ship for drunkenness. It is announced that Mr. T. Spencer, a member of th firm of Spencer and Sons, iron and steel founders, Ryton, has made a donation of £lO,OOO towards the endowment fund of the new bishopric of Newcastle-on-Tyne. Cardinal Manning, on Tuesday, consecrated Monsignor Virtue, at the Pro-Cathedral, Kensington, Bishop of the new Roman Catholic See of Portsmouth. The ceremony was witnessed by a large congregation, including many ecclesiastical dignitaries of the new diocese. The Hanley magistrates, on Saturday, committed a collier named Hancock for trial at the Stiofford Assizes on a charge of manslaughter, the prisoner havincr, it is alleged, kicked his wife so severely for going to the meeting of the Salva- tion Army that she died a few hours afterwards. The solicitor of the South-Eastern Railway Company, in a letter to the solicitor of the Board of Trade, states, in reference to Mr. Chamberlain's remarks in the House of commons on the Channel Tunnel scheme, that the railway company have acted in the matter under distinct Parlia- mentary authority' and that they deny that anything out- side the order of the Court has been done by them. The death is announced of Lord Keane, the second of the name, in his 78th year. He is succeeded by his brother, the Hon. J. M. Arbuthnot, of Churchtown, county Wex- ford. The first peer was a distinguished soldier, and for his servlces in the Peninsula and Afghanistan a pension of £2,000 a year was granted to himself and his two imme- diate successors in the peerage. THE CHARGE OF MANSLAUGHTER AGAINST A NOBLE- MAN—At the Shrewsbury Assizes, on Saturday, the Hon. George Hill Trevor was indicted with John Williams, as joint managers of If ton's Heath Colliery, with causing the death of Joseph Kynaston, a boy, on the night of June 30, through allowing the roof of the mine to be in a bad state. The charge against Trevor was stopped, and after hearing the prosecution Williams was acquitted. At a meeting of the Cobden Club, on Saturday, Sir Wilfrid Lawson proposed a resolution condemning the "international outrage "at Alexandria,and urgjngan imme- diate cessation of armed intervention. The resolution was coldly received, it being thought by the President (Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P.), and other members that present discus- sion was not desirable, in view of the principles guiding the Club. Ultimately, Sir W. Lawson withdrew the motion, expressing himself satisfied with having " made his pro- test,"

SERIODS CITARGE AGAINST A PRIEST.—A man, who gave the name eg Patrick Pacificus Wade, and who is said to be a Roman Catholic priest, was charged at the Police Court, Liverpocil,•on Tuesday, with perpetrating a terrible outrage upon a little girl, five Years old, while she was playinct with other children in Prince's Park. Medical evidence -showed that a most hideous and revolting crime had been com- mitted. Dr. Commins, who defended the prisoner, did not attempt to deny the assault, but urged that it was not of so serious a character as had been represented. Mr. Mansfield, however, remarked that that was a matter for the jury to ,Secide upon, and committed the prisoner for trial at the Assizes. A MAN SEIZED BY A LION IN WOMBWEDIAVENAGERIE. —A man named Archibald Sinclair, tesiding in the Model Lodging-house, Glasgow, was severely Irart by one of the lions in Wombwell's Menagerie, Glasgow, on Saturday night. A number of the lions are exceedingly tame, and some of the visitors are in the habit, while those in charge are net observing them, of patting the animals' feet, which frequently hang out of the cages. Sinclair, who is said to have been the worse for liquor, was using such liberties when the lion seized his hand with its paws. He was able to get away, but not before the flesh was severely torn from his hand. He was sent to the Royal Infirmary. Another ship canal is being projected, this time by our Scotch neighbours. It is now propnsed to practically abolish by a cutting 50 feet wide and 20 feet deep the nar- row isthmus which, dividing the east and west locks of Tarbert, unites the Mull of Kintyre to the mainland. Such , a canal would give a direct passage from the Clyde to the Atlantic saving about 115 miles in the voyage to the west land north of Scotland. It is estimated that the undertaking will cost only about £200,000, and the favour with which the idea has been received is indicated by the fact that at a preliminary meeting held in Glasgow on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Duke of Argyll, a large portion of that sum was subscribed. The annual revenue from shipping which would use the canal is estimated at £12,000.

CONSECRATION OF BISHOP WILBERFORCE.—The Rev. Ernest Roland Wilberforce, D.D., who was recently appointed first bishop of the new see of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, was consecrated on Tuesday, at Durham Cathedral, by the Arch- bishop of York (Dr. Thomson). A similar ceremony has never before been performed w Rhin. the ancient Minster. The proceedings were witnessed by an enormous congregation. There were present the Bishops of Ely, St. Alban's, Dur- ham, Manchester, Liverpool, Winchester, and Carlisle, to- gether with about4oo of the Cathedral and the diocesan clergy, the corporate bodies of Durham and Newcastle also attending in state. Canon Wilberforce (brother of the new bishop) preached an eloquent sermon. The ceremony of enthronement will take place in 'Newcastle Cathedral on August 3. A GIRL KILLED BY DWI/K.—An inquiry of a painful nature was held at Oldham on Saturday, touching the death of a girl named Ada Hardcastle, 18 years of age. Deceased lived with her brother, who keeps the Vulcan Inn, and it appeared from the evidence that since she was 16 years of age she has been habitually addicted to drink, having been for days together in a state of intoxication. Deceased had been drinking heavily for several days prior to Wednesday last, and on the morning of that day the brother of the deceased heard screams coaling from deceased's bedroom. He at once went to the place and found the girl in convulsions. A medical man was want for, but deceased died before he arrived. The post- morter, examination which had been held showed that deceased had died from the effects of drink, and the jury returned a verdict to this effect. The coroner remarked that it was a sad thing for cne so young to die through intemperance.

SUPPOSED FENIANISM IN LOWDON.—An extraordinary circumstance has recently occurred showing that activity in the Fenian organisation in London is still-in force. It ap- pears that a week or so ago two young men, believed to be .Inch-Americans, called at a shop in Farringdon-road, oppo- site the Clerkenwell House of Correction, and asked permis- sion of the lodger on the second floor to view the interior of the .prison from her window, promising ample payment therefor; but she declined, and referred them to the third floor lodger, who after some hesitation allowed them to enter her room. They opened the window, it is stated, and went out on the parapet, where they remained quite half an hour, evidently taking a sketch of the interior of the prison. On their return they offered the lodger some money in return for her,eourtesy, but she declined to accept it, and after giving some money to the children they departed. The sus- picions of the landlady being aroused she communicated I with the police, who have not traced the strangers. Subse- quently a number of constables were told off to watch out- side the prison in case a repetition of the circumstances should occur. The motive of the strangers' action can .only be surmised,,but the matter at least appears to be erninestly auspicious. THE ASSAULT ON THE CHIEF CONSTABLE OF MACOLY23- FIELD : EXEMKARY SENTENCE.—An exemplary sentence was passed at Chester Assizes, on Monday, upon a Maccles- field shoemaker, named Potts, for having murderously assaulted the chief constable of the borough under singular circumstances. He loitered about the chief constable's house until that gentleman went out, and then accosted him, asking if his uncle I:ad left him, Potts any money. The chief constable said ,he knew nothing about the matte% and recommended the man to go to a lawyer. Potts, however, responded by atriking the chief constable a blow in the cheek with a shoemaker's knife, cutting him, and followed up this assault with a blow on the shoulder and another stab in the neck. Then he ran away, and after being captured expressed the hope that the chief constable was dead, adding that he had caused him to be imprisoned, and that if he had had a revolver, he would have shot him. The evidence showed that Potts had been three years in a lunatic asylum, but this was eight years ago, and the gaol surgeon found no sign of insanity ab3ut him. Having this fact in view, and knowing that if one of the wounds inflicted' upon the chief constable had been a little deeper, it would have caused death, Mr. Justice Manisty failed to see why he should not give Potts the heaviest sentence in his power. He accordingly condemned him to penal servitude for life. HUSBANDS AND THEIR LEGAL HIGHTS.—A ease of an ex- traordinary character' and the first of the kind tried, came, before Mr. Perronet Thompson, judge of .the Liverpool County Court. Mrs. ERZ], Parry (by her next friend, John Riley) applied for the judge to make an order, under the Married Women's Property Act, declaring that the stock-in- trade, goodwill, fixtures, and effects connected with a certain , business were her sole and separate property, and the earn- I ings derived therefrom, and that the husband be ordered not to molest her in the carrying on of the said business.— Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Bartley and Bird) appeared for the wife. and Dr. Cummings, M.P. (instructed by Mr. H. F. Neale), for the husband. The application was made under the 9th section of the Married Women's Pro- perty Act, which enacts that the wages or earnings of any married woman acquired or gained by her after the passing of the Act, in any employment, occupation, or trade in which she is engaged or carried on separately from her husband, shall be deemed to be her property, and held for her separate use. It was stated that Mrs. Parry was married to John Richard Parry, who had been in the employment of Messrs. Cook and Townsbend. She kept a shop for the sale of fancy articles at 143, Dale-street, where they both now lived, and she had paid £95 to her mother for the stock and goodwill of this shop. The money was said to be Mrs. Parry's; that she alone conducted and managed the busi- ness; that her husband had nothing to do with it; that as the earnings from the shop and business were her own and that as the husband had taken money from the till, and had otherwise wished to interfere, the wife asked the court to make the order desired.—The defence was that the business was not the wife's ; that the money paid for it was taken partly from the husband's cash and the subsequent earnings from the shop; that the husband's name was up at the shop, and that the bills were made out and paid in his name.—After hearing the wife's evidence, his Honour hell that she had not shown sufficient ground for making the order, and consequently the application was refused.

A new church, dedicated to St. Cuthbert, was opened on Wednesday, at Usbaw College, Durham, by Monsignor Archbishop Eyre, of Glasgow. It will cost £15,000. Mr. Atthur Pease, M.P., has accepted the office of President of the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society, rendered vacant by the death of the late Mr. Samuel Gurney. A Corn Exchange building at Ipswich, erected at a cost of £22,000, was opened on Wednesday by a public dijeuiter given by the Mayor, Mr. Frederick Fish. Among the guests was Lord Waveney and Lord Gwydyr, Dundee was on Tuesday flooded by great rain. Several sewers burst, and the flax and jute warehouses between Sea- gate and Dock-street were flooded to a great depth. The damage to stored material is estimated at £20,000. Sheriff Comrie Thompson, of Aberdeen, has placed the Dunecht mystery case in a legal form. Collier, who was arrested on Friday night in Glasgow, has been released, and Charles Souter, the poacher, has been formally committed for trial on a charge of stealing the body. At Longton, on Monday, William Steele, butcher, charged with exposing tongues for sale in the market which were in a live condition of decomposition was fined £lO and costs, and told that next time he would sent to prison direct. An appeal for time for payment was peremptorily refused. On Wednesday evening, Hirini Taiwhanga, one of the Maori chiefs at present in England, attended by invitation a meeting in Salisbury-square, and delivered an address. He strongly deprecated the action of the Government in refusing to receive their petition, but said that he was not Ving back until he had got what his people wanted. The Right Hon. W. E. Forster' M.P., distributed the prizes on board the industrial ship Shaftesbury, off Green- hithe, on Saturday, and addressed words of advice to the boys, saying there were no professions in which good conduct was so sure of reward as in the naval and merchant services.

At Manchester Assizes, on Tuesday, a man who had borrowed about SOO, and given a bill of sale as security, claimed damages from the holder of the bill of sale for having, within a month, seized and sold his .property, which was worth between £5OO and £6OO. The jury found in his favour for £738, and judgment was entered with aosts. _ _ .

The return issued on Wednesday shows that during the second week of July there were 48,507 indoor and 37,901 outdoor paupers relieved in the metropolis, making a total of 86,408 as against 85,127 in the corresponding week last year, 82,794 in 1880, and 80,413 in 1879. The number of vagrants relieved during the week was 655. DEATH BY LIGIITNING.—ShortIy after ten o'clock on Monday morning, during a thunderstorm which only lasted a few minutes, the lightning struck and instantly killed Thomas Young, eleven years of age, whose parents live at 17, Hadfield-street, Newton Heath. The boy was about to fly his kite, and his companion, who was holding it up, was knocked down, but only received a slight wound on one fin- ger. The body of Young was severely bruised and burnt. Fifteen thousand pounds worth of property was destroyed by tire at Exeter on. Sunday morning. The flames were discovered in a large draper's shop in Fore-street, not far from the scene of another large fire which occurred but a short time since. The Premises, which were owned,. and occupied by Mr. Davey, were totally destroyed, and three houses adjoining were partly burnt, and the stock of a grocer, valued at £3,000, was ruined by water. The Home Secretary, replying to a resolution adopted on Clerkenwell Green, on the 16th instant, calling upon the Government •to review the whole facts of the Tichborne case with a view to the Claimant's liberation, says, through his secretary, that he does not propose to interfere with the ordinary rules applicable to convicts under sentence of penal servitude. _ _

At the Chester Assizes, on Wednesday, James Hesford, who had been convicted of the manslaughter of his wife by knocking her down some steps with a blow from a poker, whereby her spine was fractured, was placed in the dock for sentence. Mr. Justice Manisty commented upon the serious nature of the offence, and announced the determination of the Judges to put down such brutal assaults upon women. The prisoner was sent into penal servitude for five years. A remarkable fatality occurred on Tuesday at Brighton. About half-past eight in the morning a youth named Tren- chard, whose parents reside in Adelaide-crescent, Weat Brighton, was in the water at the head of the West Pier. A Mr. Franklin, in ignorance of the fact that there were bathers about, threw from the pier a box such as is used by wine merchants for the package of bottles, and weighing 25Ibs. -It struck Mr. Trenchard, who immediately dis- appeared, and whose body has not yet been recevered. THE MURDER AND SUICIDE IN MANCHESTER.—The bodies of the victims of the tragedy in St. Leonard-street, Manchester, en Thursday night, were interred on Saturday. The remains of the woman Howard were interred in Ardwick Cemetery, Hyde-road, by the registrar. 'A brother and uncle of the woman and some friends, together with a few specta- tors, were present. The body of Newby, against whom the jury returned a verdict of felo de se, was buried in consecra- ted ground in the Southern Cemetery, Withington' without any religious ceremony. Newby's father and mother followed the remains, and several of his friends were also present at the funeral. EXTRAORDINARY CHALLENGE BY HAt./LAN. The great Canadian oarsman, Edward Hanlan, has, according to advices from Toronto, dated the 11th inst., almost completely re- covered from his recent severe indisposition. The same des- patch states that he has issued the following somewhat extraordinary challenge:—" I will row any five men in the world two miles straight away, or two miles and turn, for from $l,OOO to 52,000 a side. I will row these five men with an interval of forty-eight hours (two full days) between the matches on any suitable waters on the continent of America. The challenge is open to all tho world." The champion further states that if he can get this challenge accepted, he will forego for the present at least, the visit which he at present intends paying to Australia. THE INTERNATIONAL SHOOTING MATCH.—The following volunteers have been selected by the National Rifle Associa- tion to compose the British team which will visit the United States to shoot in theinternational match, British Volunteers v. the United States National Guard. Committee : Lieut.- Colonel Sir Henry Halford, Ist Leicester; Lieut.-Colonel Walrond, M.P., Ist Devonshire; Major Humphrey, Cam- bridge University; secretary, H. Smith, Civil Service Rifles. The selected team : Corporal Bates, Ist Warwick; Private Boulter, 2nd Cheshire; Corporal Caldwell, Ist Renfrew; Sergeant Dodd, Ist Berwick; Captain Godsal, 2nd Bucks; Private Goodier, 6th Lancashire; Lieutenant Heap, 6th Lancashire ; Private M`Vittie. Ist Dumfries; Captain Mellish, 2nd Notts; Sergeant Oliver, 3rd Kent; Corporal Parry, 2nd Cheshire; Major Pearse, 4th Devon.

RAILWAY RETURNS.—A blue hook has been issued show- ing the railway returns for the United Kingdom for the year 1881. The total capital paid up and raised by loans and debentures is set down at £745,528,162, in addition to which there is a sum of £27,909,453 set down as "subscrip- tions to other companies." The total length of line open on the 31st December last was 18,175 miles, of which 8,302 miles were of single line. The number of passengers con- veyed was 623,047,787, exclusive of season and periodical ticket holders, and consisted of 37,993,944 first-class, 84,474,718 second-class, and 520,579,126 third-class passen- gers. The holde, sof season or periodical tickets numbered 538,482. The number of miles travelled by passenger, mixed goods, and mineral trains was 248,467,374. From passenger traffic the receipts amounted to £27,461,645, from gaods traffic £1,176,182, and from miscellaneous sources £2,649,205—a total revenue of £66,557,442. The total amount of the working expenditure was £34,602,616, leav- ing the net receipt at £31,955,826, the proportion of the expenditure to receipts being 52 per cent. There were 13,727 locomotives and 444,958 carriages and trucks in use on the several railways of the kingdom on the 31st of December last.

CHARGE AGAINST A SOLICITOR—In the Queen's Bench Division, on Monday, Mr. Horace Brown moved, on behalf of Mr. G. Hampden Whalley, M.P., for a rule calling upon a solicitor to show why he should not be struck of the rolls for malpractices. Mr. Browne stated that Mr. Whalley was introduced to a person connected with money-lending trans- actions in the month of January last, being anxious to pay some debts. That person introduced him to the solicitor, who obtained for him a loan of £6OO for three months, £2OO of which was paid for discount, £2OO for the solicitor's ser- vices, and £l9O was retained by him to pay off several debts of Mr. Whalley. The latter only thus received £lO out of the money advanced. The solicitor had never paid one farthing of the debts. It aftervratds became necessary for Mr. Whalley to consult the same solicitor relative to other debts, and he caused a petition to be filed. The true state of his affairs was that after payment of all his debts he had a clear income from landed estates of .£7,000 a year. On the day When the petition was filed the solicitor produced six or seven blank stamps, and requested Mr. Whalley to sign them in blank, assuring him that it was a mere matter of form. These blank stamps were subsequently presented to the first meeting of his creditors by persons who were strangers to Mr. Whalley, who sought to prove against the estate in respect of over £6,000, for which Mr. Whalley had never had any value. The solicitor has been called upon by the latter for an explanation, but he has never answered the letter. He, however, has been to Mr. Whalley and offered him £l,OOO to leave England. Sir James Hannen said the learned counsel might take a rule. EXTRAORDINARY MONEY LENDING CAM—Another extraordinary case of money lending,in which a man named Townend, of Manchester, was the defendant, came before one of the Judges at the Manchester Assizes on Saturday. A watchmaker named Sivel, but imperfectly acquainted with the English language, applied to the defendant—who trades at several places in Manchester and elsewhere, under different names—for a loan of £l2O. The interest was to be 10 per cent., and repayment was to be made at the rate of £3 per month for a time, and then per month. Sivel received a cheque for £6O, and he crossed another cheque for a like amount, which the defendant was to send to a money lender at Leeds for the purpose of redeeming some jewellery, which jewellery he was afterwards to forward to Sivel's address at Whitehaven, but did not. A bill of sale on Sivel's stock, \raised at £5BO, was duly executed, but, according to his account, he did not understand its purport. He also stated that he was told the first instalment was due on the 21st March. Oa the 7th March, however, the defendant seized the whole of Sivel's stock and had it conveyed to Manchester and sold. According to the bill of sale the first instalment became due on the 6th March. Sivel offered to pay three instalments and the cost that had been incurred by the bailiffs, hut the latter would not yield unless they got £203. The Judge said that, if what the plaintiff stated was correct, there existed in Manchester a " most mischie- vous conspiracy which deserved thorough exposure." He also commented on the different aliases assumed by the defendant, adding that what surprised him most of all was that he should keep out of the witness-box when charges of fraud of a serious character were made against him. The jury found for the plaintiff, damages rm.

The Ex-Guicowar o Baroda died on Thursday. The Parcel Post Bill was iss,led on Thursday. Its chief provision, a payment of tifty-five per cent. of the receipts to the railway companies, has already ben made known.
Some further correspondence respecting Zululand was issued on Thursday. Governor Sir H. Bulwer makes some severe strictures on Bishop Colenso's interference in Zulu affairs. _ _

A most destructive fire occurred at Exeter on Thursday morning. Six large business houses were destroyed. The fire broke out in a draper's warehouse, and the inmates narrowly escaped. The damage is estimated at £50,000. Reports from all parts of Scotland show that notwith- standing the heavy rainfall this month, an abundant harvest is expected. The crops require only a fortnight to reach maturity. All the cereals will be above the average of recent years. On Thursday morning, the Governor of Her Majesty's county prison at Nottingham, receiVal instructions to the effect that the sentence of death passed on Herbert Snell, for the murder of a farmer, at South Wheatley, East Retford had been commuted to one of penal servitude for

Early on Thursday morning, a destructive fire broke out in Cheapside-street, Anderson, Glasgow. The premises of Messrs. Joseph Walker, Parker, and Company, lead workers? and Messrs. France and Morgan, brass and. bell founders, were totally destroyed. The damage is estimated at £lO,OOO. At a special meeting of the Clitheroe Town Council on Thursday, Councillor Robert Dewburst was elected an alder- man in the place of Mr. John Mitchell (resigned). The election cause much excitement in the borough. There was a severe party fight, and Mr. Dewburst, who is a Conserva- tive, only secured one more vote than Mr. Clarke, a Liberal, who is not'a member of the Council.

On Wednesday night, an exciting scene was witnessed at Mosley near Wednfsbury. A number of youth's repaired to the Birmingham Canal for the purpose of bathing,when one named David Phillips, got out of his depth and was drowned. A number of others made desperate efforts tP save their companion, and in doing so had narrow escapes. Phillips' body was found late on Wednesday night. John Clark, a rough-looking fellow, was charged at Chester on Thursday with assaulting Thomas Truss of the Salvation Army, and with being drunk. As the " officers " were marshalling "the army" in the Town Hall Square, Clark rushed forward and struck Truss heavily twice. He was fined 20s. and costs or fourteen days' imprisonment for the assault and 10s. fine or seven days' imprisonment for drunkenness.

At Middleton, on Thursday, James Wrigley, a gamekeeper at Alkrington Hall, was charged with wounding Miles Whitehead, contractor, of Hulme. On Saturday, the prose- cutor was passing through Rhodes Wood, when the defen- dant set on him and beat him with a stick. Mr. Clark, for the defence, stated that the prosecutor was mistaken for a poacher, and that ample apology had been made, but the Bench said it was too serious a case to go without a penalty, and inflicted a fine of 40s. and costs. " Sensational " methods of obtaining money from the public are coming rapidly into fashion. The other day a man threw himself into the Thames—taking care to do so within reach of help—as a means of attracting attention to his poverty. For the same reason, a man named Devine asked a London policeman to take him into custody on Thursday morning for having attempted to damage the Mansion House. The man speedily retracted his " confes- sion," and informed the magistrates on Thursday that he had made it in order to draw attention to his poverty. The plea was not one which would be made by a man whose poverty was the result of misfortune only. He as re- manded.

Baron Huddleston gavejudgment on Thursday:morning in an important action brought by the executors of the late Lord Wenlock against the River Dee Company. The claim was for £173,000, in respect of a mortgage lent by his lord- ship on the company's property near Chester. It was con- tended for the defence that the company was not liable to refund the money, their borrowing powers under a special Act of Parliament being restricted to £25,000. The Judge held that the company having had the mobey and used it, for the purpose of their undertaking, were obliged to refund it, despite the limitation of their borrowing powers. He accordingly gave judgment for the amount claimed, and granted power to appeal. THE FIREMAN AND HIS OUTFIT. At the Liverpool County Court, on Monday, before Mr. Perronett Thompson, judge, a case of interest to seamen and outfitters was heard. John Campbell, marine fireman, Barmouth-street, sought to recover £5O from Aaron Harris, outfitter, Great Howard- street, for the non-delivery of certain goods purchased from him. Mr. Tomkies appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. H. F. Neale for the defendant. The plaintiff's case was that he shipped on board the steamer Knight of the Bath, and obtained a bonus note. With thiq he went to the defendant, who agreed to furnish him with the clothes necessary for the voyage he was about to undertake. This, he alleged, defen- dant had failed to do; that consequently the plaintiff was unable to proceed with the ship, and that he had sustained loss to the amount he now claimed.—The defence wag that the goods were there for the plaintiff to fetch, and that be failed to do so.—Verdict for the plaintiff.

A SINGULAR PEOPLE.—Some Interesting particulars are given by the Times ofindia of the Khonds, a singular people, who constitute one of the numerous remnants of the primitive races of India, which have survived the Hindu conquest. From Lieutenant Macpherson's report, which was published so long ago as 1842, we learn that no my- thology nor legend exists among the Khonds which indi- cates their origin, they believing themselves to have existed where they now are "from the beginning," having either sprung from the soil itself, like that branch of the Greeks which traced its origin to the Arcadian Belasgus, or baying been created contemporaneously with it. The two most sacred judicial tests among them are founded on the belief that rice moistened by the blood of a sheep killed in the name of the Earth-god, if eaten by litigants, destroys the ' perjured, and that a portion of disputed soil made into clay will, if swallowed by them, have a similar effect. The com- mon oaths of the Khonds are upon the skin of a tiger, from which animal destruction to the perjured is invoked; upon a lizard akin, whose scaliness, they pray, may be their lot if foresworn; upon the earth of an ant-'hill, like which they desire that if false they may be reduced to powder; and upon a peacock's feather; while the universal ordeals of boiling water, oil, and hot iron are constantly resorted to. The distinguishing qualities of these people are thus summed up :—" A passionate love of liberty, devotion to chiefs, and unconquerable resolution. They are besides faithful to friends, brave, hospitable, and laborious. Their ' vices, upon the other hand, are the indulgence of revenge, and occasionally of brutal passion. Drunkenness is uni• versal."

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

It is announced that the Government of Uruguay havo recognised the justice of the claims put forward by Spain on account of the ill-treatment of Spanish subjects in that country. The Jewish Committee at Philadelphia are sending back to this country a number of destitute Russian Jews for whose support they are unable to provide. A telegram from Constantinople Bays that the Porte discussirg the advisablness of "urgent measures" with regard to Crete. The Cretans, .or at least the Christian por- tion of them, have demanded greater powers of self-govern- ment from the Porte.

An attempt has been made to assassinate Senor Sapsta, the Prime Minister of Spain, by means of an explosive compound packed in a Rossa box, as the Fenian "infernal machines" may be styled. The box did not reach its destination, and no harm was done. SeVeral arrests have been made.

The Vienna Pressc publishet intelligence from Pesti' stating that a seriona conflict occurred on Suiaclay night at Dombroya, in the district of Dolnau, between the peasants and the labourers on the railway. Fourteen persons were killed.

Mr. M. Perkins Marsh, United States Minister at the Italian Court, died snddenly on Monday at the Vallombrosa. The Italian Government have expressed deep commisera- tion with his widow, and have telegraphed to the Legation at Washington to convey to the Government the sympathy of the Italian nation.

A few days ago it was said that an effort was being made by Germany to bring about the incorporation of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in the German Empire. A telegram from the capital of the Duchy now states that the Grand Ducal family are now selling the estates which they possess in the country. The Grand Duchy, it may be stated, formed part of the German Confederation until 1866, and Prussia had the right of garrisoning the capital. That right was renounced under the Treaty of London in 1867, when the territory was declared to be neutral, and the capital ceased , to be a fortified place. The incorporation of the Duchy in the German Empire would not only be an abrogation of the Treaty of London, but would also be regarded with very hostile feelings by the French. THE AMERICAN FREIGHT HANDLERS STRIKE: DES- PERATE AND FATAL ENCODNTER.—The last arriving mail steamer from New York brings particulars of the encounter between the Italian workmen who had been brought to super- cede the American freight handlers at 'Jersey City and a number of roughs which terminated fatally. It appears that the affair took place on the 11th instant. On that date a gang of over 500 of the strike hands went out to the Erie Ferry house to receive their back pay. They were followed by a number of roughs, who were evidently in full sympathy with them. The roughs were driven away, but on nearing the railway company's wharf they at once made a raid on the Italians who were working there. The Italians drew their knives, revolvers, stilettoes, and swords, opening fire upon the attackers. The Italians then ran along in the direction of the schooner which conveyed them morning and nigt to and from New York. On their way they met the freigtat handlers who were on strike, and, mistaking these ' for the roughs who had attacked them, they also fired on them. &everal of the freight handlers were wounded, and seven were taken to the hospital. In their eagerness to get on board the schooner, three of the Italians fell into the water; two had very narrow escapes, and one was drowned. After the affair the authorities had to put a double police force in the vicinity. no police afterwards f.earched the Italians and found on them 17 new and costly revolvers, 88 murderous-looking knives, six poniards, two swords, and two half-swords having on their blades blood. Eight of the Italians were arrested.

div.head: ANGLO-SCOTITS "_ AND HIS NEWTON
div.p: ANGLO-SCOTITS "_ AND HIS NEWTON

CRITIC. A friend of ours f om Asl,ton informs us that the new coursing ground there will consist of at least five hundred acres oNand, which will, however, not be entirely thrown out of cultivation, as many supposed it would, for the hare 'will not stay on uncultivated ground, a fact which we com- mend to the notice of your correspondent " Anglo-Scotus," who discourses on it in your columns from time to time ; and it is said that the scheme finds favour there, and especi- ally with the publicans, as well it may, for they will be the greatest gainers toy it, for they will have to provide for men and beast who may be expected to attend the periodical gatheri.ngs. We felt a little disappointed with " Anglo- Scotus '.for saying that he disliked the study of entomology. If we mistake not, it was the very one recommended by Solomon when he bade careless people " go to the ant" to study her ways. But we are glad to quote Mr. Madelev's opinion, that there are still some people left who are-as fond of the st.udy of entomology as others are of etymology. This latter science 6.‘ Anglo-Scotus "does not assume, but it is well worthy of his attention, as it is the only sure basis of reasoning, and has to do with the instruments of thoueht, words, in all their infinite variety. We have no desire- to press the matter, but before leaving the word "sketch " we will only remark that it is the modern Russian word "to gallop," as-applied to a horse, and, strange to say, contains the same idea of motion as the word "catch," which " Anglo-Scotus " took objection to in his first letter to . The Examiner. We are, however, vary glad to see that he does not intend to go off on a wrong scent, but is true to his better. instincts. He is evidently well versed in the typographic art and must feel distressed when he finds one or two of his best points blunted through a very slight error, and must console himself, as we sometimes have to do, with the thought that there are many intelligent people in Newton as .well as in London, and that they will read right what he intended to write right. But much must be left to the good nature of the public after all. We feel quite sure that that part of it which reads the Earlestown and Xewton Examiner will endorse every word he :says in praise of "the latest" and " best" if not "the only local paper," and we esteem his good opinion very much for the aforesaid reasons. He is very anxious to know more of the wonderful cow which ' could even a quarter of a century ago giye the modern com- pound known as butterine. We regret we cannot gratify him further than to say that the said animal was very like that one mentioned in the story of the house that Jack built, and that we tell the tale as it was told to us. If Anglo-Scotus had been here on Saturday he would have seen one of the finest carriage horses in the country side given to the dogs, so he need not wonder at some having a cow's head now and then. But by the same process of reasoning that very horse must have been killed for those very dogs, which we know was not the fact but a most untoward accident, the result of misdirected impulse as he will learn from your columns. If the carcase had not been removed it might have engendered bees as the animal we read of in ancient story did, and it is open to him to say that the rider may have had a bee in his bonnet at the time he im- paled the animal in the dark. We never knew but one man to whom the pun really did apply, and we met him at Frodsham. The. unfortunate gentleman had a hobby, as people said, for bees, and we heard him discourse most eloquently on their habits and intelligence, and listening to him made us wonder to see a man not many days ago attempt to hive a swarm of them with a tobacco pipe in his mouth, not seeming to know that tobacco smoke was their special abhorrence and that anyone, almost might take a wasp's nest with a pipe in his mouth: There is really much to be learned from bees. They even go to church, for there is at this moment a nest of them in a spout on a neighb)uring church. Besides, they are very thrifty and eam as much as 163. to 203. every season for as many pounds of honey, so honey makes money. At the same place on the same day we met Murphy, the lecturer, ' who met with such an untimely end, and with whom we had a rally—he was a cock of the north (of Ireland) if you like, and, like a wandering Don Quixote, must have a tilt with qnyboily that came in his way, and who seemed to have an opinion of his own, or sufficient verve to give him a nudge in defence of it. We regret the untimely end of both men, feeling sure that it was in the integrity of their hearts that they met it, for they were faithful to death in their devotion to their special subject while other men saw they had a bee in their bonnet. Times are somewhat changed in Newton since Anglo-Scotus knew it, and although a few of the original stock are left, a' generation has elapsed and they are getting still fewer every day. The foot-racing which was then indulged in on the common was "put down" as being altogether too low and scandalous, but has revived in the shape of athletic sports, here; there, and almost everywhere, and horse racing has never attained to the heighth of a truly noble science even in Newton. Pigeon flying, which was considered to stamp the native as.a sort of aborigine, though kept for pleasure, as the pigeons referred to were, has revived in another form, for there is now a gun club where pigeon shooting is practiced, and where the more select may occasionally be seen potting their dozen or two of pigeons, we do not mean literally, but making the place like a poulterer's shop, popping them alive out of one basket and into another dead the next minute. But this sport seems to have fallen off a little of late, in face of the outcry which some people in London have made in Parliament, and in the increasing interest ishich many are taking in this new project, for there is, odd to say, a fashion in these things, and one which many people will follow, in spite of their better judgments, and all that can be said to discourage and discountenance such things, by those who take other views of what is right and proper.
ANNUAL STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS OF THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.

The annual report of receipts and expenditure of the Newton Improvement Commissioners has lately been issued. The accounts are for the twelve months ended on the 25th March last, and ate included under seven heads. They have been prepared by Mr. R. Brierley, clerk and surveyor to the Commissioners, and at the annual meeting of the ratepayers held on Wednesday last (a report of which appears else- where) they were passed, subject to the approval of the Government auditor. FLACCUS.

t • • MISS MCLATCHIE AT RUNCORN. MiS5 McLatchie preached on Sunday night at St. John's pres:jteriall Chapel, Runcorn, before a large congregation. A cc.ilec- tion was made to defray expenses. Sr. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. —On Sunday, the scholars successful in passing the examina- tion in scriptural knowledge, held in this school, were pre- sented with prizes. Their names are :-1, Mary Alice Hayes; 2, Elizabeth Leach; 3, Eliz Dobson; 4, Morgan Lloyd Williams ; 5, Sarah Jane Dobson; 6, Alexander Kenyon; 7, John Leach; 8, Mary Campbell; 9, Christiana Campbell. THE SALTATION ARMY.—The branches of the Salvation Army, stationed at Runcorn and Widnes, are displaying great activity. Meetings and processions were held at both places on Sunday, and addresses were delivered by a number of curiously named individuals. On Monday' a "Holiness Convention" was held in Runcorn Public Hall, followed by a "tea fight" in the Foresters' Hall. All the services were well attended.

A BRUTAL HUSBAND.—A labourer named Charles Butter- field was at the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesay, brought up in custody charged with assaulting his wife Margaret. On the previous day the prisoner went home drunk. His wife was sitting in a chair with her baby in her arms, and the prisoner dragged her off, and struck her several blows

on the head, and blacked her eyes.—Asked if he bad any excuse to make, defendant said he was drunk.—Mr. Heald : That's no excuse. You will be fined 20s and costs, or go to gaol for a month. A WIDNES BANKRUPTCY.—A meeting of Mr. Isaac Sankey's creditors took place at the Grosvenor Hotel, Liver- pool, on Friday. A statement was made which disclosed liabilities to the amount of £9,000. Of this sum £7,000' purported to be secured. The assets combrised £7,21.7 property in the hands of secured creditors, and £172 other property. Mr. Holland, of Liverpool, who together with Mr. Haddock and Mr. Grundy, both solicitors, of Manchester, represented the creditors, ras appointed chairman. He explained the accounts ; but some discussion took place, and the creditors determined that they should be further in- vestigated, especially with regard to a bill of sale given by the debtor shortly before the failure, and resoved upon liquidation.
ANNUAL TREAT AT RUNCORN.—The scholars attending Bethesda Congregational Sunday school, Runcorn, had their annual treat on Tuesday. Assembling at the station about

twelve o'clock, the scholars proceeded by train to Sutton Weaver, walking thence to Mr. Wilkinson's farm, Aston. The number present was not so large as usual, on account of the heavy storm which had continued all morning, but the weather afterwards became bright and genial, and fresh accessions were made during the afternoon, which brought the aggregate to about 20a. Various games were indulged in by the young folks, who had tea supplied to them on the grass, those of older growth partaking of refreshments in the dairy kitchen. About seven o'clock the party assembled in front of the house and sang a hymn, and at the conclusion a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Wilkinson for his kindness. The return journey was then commenced, and R•ancern was reachcd about eight o'clock. FLOWER SERTICE AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RIINCORN.—A large congregation assembled at this place of worship on Sunday evening on the occasion of the annual flower service. The sacred edifice had been decorated with taste and effectiveness, without any attempt at ostentatious display. Behind the pulpit and on the front of the gallery were the words, in ornamental capitals. "lie clotheth the earth with beauty," the truthfulness of which statement, was testified to by the many beautiful foliage and flowering plants which adorned the pulpit and communion table. In other parts of of the chapel too plants were suspended, and as a great number of those present carried bouquets, a pretty scene was presented. The service was of a very enjoyable character. Special hymns appropriate to the occasion where sung by the choir assisted by a number of the Sunday school scholars, and J. L. Hatton's anthem Consider the lilies," was rendered by the choir. The Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor conducted the service, and preached a sermon from the 6th chapter of Matthew, 28th and 29th verses. Those persons who had taken bouquets, by request left them at the conclusion of the service. They were then collected and afterwards distributed to those homes where sickness prevailed, being thus the means of carrying glariness to many a sad heart. Widnes Accident Hospital and Liverpool Royal Infirmary also received a quantity. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—The usual fort- nightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday. The members present were the Revs. Canon Barclay (chairman), J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Ashton (vice-chairman), W. Whitlow, J. High- field, T. Norman, E. A. Wallington. J. Smith, C. Rigby, W. Pickering, James Derbyshire, H. Linaker (clerk), elle]. W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The County Rate: The precept for the county rate wes produced by the Clerk. The total amount to be paid by the Runcorn Union for the quarter was £1585 15s Bd, being made up as follows: County rate £1249 3s 9d, constabulary general expenditure £B9 3s ld, constabulary local expenditure £247 8s 10d. For the cor- responding quarter of last year the total amount required was £1833 7s 81, which showed a decrease of £247 12s.— Financial: A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the payment of £33 125 to the clerk in consideration of the extra services rendered by him, under the Union Chargeability Act, for the year ended March 25th last. The Rev. J. Lockwood moved, and it was resolved, that the accounts, amounting to £234 17s 6d, be paid.—The Master's San: On the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Henry Jones WAS appointed as assistant bookkeeper to his father, at a salary of £5 per annum.—This was all the public business.

DEATH OF MR. C. W. BROWN, OF TIALTON.—It is Our painful duty to record the death of Mr. C. W. Brown, after a protracted illness. He came to Halton as schoolmaster and organist in October, 1876, at which time he was in a delicate state of health, but the bracing air soon made an improvement in him. The school was only in a poor state when he undertook it. but with painstaking care, and appli- cation to his duties, he soon raised it to a high standard of efficiency in every respect. For some time past, however, his health had been giving way, and he tried everything, but in vain, to benefit him. After having been unable to do any duty for the last four months, he gradually declined, and expired on Sunday morning last, at nine o'clock, being only 32 years of age. The church bell was tolled slowly, and the service rendered as softly as possible, which inti- mated only too well that Mr. Brown had passed away, which was deeply regretted by all who knew him. His funeral took place on Wednesday last, when his scholars, the members of the church band and choir, some of the Sunday school teachers, the churchwardens, Dr. Carruthers, and the Vicar, assembled in front of the school-house on the Common, and then accompanied his remains, and the mourners to Halton Station, where a special van was in readiness to receive the coffin for conveyance to Tyldesley, near Manchester, where he was interred in the family grave at St. George's Church, the service being conducted by tbe vicar of Halton, Rev. J. Lockwood. There was also present at the funeral at Tyldesley Mr. and Mrs. Brown, the father and mother, whose only child he was, the churchwardens of Halton Parish Church (Messrs. Acton and Baguley), Mr. Sidesman Woodier, and Mr. Thomas Wright, the undertaker, who carried out all the necessary arrangements with great punctuality and satisfaction. The deceased has left a widow and three young children.

TILE VICAR OF FARNWORTH ON THE DRINK QUFST/6111. —Under the auspices of Widnes Samaritan Lodge 1.0.G.T. a te. -,eeting and entertainment was held in Page-lane Mission-rot,. Widnes' on Monday evening. The Rev. G. Bond, vicar ot moderate attendanc nworth presided; and there was a chairman referred to e'. ya,..opening the proceedings, the the option resolution in being talk Wilfrid Wilfrid Lawsen's local opinion consequently being elicited ipd no expression of e Government with regard to it. Speaking of the SunclV3. the rev, chairman said one of the arguments N;Bling Bill,; controverted at the meeting in favour of Sunday-el had held in Widnes recently—that a poor man had as 11.11',1 right to his public house as the rich man had to his was brought up in the House of Commons, and seemed to go down easily with the members of that body. But a club and a public house here essentially different. Men had to pay for their admission to the former; it was their own property; and in London many gentlemen lived at their clubs. Seeing their friends there and taking their meals there. In these cases the club was the bachelor's home. Could the same be said of the public-house? A man's house could not be closed on Sunday, but there was nothing to prevent the closing of a public-house; and there was a preponderating majority in favour of that step being taken. He questioned if Sir Wil- frid Lawson's Local Option measure would in its present form reach the object he had in view even if it became law.l He (the chairman) suggested another plan, concerning which be was now in correspondence, with several prominent members of Parliament, and which had been received with considerable favour. Why should not Government take charge of the public-houses themselves, and conduct them on pure principles? They could then close a portion of them when there were too many, and also supply pure liquor. The houses would then become what they ought to be—places of rational entertainment for the workingmen ; and he' suggested that they should be kept by retired policemen or retired army sergeants, whete they now had no pension. It might be objected that this would be a costly scheme. Yes, it might cost 200 millions of money, but the Government had before—witness the emancipation of the slaves—spent large sums of money for philanthropic pur- poses, from which they gained nothing, except the con- sciousness of having done a good action. The Government, too, could borrow money much cheaper than any one else. As it was, the public-house was generally the hot bed for all the mischief done in the parish; but under the system be suggested this would cease to be the case. He did not wish to air his own crotchets. His only desire was for English- men to become more temperate, Mod thus make themselves and their homes more comfortable.—During the evening a programme was creditably gone through, the following taking part in the proceedings :—Brothers Pickersgill, W. C. Duncan, R. A. Duncan, Barrows, and Kiddie' and Sisters E. A. Linden, M. Linden, A. Duncan, Wells, and Miss Marsh.

We are more concerned with tea"4o futtire than with the past; and looking a-head we 1,413: express the hope that the approaching campaign be a short and decisive one. Admiral Seymour -"u• his blue. jackets commenced it well, and the high rit in which our; troops are being landed on _gYPtian soil may be accepted as an indication that what has been so well 'begun will be followed to a ealicciessful issue. A temporary reverse would do a ezt.:ef mischief, and raise the spirits of the rebels, ;4' it is consequently all the more desirable that the ic'e,tece Uses should be sufficient to crush the enemy at catset. It will be seen that in order to prosecute campaign the Government ask for only ,',P0,000 of which £1,400,000 is for the navy, and 4900 ,c"00 for the army. This amount, it is stated, enable us to equip a force of 2,400 cavalry, 43400 infantry, and 1,700 of horse and field artillery. 21 also, it is expected, cover the cost of 3,700 -"sea artillery and engineers. It is proposed to ' ttli4e th amount by putting 3d. on the income-tax 'ae second half of the current year, making the Atitirellee equsi to 4d. in the £ for the whole year; Ive %kr feel sure that if this expenditure should ' w 6 for us greater security for our interests—politi- -41;1 tie well as commercial and financial—in Egypt, 484114 rid the Egyptians themselves of the. military tobil°tisra and obtain for them something like a stable tri'lrament, then the British tax-payer wilt not be- age the money.
