div.head: EXAMIYER, SATURDAY, JULY 20,
div.p: THE EXAMIYER, SATURDAY, JULY 20,

IRUNCORN PUBLIC Feu:max.—At the Runeotn Police-Court on Monday, Mr. W. H. Linaker, law clerk to the Improvement Commissioners, applied to the magistrates, Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. John Brundrit, for an order to close the fountain for a further period of two months, the mooth previously granted baying expired. He called Mr. Barker, the surveyor, to prove collecting the sample of water, and read the analysis of the water made by Mr. Davies, of Liverpool, which has previously been published in these columns. The Bench at once granted the order. ' DROWNED IN THE CANAL AT CLIFTON, —Mr. J. V. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at Stocks Farm, Clifton, on Saturday, on the body of Thomas Clare Dodd, aged seven years, son of John Dodd, who was found drowned in the Weaver Canal, Clifton, near Frodsham Bridge. It appeared that the boy was playing near the canal, which is only a short distance from his home. Subsequently, he wax missed, and, being unable to ind him, the canal was dragged and his body was brought to the surface.—The jury returned a verdict of found drowned.

ROBBING AN ORCHARD. - Peter Lightfoot, Michael Mc Grevy, Edward Currie, Thomas Dean, and Sohn Fowler, boys, were brought up in custody at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, charged with stealing gooseberries from the farm of John Halsall, farmer, Halebank. Mr. Husband appeared for the prosecutor, and detailed the circumstances of the case, which won reported on Monday.—A boy named Rosever!, who had been fined under tho same charge, was called as a witness, and stated Lightfoot and Currie had not taken part in the robbery. The Bench consequently discharged those prisoners, and fined each of the others 7s. 6d. and costs, with the alternative of 14 days' imprison- ment.

LECTURE rty THE REV. J. D. THOMAS AT RUNCORN.— An interesting lecture, entitled "The land o' cakes," was delivered by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, in the Bethesda school- room, Runcorn, on Monday evening. The children of the Sunday school, for whom the lecture was specially prepared, attended in large numbers, and listened with a gratifying appreciation, aS Mr. Thomas described a trip to Scotland, which he made some weeks ago. Incidents on the voyage from Liverpool to Glasgow, the beauties of, and notable places in, that town and Edinburgh were graphically pour- trayed, and the conclusion of the lecture which will be given ia a short time will be looked forward to with pleasure.
" Tua On) TorL-HousE.—On Thursday week, in
the Chambers of the Queen's Bench Division, Mr. Justice Denman granted an injunction, restraining the defendant in

he action Cave v. Russell, his agents and servants, and any of them, from further publicly performing the above-named drama, or any part thereof, at any place of public enter- tainment, together with full costs. The application was made by Mr. Thomas Lewis Allen, solicitor, on behalf of the plaintiff, Mr. Joseph Arnold Cave, of the Marylebcne Theatre, the regi•tered proprietor of the sole liberty of per- formance (and who was also one of the two joint authors) thereof. The defendant, Mr. Tom Russell, a provincial theatrical manager, had performed the drama on the 26th and 27th ult., at the Theatre. Widnes, without the consent in writing first being obtained from the plaintiff, or of Mr. Harry Wall, his authorised agent, contrary to the provisions of the statute 3 and 4 Wm. 4, cap. 15; and had paid £4, the minimum amount of damages fixed by the Act, as claimed by the plaintiff for the two performances in question. CAUGHT AMONG THE Goos EB EERY BUSHES AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. F. H. Gossage (chairman) and Holbrsek Gaskell, jun., Thomas Lightfoot and Wm. Rosevere, lads, living %t Widnes, were charged with stealing a quantity of goose- berries, of the value of 5a., the property of Mr. Thomas Halsall, farmer, of Manor Farm, Hale Bank.—Mr. Husband appeared for the prosecution, and said opposite to the prose- cutor's house was a garden' in which were a number of gooseberrY bushes, and on Sunday Mr. Halsall perceived about seven boys among the trees stripping them of their fruit. Two of his sons went out, whereupon the lads took to their heels, but they were chased a distance of two miles, to Ditton,where the prisoners were captured and given in custody. The other boys escaped. Mr. Husband asked the Bench to make an example of the offenders, as Mr. Halsall had suffered very much from depredations of that kind.—Mr. Halsall having proved the facts of the case, the prisoners pleaded guilty, and were each fined ss. and costs Os. 6d., and ordered to pay the damage ss. between them. ASSAULT ON A WIPE: A. CANDID HUSBAND.. —At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, a boatman,named James Bushell was charged with assaulting his wife Ellen. The complainant said on the Bth inst. she was walking up High- street, when she met the defendant, who asked her to give him the 5s 10d which he bad given her previoualy. She replied that she had spent it in purchasing food. The defendant then seizod her and thumped her &avagely, and dragged her by the neck from High-street to her home in Bridgewater-street. He had frequently ill-used her. She -was in peril of her life, and wished for a separation order. Mary Ann Simpson gave similar evidence. The defendant said there were six of one and half-a-dozen of the other ; she had not acted right to him and he had not acted right to her. The Chairman said there was a very black list against the defendant, who was fined 20s and costs lie 6d, or in default 14 days' hard labour. The Bench did not think the facts warranted them in making a separation I order, but bound the defendant over to keen the peace for l six months, himself in £lO and one surety in a similar I amount.

A TOUGH STRUGGLE: EXEXPLARY PUNISHMENT:FOR OBSTRUCTING THE POLICE.—g young man named Robert Moore, was at the Runcorn Police Court on Monday, charged with using obscene language in Heath-road on the 15th inst., and also with assaulting P.C. Mellor whilst in the execution of his duty on the 22nd July.—P.C. Cooper and Sergeant Loundes proved the first charge.—With regard to the second, P.C. Mellor said on the 22nd inst. at 11 o'clock, he was on duty in Heath-road, when the prisoner and another man went to him, and said "This is the bobby who searched me the other night. and served me with a summons." The prisoner then deliberately struck the officer oa the chest, the force of the blow knocking him against the wall. He afterwards seized the officer by the cape, dragged him across the street, and assaulted him in a very violent manner, kicking him several times on the legs. The constable threw the prisoner to the ground several times, and with the aid of Joseph Bell, managed to get the hand- cuffs on his wrists.—The prisoner, who had been before the court on many previous occasions, was fined 10s. and costs lie. 6d., or in default, 14 days' imprisonment on the first charge; and for the second, which the Bench considered
_„ • much more serious, he was committed to gaol for a month without the option of a fine.—Mr. Superintendent William- son said he was extremely obliged to Mr. Bell for assisting the police.

BREACH OF THE LICENSING ACT AT FA.RNWORTII.— On Wednesday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions—before Messrs. W. L. Heald and Holbrook Gaskell, junr.—Aubin Young was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of John Smith, Griffin:Jon, Farnworth,—P.C. Ross stated that on Saturday night, the Ist inst., he saw the de- fendant standing at the bar of the public-house. He was so drunk that he could hardly stand, and Mrs. mitli refused to serve him with any liquor. Eventually he left the house, when he staggered so badly that a person took him home. He had known the defendant about eight months, and was sure he was the man.—P.C. Coutts corroborated, and Mrs. Smith being called stated she remembered refusing to serve a man with drink in presence of P.C. Coutts and P.C. Ross, but she was unable to identify him.—Defendant contended that the police had made a mistake, and denied that he was in the He called two witnesses named Wilson Wallace and James Wild, who gave evidence that they left the defendant in Butterworth-street about 830 on the night in question, and he then said it was his intention to go home. —Mrs. Young the mother of the defendant, said that on the Ist inst. her son went home about nine o'clock, and about half an hour later he went to bed. He was teetotal to within a fortnight ago, and she had never seen him in- capable in her life.—Cross-examined by Superintendent Barker: Witness could give no reason why she remembered the date.—Defendant then called Miss Smith, the daughter of the landlord, but she stated she was not present on the eeision.—The Bench fined the defendant 103. and costs. A. wiDNEs.__At EINIINAL ASSAULT ON A GIRL AT mpolice Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Gaskell. jun., Wm. Walton was charged with com-rial Hannah Nixon, sometime about Eriminal assault upon. Widnes. It appeared that the prisonerlth June last, at lived on the Old Marsh ' • and the girl resaabourer and parents in King-street, Widnes. On the 30th nit ;;th her soner called at Mrs. Walton's house, and asked for the-ri- to go to the shop of a man named Farmer on an errand 'for him, promising to give her 2d. if she would do so. The girl objected, but the mother insisted on her going, and subse- quently the prisoner and the girl left the house together. They crossed the bridge by the "big offices" and passed under the canal bridge and came to the adjacent arches. On their arrival there the prisoner, who had previously said be was going to his home, stated he did not intend to proceed thither, and pulled the girl under a wagon. The girl screamed several times but no one came to her assistance. and the prisontx accomplished his purpose. From the girl's further evidence it seemed that this was not the first time the pris,,ner had acted in this manner; it had occurred many times previously; but she could not give the exact dete of the first occasion. She knew, however, that it was in winter, and thought it was before Christmas. She had never told her mother on any of those occasions, because she was atraid the prisoner would beat her. He had warned her not to tell her mother.-1 he mother was called, and said the prisoner had frequently gone to her house during the past six months, for the purpose of asking her daughter to go errands for him to Farmer's, a coal dealer. Sometimes the child had seemed unwilling to go, but she (witness) had compelled her—had even " thumped " her for refusing. She had no idea the prisoner wanted the girl for any improper purpose; and did not suspect that anything was wrong.— Dr. Cooper and Dr. O'Keeffe gave evidence at great length as to the condition of the girl, who was suffering from an infectious disorder—The father of the girl stated she was born in March, 1870. and was consequently in her 13th year. —The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

rAyrucm- THEATRE, WlDNES.—Crowded audiences have Patronised the th'tre during the past week, but next week ..1: there will no &mist be A more successful run. Mr. Russell, the proprietot, annewnees the:. t the present season will ceaSe on Saturday nett, and the estashment will then be tem- porarily closed. An attractive projramme has been [re• pared, and Mr. Ernest Lawton and Misg Kate Winstanley, who have been specially engaged, will make their appear- ance in several popular dramas. ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES.—On Thursday morning a man named McCann, etisployed at the Vine Chemical Works, fell into a pan of strong chemical liquor, and was badly burned. He was taiken home and attended by Dr. Booth.— There is at Widnes Accident Hospital, a maw named Henry Wailes, who is suffering from injuries received by stepping into a trough of caustic liquor. Under tke care of Dr. O'Keeffe, he is recovering. ALLWED THEFT OF CISOTHING AT RlNCORN.—Tester- day, at JrAncorn Police Court, before Mr, William Brakes, a boatwoman named Alice Vere was brought up in custody charged with stealing two shirts and one sloprthe property of Catherine. Walker, living at IS, Lock-street, Runcorn. ..ft- appeared that the pesoner lived'with the prosecutrix a short time, but disappeared on the glst inst., and it was subse- quently ascerta'nted she had pledged the articles named at Mr. unison's pawnshop on Thursday afternoon. P.T. Noden received the prisoner in custody from the Nortilampton police. She was remanded to Monday. GOOD TEMPLAIV7 IN WIDNES.—The annual electi-on n

officers of the Star of Widnes Lodge LO.G.T., took place on Wednesday evening. The following were the appointments: —W.C.T., Bro. H. Hupton (re-elected for the 3rd time) ; W.V.T.,sister Prescott ; W.C.,8r0. Taylor ; W.§.,8r0 Evans; W.F.S., Bro. Hodgkiuson ; W.T., Bro.. Coleburn; W.M., Bro. Bushel!; W.J.G.,8r0. Kenyon ; W.0.G.,8r0. Smith ; W.A.S., Bro. Bullivant ; D.M., Sister Fairclough. A fruit banquet and entertainment followed, and a pleasant evening was spent.—On Wednesday evening the quarterly meeting for the election of officers of the Sunbeam Juvenile Temple 1.0.G.T. was held. The appointments were :—C.T., Bro. George Wendt ; V.T., Bro. J. W. Jones; chaplain, Sister Gough; secretary, Bro. Spilby ; F.S., Sister Bullivant ; treasurer, Bro. Brady; marshall, Bro. Kenyon; W.J.G., Bro. Galilee ; W.0.G., Bro Welling ; D.M , Bro. Wolstencroft ; A.S., Bro. J: Broderick.

WESLEYA.N CONFERENCE: STATIONS MINISTERS —Among the stations of ministers as given at the third reading at the Conference are the following :—Warrington : John Eglinton, Joseph Agar Beet, Thomas Rippon. Cadis- head (Warrington): Robert Dillon who shall change on one. Sunday in every six weeks with die m'nisters of the Man- chester (Great Bridgewater-street and City-road) circuits, alternately. Runcorn : Edward J. Robinson, George Hack, Sidney Mees (Halton). Frodsham : John M. Bamford, who shall change on one Sunday in every six weeks with the ministers of the Runcorn circuit; Frederick F. Edmunds, Supernumerary. Widnes: Richard Harper, John Tessyman. St. Helens and Prescot : John M. Wamsley, George Smith (a), Joshua M. Fairbourn (Earlestown,Newton-le-Willows); Samuel Taylor (Rainhill), supernumerary. Pendleton (Manchester) : Henry Valentine. Ashton-under-Lyne : John Nowell. Alderley Edge (Manchester) and Knutsford: John Jenkin, Thomas Harrison (Knutsford), Joseph Sykes, super- numerary. Altrincham : Joseph Bush, Joseph C. Wood- cock (Sale, Manchester), Henry J. Forster (Bowdon), Alfred Roebuck (Sale, Manchester) ; Thomas Llewellyn (Bowdon), supernumerary. Sandbach : James Kent, who shall change on one Sunday in every six weeks with the ministers of the Congleton circuit. Nantwich : John Bramley, Samuel Green. Crewe: William Lees, Ebenezer Cole, Cle.,ar Caine. Northrich : Frederick Haines, Henry T. Brumwell (Middle- wich), Clement S. Reader (Winsford, Cheshire), Thomas Slader. Chester:John S. Workman, Alfred Sar4eant ; John M. Budden, supernumerary. Tarporley: John P. Yates, William Greenwood. Oswestry : Charles Bingant. BREACH OF THE NAVIGATION COMPANY'S BYE-LAWS AT RUNCORN.—On Monday at the Runcorn Police-Court— before Messrs. C. Reynolds and John Brundrit—Joseph Jones was charged with having on the 29th June in the township of Runcorn, then being the owner of the vessels Speedwell and Waterlilly passing on the Runcorn and Weston canal failed to comply with the requirement regula- ting the right of way .of vessels, which states that when vessels using the canal shall meet, the right of way shall be given to the one going in the direction of Runcorn from Weston. Mr. Meadowcroft said he was the agent of the Bridgewater Navigation Company. On the -29th of last month the two boats named, which were narrow ones, and owned by the defendant, were proceeding in the direction of Weston ePoint on the Runcorn and Weston Canal, which connects the Weaver Navigation with the Runcorn Docks and the Bridgewater Canal. The de- fendant's son, Henry Jones, was the master of the boats, and when about 200 yards from the lock which connects the higher with the lower levels, he ran to the lock. There was a float about to enter the lock from the lower level, but Henry Jones persisted in closing the lower gate in face of the float, thus taking the right of turn from the boatman. The lock tenter • protested against the procedure, but the oaptain disregarded his authority, and was also somewhat abusive in his language. The captain's proceedings was clearly in contravention of the 29th bye-law, which regulated the turns of the boats, and which compelled the company to prosecute the owner of the vessel, although the defendant was not at that time working the boats.—Wm. Clark, the lock tenter, confirmed this statement ; and Wm. Watson, captain of the float, stated that the defendant's boats were 200 yards from the lock when Henry Jones closed the gate, while his float was only five yards away.— Wm. Green said the defendant's name was on the boats, and Wm. Simister, the tonnage clerk at Top Locks, deposed that the defendant was registered as owner of the boats.—Mr. Hitcheo, who appeared for the defendant. contende4 that the defendant was not the owner of the boats according to the bye-laws. Henry Jones, his son, who had hiredlte boats, which were not under the control of the defendant, was really the owner; and Mr. Hitchen cited a case where it had been held that a person hiring a carriage, and pro- viding the horses and coachman, was considered the owner, and liable for any accidents which might ensue.—The Bench overruled this objection, and said they considered the de- fendant the owner —Mr. Hitchen then addressed the Bench in mitigation of the offence, and the defendant said he had had boats on the canal for a period of 49 years, and had never been summoned before.—Mr. Reynolds said the magistrates -sere compelled to support the order of the com- pany. The boatmen knew perfectly well what the bye- laws were, and the defendant would be fined 108. and costs 14s. 6d.

DESPERATE A.FSAULT BY A CHIMNEY JAME AT WARRING TON.-At the Warrington Police Curt, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and Councillor Pairclou;b, Thomas Hemus, a "chimney Jack," was charged with wounding his master, James Jewitt, a contractor and builder carrying on business in Hightown, Manchester. It appeared that the prisoner was engaged, on Saturday, fixing a lightning conductor on one of Messrs. Crosfield and Son's chimneys, and about half-past four in the afternoon the prosecutor went to the job and asked prisoner what he had been doing. His reply was "I have fixed the rod once, and I shall not fix it again. One of of Messrs. Crosfield and Son's foremen has pulled the boldfast out, and I shall not put it right again." Prosecutor then told him that he would have to make the rod right, whereupon prisoner began to use very foul language, and deliberately struck his employer several times in the face with his fist. Prosecutor defended him- self as well as he could with an umbrella, but the prisoner picked up an iron block and dealt Mr. Jewitt a very severe blow on the forehead, stunning him and caus;ng blood to flow very copiously. The prisoner also attempted to strike his employer with a brick, but was stopped by two of Messrs. Crosfield's workmen, who also held him in check whilst the prosecutor made his way as best he could to the lodge to have his wounds attended to. About six o'clock Inspector Singleton had received information of whst bad taken place. He made inquiries for, and subsequently found the prisoner in possession of the prosecutor's hat and umbrella in the Wool Pack Inn, Sankey-street. He asked prisoner what he was doing with Mr. Jewitt's bat and umbrella, when he replied in the first instance that they were his, but subsequently his mister's, and that he intended taking them back to his master. He was then taken into custody and locked up.—The prosecutor, who appeared in court with his forehead covered with plaster, stated that Hemus was a most desperate character.—The prisoner pleaded as an excuse for the assault that he was drunk at the time, and did not know what he was doing.— Councillor Fairclough remarked that drink was no excuse for committing such an offence, and prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, or, in default of payment, one month's imprison- ment with hard labour.

STil LANCAgIIRE (WAREINGTOII) RIFLE VOLUN- I TEERS.—During the past week the usual preparations have been made to maintain the reputation of this corps at the forthcoming inspection, and to render the event as successful e possible. The annual training Ras commenced on Satur- wee,qt. when the regiment assembled at .six o'clock. There Colonel ty,,le Lieutenant-Colonel Greenall, Lieutenant. Hepherd, 8i1k,,_.1%,..,,tant), Captains Widdows, Ridgway, Buckton, Gooch, and 0-ilton, and Lister; Lieutenants about 300 men. After eqrialis., Watkins, and march-past was practised, and then a'. ..Suraeon companies, the ments, which, considering that this was the 1.,..1;0n move. which so large a number had assembled during tno9 at passed off satisfactorily. At the conclusion of the evolu- tions, Colonel Greenall addressed the men, and remarked that he was glad to see such a good muster, and he hoped the men would consider themselves bound to do all that they could to make themselves as efficient as possible for the inspecting officer. He thought. in these times particularly.' the volunteer force was called upon to show their zeal for ' the service, and mentioned the fact that one volunteer corps 'in London—the Post Office Corps—hal offared their services te the Government if they were required for the purpose of going to Egypt, or for performing any duties that they were considered competent to undertale. This, he considered, was very satisfactory, and reflected great credit upon the force at large. After a few further re-narks be reference to the present position of the corps, the band assembled, and. the regiment marched to headquarters where, as is custom- ary on these occasions, the men sat down to refreshments, and the officers to their usual mess. The band, under the ! conductorship of Sergeant Newns, played the following ! selection of music :—March, "Ye fancye fayre," G. H: Newcombe, Warrington; fantasia, 'Queen's messengert R Smith • valse, "Balmoral," M. Olgoe ; chorus, " Halle- lujah, Handel • God save the Queen:

THE BEY. ''PESTON, OF RUNCORN, " r .ON P incorn on Sunday, Preaching at holy Trinity Chufo, . prince of the from the text "Am there shall be no mote land-of Egypt," Ezeh?ed, xx.x c., 13 v., the get% W• Preston said the boom of Bridge cannon which ,had destrOYed. the threatening forts of Alexandria, might do- more than direct the eyes of the world to Egyjet and Egyptian affairs; or solve the dilemma, or cut the Gordian knot of .1313:7Pti4n 4iffie- culties, or hasten on a trying" and dangerous cis, whiC." might involve Europe in a general war. There Witeanother result which might be the issue ef our present bohll It might be the initial step towards great beginnings in the East ;the beginning of the end which: the student of prophetey had long been looking for, and forward to, when Paleetne should again be colonised by its own- ancient people; when the Jews should return to their own, native soil: which I events would be the actual precursors' of a still inure im- portant, more-glorious, and more longed .for return, that of Him who hassromieed " I will come ew.in unto you," and for whom the waiting church bad for 18 tentative been cry- ing in earnest tones "Even so, come Lerd, Jesus ; come quickly." The period of the Lord's cone:ttg was nearing. and it might be that the events which were toettety trans- piring were but the agents which were hasteeitig, it onwards. , It was then, a season when Christians might property betake themselves to their watch houses and inquire cf-WaceeSmen, what of the night." The light of God's Word he:ped.to.Oispel the darkness, and to illumine the future; we arennt lett in complete obscurity. There was a remarkable prophecy set forth in Daniel, xii C. 2nd v., "From the time tbeerthe dily .secrifice shall be taken away, and an abomination that .maketh desolate there shall be 1290 days." Bffi prophecy, a day stood for a year. In e:0-3: A. the tyrant Emperor l'heeeee with forged decretalu gave the Bishop of Rime permission to assume the title-of "'Universal Bishop," an assumption hitherto held bee no' bishop, but declared by Pope Gregory the Great to -03 the- ,mark of Antichrist, and diet: he who assumed it was-the- "forerunner of Antichrist." It was this very year that Mahomet retired to his cave to forge his imposture, which. he began to propogate at Mecca. in 608 A.D., and compelled' acceptance of by the sword. These two abominations w
re

set up about 60-6. AD. ; a period of 1,290 years had been - assigned to their continuance or to the continuance of "an abomination," and these added together brought us to the year 1896; a date not so distant. It was also noteworthy. that if another special period, mentioned by Daniel (xii c. 7 v.,) 1,260 years, he considered as having begun in, 622, when the Hegira or flight of'lllabomet was said to have taken place, they terminated on Saturday, July 16, on which very day in 622-A.D. the said flight occurred, Was it not a remarkable coincideoce that our action in Egypt should synchronise with the expiration of this period ? Its close might be signalised by. some new phase of the Eastern Question and of the situation in the East with special . . .

saferew to Mahomedanism, of which present events were but the inauguration. Alter briefly noticing the history of Egypt, and the changes which liad-occwred in its Govern- ment, the rev gentleman.said whether the events now tran- spiring would effect a further change in the government of the Kingdom was difficult to foretell. It might be that Egypt would be detached from Ottoman rule, which was to be expected for the Turkish Einpire was the mystic Euphrates of prophecy which was to be dried up, i.e, disap- pear ere the millenium sets in, For years its dismemberment had oeen going on, and since the year 1-820 the exhaustion

of the Turkish power had ben progressing with marvellous rapidity; Greece, Moldavia, Waliachia, Algiers, had cast off her yoke, whilstl from pestilence and civil commotion there had been a great depopulation; and perhaps the events of to-day were but the agents designed • to produce a still further disintegration, and so a further fulfilment of prophecy; and another step, towards that peaceful time when "the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord

as the waters cover the sea." From ail history the truth of Ez?kiel's predictions was attested. Here we had one convincing evidence of the truth of Holy Scripture, and that it is not a cunningly devised fable of designing men or

priestcraft How could mere human wisdom —or c—onjecture foretell so accurately that so great and prosperous a king- dom would become debased; that so rich a country would become tributary; and that its native princes would be _ _ _
dethroned and strangers take their place and sway, Jehovah
declared more than 2,000 years ago " Tbere shall no more be a prince of the land of Egypt," and to this day had that assurance held good.

div.head: DREADFUL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES; INQUEST ON THE DECEASED.
div.p: THE DREADFUL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES; INQUEST ON THE DECEASED.

The young man named Peter Kinsey, who was severely burned through falling into a caustic filter at Messrs. Mus- pratt's works on Sunday week, succumbed to his injuries on Monday last. Although burned in a most frightful way hopes were at first entertained that he would recover, but he gradually became worse. Mr. C. E. Driilield held an inquiry on the body at the Mersey Hotel, West Bank, on Wednesday, and full particulars of.the accident are reported below.

Miss Janet Downie, matron at the Widnes accident hospital, said the deceased was brought to the hospital on Sunday, the 16th inst., straight- from the works. It was about eleven o'clock in the forenoon-. He was severely scalded over almost every part of his body, from immersion in caustic or acid liquor, at, she understood, a cool tempera- tyre. Dr. Cooper and Dr. O'Keeffe both attended upon him, and one or the other saw him daily, sometimes twice. She believed all was done that could be, butdeceased showed little amendment, except during the first few days, afterwards he became delirious, and died on Monday afternoon. Deceased gave her aa account of the accident.. He said he was kneel- on the edge of the filter tank with a stick in his hand. The stick fell, and in attempting to catch it, he dropped in the liquor head first. ILa did not attach any blame to anyone, but he did not distinctly say it was his own fault. In anstrer to a juryman, Miss Downie said the deceased repeatedly said it was a pure accident. Peter Kinsey' of 51, Viaduct-street, West Bank, said he was a labourer in Messrs. Musprates'works, and the deceased was his son, aged 19, and. resided with him. He narrated his son's account of the accident. The deceased was attempting to push down the syphon with a stick, when the stick slipped off, causing him to fall into the filter. He said he used the stick as he bad often done before. By the Coroner: The stick was not provided for the purpose; it was jnst an ordinary piece of wood. The Coroner: Was there any necessity for the deceas.d to push the syphon down in this way ? Well, if the syphon gets stiff, it must be pushed down some way, for it won't go down itself when the joint gets clagged with lime. When I was in the job myself, I had often to get hold of something to push it down, but the tank was not so deep as this one.

In answer to further questions, witness said he was not aware that his son had complained of the syphon sticking, or that in consequence he wished for some appliance to make it right. The deceased was very active in his work, and ha had often warned him to be careful, as he was very venturesome.

George Mansell, of 9, Carey-street, Simms Cross, labourer, slid he was employed at Messrs. l%luspratt's works, and worked within 20 yards from the spot where the acci- dent happened. He heard the shouts of the deceased, and turning his head, saw he was just climbing over the edge of the filter. He ran to him, and shouted for assistance, at the same time aiding him to get away. The liquor was burn- ing the deceased very much. Another man, named Thos. Beswiek, arrived quickly, and each hold of an arm of the deceased conveyed him to the blowing shed, where the usual remedies were applied. The woollen pants he had under his canvas trousers were very much burned. Subse- quently he was conveyed to the hospital. There was a stick about a yard long floating in the filter, and it appeared as if it had been used previously. In answer tc a juryman wit- ness said the syphon usually required considerable pressure to push it down.
The Coroner : Have you ever heard of any man complain- ing that there ought to be more applianus for the purpese? No, sir.

lilt.. J. H. Lewis, manager of the works, was then called, and produced a plan of the filter tank, and explained how the syphon was worked. Attached to an iron arm of the syphon was a chain with a hook attached, by which it could be dropped or raised. Of course, if it got clagged with lime other means would have to be used to lower it sufficiently to take off the surface liquor. _
The Coroner: But where are those other means? Mr. Lewis: It has never been reported to me that they have had to use other means.

The Coroner: How long have you been there? Mr. Lewis: About seven year. I didn't know it was the practice to push it down with a stick until the accident occurred. There has never been a single complaint. The Coroner said it seemed to him that Mr. Lewis might have acquainted himself with the fact that it was dane before this. But now they were acquainted with it, what did the firm intend to do to remedy it? Mr. Lewis said he intended to remedy' it in this way. The chain he had alluded to was flexible, and consequently it could not be used as a pushing medium, but if an iron rod was made to work with the chain they could either push the syphon or drop it equally well, and it would always he at hand when required. The Coroner : You should not have left it to the stick. Mr. Lewis : If I had known the men were using a stick, I should at once have stopped the practice. He now under- took to provide a remedy. The factory inspector, who was rpractical man and an engineer, and was perfectly able to hX-P. said the present method was right, but that they might The ut. rounded surface'. r::'''' agree with iiohen addressed the jury, who, he said, would ceased's misus,: ithat the mistake in the case was the de- oecurred, he hoped 'stick, which naturally slipped off the • --,nhon. ' A TURKISH OCCUPATION' DECIDED UPON' The following appeared in a second edition of the Daily Telegraph :—At Thursday's Conference the Ottoman..dele- gates repeated their statement that they were ready to send troops to Egypt on certain conditions. They were, there- fore, requested by the Conference to put these conditions into writing. For this purpose a Cabinet Council was called, which continued in session all last nightiond until a !ate hour this afternoon. On its conclusion Said and Assym Pas has started for Therapia, and on the Conference reas- sembling they brought the reply that the Porte would send a military expedition to Egypt on the terms ltd down by the Powers, but the Porte trusted 'that when an Ottoman force should be established in the country foreign arma- ments would be withdrawn.
SIR GARNET AND HIS STAFF. Sir Garnet Wolseley and other offic.,rs proceeded this morning to Osborne, to take leave of Her Majesty. Sir Gartet and Staff leave for Egypt, via Brindisi, on Friday next.

Miss Anna Parnell, sister of Mr Parnell, is lying very ill in Dublin, the news of the death of her sister, Miss Fanny Parnell, having prostrated her. Her hibours in connection with the land agitation had previously.thrown her in a weak, state of health.

As the result of a conference between the coal and iron masters of North Staffordshire and a deputation from the National Association of Miners, on the subject of a five per cent, reduction in wages, the notices of which would have. expitV to-day, the employers have withdrawn the notices, and what might have been a gigantic strike has therefore been averted.

At the Chester City Quarter Sessions yesterday, Jane White, with several aliases, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for having stolen articles from two different persons. Prisoner had eight times previously been con- victed of serious offences. She was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude at Liverpool in 1865',•and immediately after the expiration of that sentence was convicted and sentenced to a similar term of punishment. , On Thursday evening, Mr. Churton, coroner for Cheshire, held an inquest at Ellesmere Port, on the body of a boy aged three years, named Alexander Coppack. The little fellow chased some young ducks across a road into a plantation in which there was a deep pit, and in endeavour— ing to catch them fell into the water and was drowned. The boy's father was on the spot almost immediately and plunged into the pit, but the child was dead when he got [din out.
THE MARRIAGE OF THE DUKE OF WESTMINSTER.

Lie Duke of Westminster's marriage with Lady Catherine Cavendish, at E irl Leicester's seat at Halkham' to-day, will be strictly private. After the wedding the Dake and his- bride will tra% el to London, and will stay an hour or two at Grosvenor House, en route to Fonthill, near Salisbury, where they will stay two or three weeks. After that it is expec ed.' that the Duke and Duchess will goo Eaton Hall.,

div.p: THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE _ _

At the Wesleyan Conference in Leeds yesterday morning, the Committee on Memorials and Suggestions presented their reprt, which was accepted. *The Rev. William Arthur continued the discussion on the book of offices, and spoke in favour ol the adoption of the amended form.for the administration of baptism to•adults and infants.

div.head: PH(ESIX PARK MURDERS.
div.p: THE PH(ESIX PARK MURDERS.

The Dublin detective department beyond making inquiries into the statement made regarding the movements of West- gate, had made no important discovery up to yesterday morning, but the opinion is growing that the man in custody. in Ventzuda is not one of the Phenix Park assassins. THE REPRESENTITION OF BOLTON.

In view ot the Conservative meeting to-night, the Execu- tive Committee have issued a report stating that there is much opposition among the party to Mr. Richardson's can- didature. Mr. Richardson has also issued another address, asking the meeting to-day to suspend judgment, as he intends to address the electors next week. He admits that he may not receive the support of the elite of the Conserva- tive party, hut thinks he will have the support outsile that circle, which will abundantly compensate. . A DANGEROUS PRACTICE.

M the.. Blackburn Borough Police Court yesterday Walter Lingard, grocer, Darwen, was summoned for leaving a train whilst in motion. The defendant attempted to alight before a train stopped, on the 15th inst., b ut slipped and only saved himself from falling upon the line by seizing the carriage handle. He then had to lie on the foot-board until the train stopped. He was fined 40s. and costs and the magistrates condemned the dangerous practice now so prevalent at Blackburn.

div.head: STABBING A POLICEMAN.
div.p: STABBING A POLICEMAN.

At Accringtom, yesterday, Turner Calvert, an operative, was chard with cuttinc, and wounding Police-constable Byers. The officer tool the prisoner into custody for drunkenness yesterday morning, and while in the police office the prisoner stabbed him with a pocket knife, inflict- ing a wound an inch deep on the arm, and the prisoner was attempting to stab another officer, but was knocked down. He was committed for three months with hard labour for the assault. and fined for drunkenness.

The prizes were distributed at seven o'clock by Mrs. Cross, of Mossbrook, Farnwortn. There was a large number of people present, including the Rev. G. Bond, Mrs. Bond, Miss Bond, Major Cross, Miss Cross, Mr. H. Wade Deacon. Mrs. Carey, sen., Miss Cooper, &c. At the conclusion of the distribution Mr. H. Wade Deacon proposed a vote of thanks to Mrr. Cross, which was carried with acclamation. In responding, Major Cross said it had. been a great pleasure to Mrs. Cross to perform the task she had just completed. He wished every success to the Widnes Window Plant Association, and hoped that another year a larger number of prizes would testify that the cultivation of window plants had made even greater progress in Widnes than it had up to the present time. The proceedings then terminated. We may add that materials were contributed for the decoration by the firm of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co. Flags were also kindly lent by the National and Cunard lines of steamers Liverpool. There was received for entrance money £l.B Os. 31, which is a little better than last year, when the receipts were £l6 Os. sd. A great loss is sustained in the gate money through the exhibition not being well patronised in the afternoon.

MILITARY INTERVENTION BY ENGLAND. THE OPENING OF THE CAMPAIGN. We may now be said to have commenced in earnest the campaign in the interior of Egypt, and towards strengthen- ing our forces preparations are being actively pushed for- ward. Her Majesty has, it is announced, approved the following appointments in connection with the expedition to be sent out, namely, to command it, Lieutenant-General Sir Garnet J. Wolseley ; to be chief of the staff, Lieutenant- General Sir J. M. Adye, Royal Artillery. The Duke of Con- naught, Sir Archibald Ali Son, and Sir Evelyn Wood will each command a brigade in the expedition, and Colonel the Hon. J. C. Dormer will act as assistant adjutant-general. Sir Garnet Wolseley and the principal members of his staff will, according to present arrangements, leave England early next week. The whole of the arrangements for the despatch of the expedition are stated to have been completed so far as the War Department is concerned, and everything is in readiness for the machinery to be put in motion as soon as the Admiralty has provided the necessary transport for the troops. It is proposed to send out in the first instance a force of about 10,000 men, and this, with the troops al- ready despatched, would make the total number of troops imtnediately available for active service in Egypt close upon 14,000. Ourabi has issued two proclamations, in which he describes himself as the military dictator of Egypt, de- nounces the Khedive as a traitor because of his alliance with the English, 'declares war to the death against us, and appeals to the religious fanaticism of the people to support him in the struggle. To that fanaticism he had not appealed in-vain, as the reports ef the dreadful massacres at Tantah and other places show. The English, we are told, were hunted like game, and a Syrian was murdered because from the fairness of his complexion he was believed to be one of the hated nation. The Khedive, on the other hand, has issued a proclamation declaring Ourabi to be a rebel and outlaw, and requesting the Egyptians to assist the British, who, it is declared, are only present to restore order and pro- mote the real interests of the country. ,An order has been issued by His Highness forbidding the Egyptian army to obey the commands of Ourabi, and requesting the people not to pay any taxes levied by him. It is not believed at the Palace that this proclamation will alter Ourabi's course. On Saturday Sir Archibald Alison pushed forward 250 Rifles to blow up the railway beyond Malaha in order to prevent Ourabi's approach. The men exchanged shots with Ourabi's cavalry. It is stated that the Egyptians flerl, leaving a few Arabs dead on the field, and that the British having finished the work entrusted to them withdrew with- out any casualties. On Sunday, upon the arrival of a steamer from Constan- tinople the captain, a Greek, and an Egyptian officer were arrested by order of the Khedive. It is stated that they were known to be the bearers of despatches for Ourabi, which, however, were landed before the arrests were made. A SMART ACTION: OCCUPATION OF RAMLEH. On Monday there was a smart little action near Alexan- dria, brought on by the advance of Sir A. Alison against the Egyptian position at Ramleh, four miles to the eastward of the city. The troops of Ourabi showed some spirit, and used both rifles and cannon against our men, but little exe- cution was done on either side, and the " rebels " finally retired, leaving Raml eh in our hands. A further reconnais- sance showed that the enemy were entrenched and in con- siderable force on the narrow isthmus between Lakes Aboukir and Mareotis, and the advanced party of British fell back to the village. The Daily News gives the follow- ing account of this transaction :—" I have just witnessed the opening of the land campaign in Egypt. Sir Archibald Alison advanced early this morning, with six companies of the Rifles and two small guns drawn by sailors, to a strong position near the ,Ramleh Palace, a hillock where are the pumps of the waterworks. The Arabs showed in force beyond the railway junction, where they had water on both flanks. The English held the railway bridge, and skirmished down towards a grove of palm trees near the water. A sharp fire was exchanged between the skirmishers at about half- past eight, and presently the Arabs began to throw shrapnel shells upon our advanced line. The shells burst too high and stemed to do no damage, but they had a pretty effect, soar- ing up with white smoke clouds above the feathery tops of the palm trees. We could see groups of Arabs on the rail- way line working either to repair it or tear it up, it was diffi- cult to tell which, and the enemy's guns beyond the water could be distinctly seen. There were six or eight guns, I think, though I was only sure about the position of four of them, and there must have been from 800 to 1000 infantry, besides a troop of horse. These latter were the foremost to engage us, and one at least of their chargers was rolled over by an English bullet. Our guns had not taken any part in the affair when I came away, being held in reserve in case the Arabs should make an attack. The English troops were in high spirits, did their spade work with right good will despite the heat, and only wished there might be a real fight. As to the sailors they tugged those two little guns over the sandhills like human traction engines. The skirmish continued for more than half an hour with anima- tion. Then the Arab guns ceased firing, and a few straggling shots only were exchanged. Each side seemed to have found out all it wanted to know about the other. Each has a strong position for defence, but a dangerous one to advance far without a superior force. ARABI'S POSITION. The Daily News correspondent at Alexandria gives the following general account of the situation with which we Lave to deal :—Major Morice Bey, of the intelligence de- partment, hearing that Arabi was moving ap troops towards Rosetta and Aboukir, volunteered to go out by sea and go ashore and make inquiries. The Admiral sent him round in the Cygnet. He was accompanied by Lieutenant Streeten, of the Inconstant. They landed close to the forts, with a white pocket-handkerchief on a stick. Morice Bey was met by an officer and ten men, who received him in a friendly manner, inquired after the Khedive and the position of affairs at Alexandria' and said the soldiers in the forts were all well disposed to his Highness. On Morice Bey askir them to show their fidelity by coming away with him, th said they must remain to protect the Khedive's interr:sts there. They refused to allow Morice Bey to visit the f irts, and said there were 10,000 men there. Morice Bey saw 15 large rifled Armstrong guns, but not many men. The flag of truce is still flying, and perhaps it is better to keep the men there than take the forts and liberate them. Arabi Pasha has circulated all kinds of atrocious statements at Cairo to the effect that the English were pillaging and ruining the country, that the fires at Alexandria were not only caused by the guns of the fleet but by inflammable projectiles used on purpose to destroy the town, and that the Khedive's Ministers. were kept prisoners by the British. Ali Pasha Mourabeck and three others have accordingly been deputed by the Pashas and residents of Cairo to proceed to Alex- andria. and report upon the actual state ef the case. After some difficulty at Karr Dewar, where Arabi tried to frighten them by saying he was sure they would be killed at Alexan- dria, Aiy Pasha Mourabeck arrived at the Palace of Ras-el- Tin on Tuesday morning. He was surprised and delighted to find the Khedive surrounded by old friends, and as happy and comfortable as possible under present circumstances. At Kafr Dower, Arabi is very strongly entrenched, and has 30,000 armed men not all soldiers, but men armed with Remington rifles, of which he has 120,000. in different places. He has proclai.ned a jehad or holy war, and fanatics are crowding in by thousands asking to be armed. They have plenty of supplies. All the mule drivers engaged by the Commissariat Department ran off on Tuesday to join Arabi, who has called into his service all the Bedouins at Ramleh, who, being scattered and isolated, are afraid to remain, but at Kifr Dower the relations between Arabi and the Bedouins are not amicable. As a body, they have behaved well during the troubles of the past five weeks. There were very few cases of pillage by Bedouins at Alex- andria. Five hundred have offered their services to the Khedive, who believes that by good management and liberal payment of services the Bedouins might be secured to ensure the safety of the Suez Canal, ARABI'S CUPIDITY. The Standard states—" A rumour is in ciiculation that, in order to replenish his empty treasury, Arabi Pasha pro- poses to sell the Boolak Museum, and has ordered Professor Maspers to value that priceless collection of Egyptian anti- quities. Though it is difficult to see how the purchaser of this piece of national property could convey it out of the country, there is nothing improbable in the report, and con sidering the imminent peril in which the life labour 91 Marlette Bey and his successors is placed, possibly_Riste could scarcely perform a kindlier office to hisssysteA of the native land than to dispose of the tombs andi the illiterate Pharaohs to custodians more revent;eEgyptologists have rabble of Cairo. For weekteaction of the city of the trembled lest the one .se-a-nen a prey to the cupidity of the Mamelukes shouldifd rage for destruction." Arabs or to ke t rARLIAMENTARY PAPERS. .der papers relating to Egypt have been issued by the ,reign Office, bringing down the correspondence to June 23. On June 1, Admiral Seymour, having reported by tele- graph that four new earthworks had been thrown up by the Egyptians at Alexandria, and that the safety of his en- armoured vessels was compromised, received telegraphic instructions to arrange with the French admiral to dispose the ironclads so as to silence the batteries if they opened fire. Subsequent despatches describe the armaments of the forts and the progress of operations. On June 11th, Vice- Consul Calvert informed Earl Granville by telegraph of a serious riot, in which Mr. Cookson was wounded and the engineer of the Superb killed. Admiral Seymour's report of the same affair follows, and his account of the arrangements made' at the port for the removal of European refugees is added. A communication, date June 17, from Sir Edward Malet to Lord Granville, mentions that about 20,000 Christian refugees had embarked. Reports from Sir Beauchamp Seymour to the Admiralty on theoutbreak at Alexandria were issued on Monday. The Viceroy stated that if men were landed there would be a general conflagration throughout the country. The admiral believes the course he adopted in not landing a force on the occasion of the riots was correct. Captain Molyneux, tem- porary consul, describing the occurrences on the night of the riots, says the Governor begged him to withdraw the Eng- lish boats out of sight or the soldiers would join the rioters. This was done.
THE GREAT STRIKE IN THE COAL TRADE. DECISION OF THE MEN TO CONTINUE THE STRUGGLE.

There is no new feature to report in connection with the dispute between the firm of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. and their hands, who are out on strike against a proposed reduction of 10 per cent. in their wages and a proposal to revert to the system of fortnightly pays instead of weekly. About 700 of the men came out on the 4th instant, three weeks go. last Tuesday, while the remainder, estimated to number about 3,000, stopped a fortnight ago. Since that time several attempts have been made to come to an amicable arrangement, but hitherto they have all failed, and the lispute is almost as far from a settlement as ever. Another deputation from the men again waited on Mr. Glover, the manager of the firm, on Saturday morning last, but as at all other previous interviews, no definite decision was come to, and the men returned in no better position than when they went. The deputation comprised two men from each of the pits belonging to the firm, who, before waiting on Mr. Glover, met at a preliminary meeting at the Ram's Head, Hay dock. The men asked Mr. Gover if he had any new terms to offer, or any concession to make with the view of settlement being come to, and the reply they received was a negative one, Mr. Glover intima- ting that he had not. He told them that he had not offered to make a rumoured concession of 5 per cent., but a deputa- tion from Golborne had proposed those terms to him, and further, that he still meant to adhere to the 10 per cent. reduction. On the return of the deputation to the Ram's Head, a resolution was passed that they should not again wait on Mr. Glover, and recommended all colliers, young men particularly to leave the district. With the object of soliciting subscriptions on behalf of the men out on strike, a circular headed " Haydock Miners' Strike," and issued "From the committee of the Haydock Miners' Society " has been issued. It is worded as follows :

Fellow-Workmen and Friends,—We are desirous to make an appeal to you for your support and sympathy in our present unfortunate struggle against the arbitrary reduction Of our wages of 10 per cent., and against the old system of payment of our wages fortnightly instead of weekly. We have done everything reasonable,to avert, if possib:e, a disastrous strike. We have offered arbitration, we have asked for fair concessions, but all our attempts have been 'pored. Our position is most distressing. The day wagemen's wages wi,l not average more than 13s. per week when stoppages are deducted, and the col- liers' wages not more than Ll per week. We re-pectfully ask how can the poor miner maintain, in many instances, very large families, out of such a mean pittance? On these grounds, we hopefully appeal to you to do your uttermost endeavours to help us in our strife for fair wage and liberty. We are, yours on behalf of the committee, THOMAS DIX, president, WM. DEIRDEN', secretary. It is stated that the appeal is being liberally responded to, and it is confidently anticipated that a sufficient sum will come to hand weekly to maintain the non-society men while the strike lasts. The men in the society are being paid at the rate of 103. per week and is. for every child out of the funds, the outside subscriptions being set apart almost en- tirely for the benefit of the non-society men. A large num- ber of the latter have recently left the district, and the men express themselves confident to maintain the struggle until Mr. Glover agrees to make some concessisn, or until the notice of reduction is withdrawn.

ACTION AGAINST THE RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS. The case of Beasley v. the Runcorn Commiss'oners came before Mr. Justice North, at the Manchester Assizes, on Saturday. This was an action for damages for maliciously issuing a search warrant for goods alleged to have been stolen, being the property of the Runcorn Commissioners. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. C. Russell, Q.C., M.P., Dr. Commins, and Mr. W. R. Kennedy; and the defendants by Mr. W. C. Gulley, Q.C., Mr. G. Segar, and Mr. C. L. Shand. Mr. Russell, addressing his lordship, said they had arranged a course in this case, of which he was personally very glad, and it would save the necessity of troubling the jury. It was due to the plaintiff, however, that it should be stated to his lordship in the court what the nature of the case was, and how the action came to be brought. It appeared the plaintiff, Mr, Thomas - Beasley, was a solicitor, who had practised for a number of years at Widnes, in Lancashire,—he thought he was of some 20 years' stand- ing—and who had during that time held official positions and appointments as clerk to the Widnes Local Board and also clerk to the magistrates. He became tenant to the Run- corn Commissioners of a house in Runcorn called Waterloo House, and his tenancy of that house came to an end in the month of June, 1881. He thereupon removed, or gave directions for the removal, from the house of the furniture and property which belonged to him in the house, including certain fixtures, which were his property, to the house 125. Church-street, which was also in Runcorn. When he had so removed his property some persons, members of the de- fendant Board, called the Properties' Committee, inspected the house, and they came to the conclusion, as it turned out quite erroneously, that certain things had been removed, as they assumed, by Mr. Beasley, from the house, which were not his property, but the property of the Commissioners. Accordingly, without any communication with Mr. Beasley at all in the matter without any demand for an explanation, they came to a resolution by which the Law Clerk was instructed to take such proceedings as he might be advise!, to bring Mr. Beasley before the justices at the Petty Sessions for fraudulently removing the property of the Com- missioners. Upon that resolution coming to Mr. Beasley's notice—he had not been himself a party to the removal of the goods at all—he went and examined the things which had been removed and found they were all his own property with one exception, that being a cornice pole value about 2s. 6d., or something of that description. Mr. Gully here interrupted, and Mr. Russell said he would sit down, and resumed his seat remarking that Mr. Gully had made remarks tanta- mount to saying that he was leading his lordship to a misunderstanding. Mr. Gully: Oh! no. Mr. Russell said he must mention the matter his own way, and went on to state that on the 4th July Mr. Beasley directed the return of that one thing, and wrote to the chair- man of the Commissioners intimating that this one article which alone was not his was returned. It was returned on the 4th July, but there was no one to take possession of it, and it was deposited at the house on the sth July. Not- withstanding that-, and still without any reference to Mr. Beasley, the Commissioners proceeded to take out a search warrant for the premises No. 125, Church-street, alleging that the property had been feloniously stolen and fraudu- lently removed from their house in Waterloo-road. Aecordingly the warrant was issued, and the house searched, with the result that nothing, by the admission of the Commissioners themselves' was discovered, which wag the property of the Commissioners. It was because of that ivrong, the malicious act of taking out those proceedings that the present action was brought against the Commissioners. Mr. Beasley did not allege that he had been injured by this, and he did not bring the action for the purpcse of putting money into his pocket; but, inasmuch as it had become known in the com- munity in which he lived that thele.proceedings had been taken against him, he had been compelled to take action in order to put himself right, and having brought it he asked for nothing more than an indemnity for the course he had been bound to take, and for the opportunity of vindicating his own position and character. His learned friend had in- structed him to say- there was nothing in the facts of the case which would involve any imputation whatever upon Mr. Beasley, and he must take a judgment from his lord- ship for £553., and an undertaking for costs to be taxed as between attorney and slient. Mr. Gully said this was a form of action in which the question of whether or not Mr. Beasley was guilty oe., ere duct sech as-was suggested in the proceedings ee' whether taken was not the question. The rp----te:inte, pad of the eromt of law ; and that question, ~,tcl raise the question of justifica- there was reasonable and probahLeu that was any satisfac- ,_,ey was guilty of conduct suggested on the part of in the sense of whether or not Cat: so: nmh oms for sor nsr whistidiossnsbe:or_ns e.tf rho:re. they actingH,.aact, tn, ade no imputation whatever upon timb Mr. Beasley and he withdrew any imputation that might have been made. No doubt the facts, as stated by Mr. Russell, in substance were correct; but if he stated the fscts from his brief he shoed qualify some of the details. But it was not worth while -going into that. The Commiseioners in what they did acted simply and solely, whether rightly or wrongly—and they admitted they were not justified in what they did—accerding to their own lights of their duty to the public in the protection of their property. He had advised them, and strongly advised them, they went beyond their right in what they did, and he thought it was a substantial invasion of the rights of Mr. Beasley. He had advised them they had no defence to the action, and that the proper course to take was that which he did,—to withdraw any imputation which had been suggested against Mr. Beasley personally in the matter, and to consent to a verdict upon the terms Mr. Russell had mentioned. His Lordship: I give judgment accordingly. Mr. Russell: We take judgment for .£5 53. on the terms mentioned. His Lordship : And the costs taxed in the way mentioned by Mr. Russell.

THE FORCES OF ANARCHY. All Mubarek Pashl has reported to the Khedive that a number of vagabonds from Alexandria are at present in Cairo ready to burn and plunder the European quarter of that city. The Mussulman inhabitants are also much terri- fied, and considerable panic prevails. Besides those ma- sacred at Tanta and Mihasla, a number of Christians, in- cluding several Copts, have been murdered at Kafrzcyaa and Damanbour.
At the Wimbledon Rifle Meeting, last week, Sergeant West, 21st L.R.V. St. Helens), obtained a prize of £5 in the Olympic competition with a score of 32.

div.head: LETTER FROM ARABI TO MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: LETTER FROM ARABI TO MR. GLADSTONE.
The following letter was addressed by Arabi Pasha to Mr. Gladstone a few days before the bombardment of Alexandria, but did not reach his hands until after that event : .

"TO THE RIGHT HON. W. E. GLADSTONE, M P. " Alexandria, July 2, 1832. "Sir,—Our Prophet in his Koran has commanded us not to seek war nor to begin it. He has commanded us also, if war be waged against us, to resist, and, under penalty of being our- selves as unbelievers, to follow those who have assailed us with every weapon and without pity. Hence England may rest assured that the first gun she fires on Egypt will absolve the Egyptians from all treaties, contracts. and conventions, that the control and debt whl cease, that the property of Europeans will be confiscated, that the canals will be destroyed, the com- munications cut, and that use will be made of the religious zeal of hfahomedans to preach a holy war in Sp ia, in Arabia, and in India. Egypt is held by Mahomedans as the key of Mecca and Medina, and all are bound by their religious law to defend those holy places and the ways leading to them. Sermons on this subject have already been preaahed in the mosques of Damascus, and an agreement has been come to with the religious leaders of every land throughout the (Mahomedan) world. I repeat it again and again, that the first blow struck at Egypt by England or her allies will cause blood to flow through the breadth of Asia and of Africa, the responsibility of which will be on the head of England. The English Government has allowed itself to be deceived by Its azents, who have cost their country its prestige in Egypt. England will be still worse advised if she attempts to regain what she has lost by the brute force of guns and bayonets. On the other hand, there are more humane and friet-rdly means to this end. Egypt is ready still, nay desirous, to come to terms with England, to be fast friends with her, to protect her in- terests and keep her road to India. to be her ally.. But she must keep within the limits of her jurisdiction. If, however, she prefer to remain deceived, and to boast and threaten us with her fleets and her Indian troops, it is hers to make the choice. Only let her not underrate, as she has done, the patriotism of the Egyptian people. Her representatives have not informed her of the change which has been wrought among us since the days of Ismail's tyranny. Nations in our modern age make sudden and gigantic strides in the path of progress. England, in fine, may rest assured that we are determined to fight, to die martyrs for our country—as has been enjoined on us by our Propnet—or else to conquer, and so live independently and happy. Happiness in either case is promised to us, and when a people is imbued wsith this belief their courage knows no bounds. ARMED ARABI."
TRAITORS IN LONDON. ENGLISH AID TO AItA.BI.

A London correspondent telegraphs :—On Tuesday the Foreign Affairs Committee—a body which sits at the Adelphi Hotel—took an extraordinary step. Not only do they ask the Government to hold their hand and to abandon their scheme of intervention, but they propose to aid Arabi Pasha with a strong battalion of Englishmen which should engage to sfveep the foreigner, of whatever nationality, from the shores of Egypt. It is strange that a body of sane Britishers should at this moment think of equipping another "Gari'xildian Brigade," and to offer its services to the vulgar cut-throat and pillager who permitted, if he did not actually push forward, the massacres at and the pillage and destruction of Alexandria. It is stranger to note that Lord Stanley of Mderley should sympathise with a movement of this sort, though it is not surprising to find Mr. Maltman Barry taking the leading part in this insane proceeding. It would be interesting to see how many " volunteers " would come forward in answer to the request of the committee for the purpose of fighting against their own countrymen. It is possible that if the number were considerable the Govern- ment might have a word to saw on the subject of the corn mittee's operations.

div.head: FORCE LANDED AT PORT SAID.
div.p: A FORCE LANDED AT PORT SAID.
The Alexandria correspondent of the Central N,ws says a force from the English ships of war has been landed at Port Said.
PROPOSALS OF ARABI.

The correspondent of the Daily Telegraph at Alexandria, telegraphing on Wednesday morning, says:—Rumours are current that Arabi has been attempting to treat at Alexan- dria for conditions of surrender. I have not been able up to the present to learn on what basis these reports rest. but whatever he may have done or may be doing in this respect did not prevent him last night from attempting a surprise on our outposts. It appears to be part of Arabi's policy to make a treacherous use of the white flag. At sundown last evening the white flag was reported to be flying over his en- trenchments, and this probably was the foundation for the rumours to which I have just referred. Nevertheless, at nine o'clock a decided attempt was made to surprise 0..3r outposts, and but for the gallantry of Major Alexander, of the 35th, it might have succeeded in cutting off our outlying picket. Under cover of darkness, a force of 600 men came on in three bodies, and approached close to our most ad- vanced posts. Our men opened fire sharply and the enemy retired precipitately. During the rest of the night nothing of any iniportance occurred, but Arabi's men continued moving about just out of range.

div.head: TURKEY'S DECISION TO LAND TROOPS.
div.p: TURKEY'S DECISION TO LAND TROOPS.

A St. James's Gazette telegram from Berlin says :—lt is stated here that the Porte, in accepting in principle the invi- tation of the Conference to send troops to Egypt, has declined to limit the period of occupation to three months. The Porte has furtber declared that it has consented to join in the deliberations of the conference not as a simple member of the European concert, but as the Sovereign of Egypt, and that it participates in the debates on condition of their being exclusively confined to the Egyptian question. If these conditions should be respected, the Porte hopes soon to see the establishment of a satisfactory and enduring condition of affairs in Egypt. The German newspapers recall Mr. Gladstone's menacing refusal to admit the Sultan's voluntary offer of intervention in Egypt when it was made in October last, and ridicule the desire he now displays for Turkish co- operation. _ _

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The County GeW eman hears of dreadful losses upon the Stock Exchange through the crisis in Egypt. One gentle- man, well known in the hunting world, is said to have lost £lOO,OOO. Volunteers for the first time since the enrolment of the force in 1859, are to be sent abroad. Our difficulty with Egypt has led to the issue of a special order calling upon members of the 24th Middlesex (Postoffice) Rites to volun- teer for an Army Post3l Corps. It is to consist of three officers and one hundred rank and file; and, subject to the approval of the Postmaster-General, Major Sturgeon will be in command. Half the force is to be at once despatched on foreign service, the rest constituting a reserve company. All are to be at once enlisted for six years, but the men will retain their pay and position in the London Postofflw. In addition, sergeants will receive 2s. 4d., corporals is. Sd., and privates is. per day, besides free kit, rations, kc. This applies to those who are sent abroad, the reserve company receiving the pay of the first-class Army Reserve, in addi- tion to their postoffiee pay. More than 500 men volun- teered to go out, and as the majority are said to be eligible, their will be some difficulty in making the necessary selec- tion. _ _

The Malabar arrived on Sunday night at Alexandria with the 46th Regiment, half of the 35th, eight artillerymen, and four 40-pounder siege guns. The total force at Alexandria now consists of 3,687 of the line, 900 marines, besides artillery and bluejackets. In a letter from an officer of the Invincible to the Western Morning News, mention is made of a hitherto unpublished fact in connection with the spiking of the guns at Alex- andria. When the volunteers were called for to go ashore and spike the guns, nearly every hand in the ship expressed a desire to be selected. Ultimately ten torpedo men were chosen, and they landed in charge of the flag lieutenant under cover of the ship's guns. The dingy was conveying the men from the shore to the steam launch when it was struck by a shot, and foundered. The occupants all suc- ceeded in swimming to the launch, and were brought safely on board. The admiral shook hands with each of the men employed on this dangerous service, and told them how proud he was to feel he had such men under his command. Admiral Seymour's kind attention to the wounded is marked, and on all hands gratification is expressed at being under the command of such an officer. s Great uncertainty prevails as to the strength of,Niiona army. In one account it is fixed at 100,000, mot-t all the are burning with religious zeal to cut it.IT 4.! Zs of as not more than Europeans; another says that the P these are merely an 30,000 men under his orders, adiaml safe. however, to the last armed rabble. It would estimate. Ourabi has with him, degree to accept thi. well-armed and disciplined troops, no doubt, thoy,,V as they did in Roumelia, and who are who will 8-37 works which are every day being strengthened. Prstward of Ramleh, on the point of Aboukir Bay, is the \ castle of Aboukir, and this fort is held by an officer who professes to be loyal to the Khedive, but is really an instru- ment in the bands of Ourabi. A flag of truce is kept flying over the fort, but the British ships will- probably be instructed to reduce it as soon as a further movement from Alexandria shall have begun. The following ships are at present guarding the Suez Canal, several having arrived from distant stations within the last few days :—Agincourt, Tourmaline, Carysfort, Beacon, Euryalus, Ruby, Dragon, Harrier, Eclipse, and Philomel. The Dryad, Woodlark, and Arab are within a short distance of Suez. The Government have chartered the ship Recovery for use in Egypt. She will be in readi- ness in the Suez Canal to lift any obstruction Arabi's party may place there to block the Canal. She has enormous lifting power.

A ;Pe correspondent at Alexandria, after reporting Sir A. Alison's success at Ramleh, states that the water question is becoming very serious. The supply in the Mahmoudieh Canal is rapidly decreasing, and by Ourabi's orders salt water has been turned into the channel. The troopship Euphrates, with the Munster Fusiliers and the Devonshire regiment on board, sailed from Portsmouth on Satuday. Just before the vessel sailed, Prince Edward ef Saxe-Weimar, who was accompanied by the Princess and his brother, Prince Gustave, made a final inspection of the troops, and in bidding good-bye to the officers in the saloon expressecl his best wishes for their success and safe return. When the Euphrates got cicar of the dockyard the soldiers, who lined the upper deck forward, and cjustered thickly in the shrouds, gave hearty cheers, the enthusiasm being taken up by those on shore. A supplement to the London Gazette, published on Tues- day night, contains a royal proclamation summoning the first-class army reserve on permanent service on the 26th to proceed on or before August 2 to the regimental districts appointed by the Secretary of State for War. An order in council is also published extending the period of training from 28 to 56 days for certain militia battalions.
