div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday at the Workhouse, Whiston, when there were present Messrs. Marsh (in the chair), Hall Fidler, Syder, Newsome, Jackson, Gerrard, Buckley, Birchall, Dobell, Hulme, Gilbody, Sadler, Griffith, Tyrer, Eatock, Tuson, Birch, the Rev. J. Barnacle, and Mr. Hartley (clerk.)

div.head: BELIEF CASES,
div.p: BELIEF CASES,
A woman named Maria Flanners applied for relief which had been discontinued to her on the revision of the relief list.
Mr. STEWARD, relieving officer, (Windle district) said the woman's husband had deserted her two years ago. The CHAIRMAN: Have you never heard from him for two years. Mrs. FLANNERS : No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN : Did he go away with another woman? Mrs. FLANNERS : Yes, sir, he went awajwitla a married woman.

The CLERK said all they could do in cases like that was to give an order for the Workhouse. An order for the woman and her two children was accordingly given. Jam?,s Ashall another applicant for relief was granted 3s. pr week; Margaret Fay, an orphan 12 years of age, was allowed a like amount; an order for the Workhouse was granted to James Seddon and his family. Another applicant for relief, named Ellen Ryder, was also offered an order for the Workhouse but refused to accept it.

div.head: WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.
The Master of the-Workhouse reported that there were at present 441 inmates in the Workhous;e, against 445 the preceding week, and 491 the corresponding week of last year.

div.head: SUITABLE PRESENT.
div.p: A SUITABLE PRESENT.

The Workhouse Master reported that as the communion service presented at the time of the opening of theshapel was not sufficiently portable for use in the hospital, the Rev. T. Chambers had presented a silver pocket communion ser- vice for the use of the chaplain in the sick wards, and also a silk fall for the reading desk of the lectern. Mr. DOBELL said he thought Mr. Chambers was entitled to a vote of thanks for his handsome present, and he had pleasure in moving that one be accorded him. The vote was given unanimously. • COMPLAINT.
Mr. BARNACLE referred to the bad attendance at the meet- ings of the House Committee. At one meeting there had only been himself present, and at another there had only been Mr. Fisher and himself.

Mr. NEWSOME: Perhaps we will not have far to travel to get a reason for that. Mr. BARNACLE had thought it was rather an important matter from what he had heard some weeks ago. The house committee was one of the most important committees at which their was a great deal to attend to not of immaterial importance but of great importance he thought. The matter then dropped. •

div.head: TRE GUARDIANS AND THEIR AUDITOR.
div.p: TRE GUARDIANS AND THEIR AUDITOR.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that they bad received a report from Mr. G. Hozle- hurst, the assistant auditor, respecting the audit of the ac- counts of the officers of the Union in which he stated that the cheques for payment of school fees were made payable to the order of the Clerk to the Guardians. The Board re- quested that they might be furnished with the observations of the Guardians on the matter to which the auditor had drawn attention. The CLERK said the order of the Local Government Board with respect to these school fees was that they should be "paid by the Guardians thrhugh the enquiry officer or otherwise at such quarterly or such period as may be agreed upon." The Guardians re- quired him (the clerk) to give a substantial bond for the faithful performance of his duties while the enquiry officer was not required to give a bond and did not give one, and he had therefore drawn three eheques in his own name for the purpose of protecting the Guardians. As a matter of fact the cheques would have to go through his hands any way. He should like to ask the Local Government Beard what the word "otherwise" in their order meant, if they were to be reported for doing these things otherwise than through the enquiry officer. If they would permit him he would send the Local Government Board the following letter The CHAIRMAN : Draw atter.tion to the clause which you have just read. The .CLERK then read the following letter which he had drawn up in reply to the Lecal Government Board :—"I am directed by the Guardians of this Union to acknowledge the receipt of your letter on the 22nd July, respecting a report sent to you by Mr. Hailehurst, as district auditor, of the accounts of the officers of this Union in which he states that the cheques for payment of school fees were made pay- able to the order of the Clerk to the Guardians, and in reply I am to refer you to article 9 of your order relating to pay- ment of school fees of non-pauper children. lam further to state that the Guardians corrsider most of the reports of the auditor are trivial and unworthy of your consideration." Mr. NEWSOME: I beg to move that reply be sent. " The CLERK said this was the only letter sent to the Guardians, the others being sent to himself, and the Guar- dians' otservations were asked upon it. The matter was simply absurd, and there was nothing in it. Mr. Newsome's proposal was then agreed to. The CLERK intimated that the next audit would be on the 14th August.

div.head: EXPENSES RECOVERED.
div.p: EXPENSES RECOVERED.
The CLERK said that since- the last meeting he had received from the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster £194 19. 2d., in the case of Winstanley, a lunatic. The CHAIRMAN: He is dead, is he? _ _

The CLERK said the relatives of the man Winstanley op- posed the application of the Guardians with regard to claim for his maintenance, and took council in the matter; but he (the Clerk) attended Liverpool and showed that the Guardians had expended certain money in his maintenance and the court said they were entitled to the money granted so that the Guardians have done very well. The Clerk further added that there was also a case of a person named Makin, an old lady, whom he thought most of the Guardians would remember. She was now dead, and her property, of which they bad received the rents would have to be handed up to the executer, Mr. Hurst, along with the rents which had been received since her death. He had communicated with Mr. Hurst, who wrote as follows :—" I shall be quite willing for the money made by Mr. Makin's property to ba used for the mainte- nance of Mrs. Makin up to the day she dies, with the under- standing that you have no further claim upon me." He (the clerk) had arranged that this should be done, which he thought would be agreeable to the Guardians. The CHAIRMAN: How much money have we received? The CLERK said the rents lately had been a trifle more than they bad been paying for her maintenance, but taking former expenses into account they would b:_ittbout straight, and the Guardians had made uothing out of it. The Clerk's suggestion was thew agreed to. A REQUEST FOR AN ORGANIST. A letter was read from Father Henry, of Portico Cilapel, stating that they intended to hold Roman Catholic services regularly at the chapel, and asking the Guardians to allow an organist for the Catholic services. Miss Twist, who played the organ at the Church of England services would be willing to undertake the playing for the services, services as well. With regard to a sacristan, who was indis- pensable, he had himself trained one, a lad named Patrick Larkin, 15years of age, who was at present employed at the bakehouse, whom he hoped the Board would allow to act in that capacity. The CHAIRMAN supposed that there would be no cost or anything of that kind to the Guardians, as he presumed they would make their own arrangements with Miss Twist.

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- _ SION ERS. WATERLOO HOUSE, dx. An adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- 'goners was held in the Board-room. Town Hall, on Thursday wvening, for the purpose of considering the following reso- lution which was recommended for approval by the Proper- ties Committee :—" That the surveyor be instructed to review the valuation of Waterloo House, the Commissioners' present offices, the Market cottages, and the town's yard; and that advertisements be inserted in the following news- papers, viz., Runcorn Examiner, Runcorn Guardian, Liver- pee Deily Post, and Manchester Guardian, inviting tenders for the several properties, the Commissioners not being ' bound to accept the highest tender." In the absence of the• chairman kDr. Steele) Mr. Thomas Norman was voted to the chair; and there were also present, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. P. Briscoe, W. Handley, Meadowcroft, Shaw, Lake, J. J. Speakman, P. Speakman, Williams, Fisher, W. Brooks (secretary), and Barker (surveyor). Mr. LAKE, as chairman of the committee, moved the adoption of the resolution, and in doing so said some of the members of the committee wished for the review of the valuation of the property because they thought it rather high. The properties of the Board were at present so scat- tered that the committee considered it would be an advan- tage to dispose of them, and erect some building in a central part of the town, of such a character as would be worthy of the public offices, and Capable of accommodating the Free Library and every other office connected with the govern- ment of the town. It was thought the sale of the property Would realise a sufficient amount of money to erect or pur- chase the building required. If they could not sell the pro- perty some other resolution could be adopted, but he thought the course recommended a desirable one. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded the resolution. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN asked what was the ultimate object of this proceeding; and how much was it going to cost. The ISard had no money to spare. (A laugh.) The CHAIRMAN Oi.tjf'rved that it was at piesent only intended to advertise for tem.4.frs• Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN was unable t's: sle the use of going to I the expense of advertit;.7, th 'object I Ne'een --ere was no re. rew. Suppose the Board removed to Waterloo House was too large for them, and they could not calculate upon the other public offices becoming tenanted, nor in any build- ing the Board might erect. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Labe had made no reference to removing to Waterloo House. The cost of advertising could not possibly be much, and if they did not make an attempt to dispose of the property, what were they going to do with ? if they could sell all the property, with the exception Of Waterloo loose, let the Boaid retrieve there. At present Waterloo House was a "white elephant," and it was impera- tive that action should be taken. Mr. W. HANDLEY said he thought Mr. Lake in his Opening remarks gave the best possible reason why they should not accede to the request of the Committee. Mr. Lake stated that the valuation of the 'property was higher than it could be expected to realise at the present time, and therefore he (Mr. Handley) asked why should the Board sell it if they could not get the price which it was worth. It was a serious step they were asked to take. If there was no ultimate aim in disposing of the property, it was a waste of money to ask anyone to send in tenders; the Board ought not to advertise until they seriously meant to sell, for the expense of doing so would be considerably more than the £5 men- tioned. He saw several reasons why they should not attempt to part with the property. They should not attempt to part with Waterloo House, because it was granted that they could nOt get the price the Beard paid for it. It was a " white elephant," and like most of them, it was very expensive keeping unless they had something for it to do, and the longer they kept it in that state the more expensive it was likely to become. With regard to the present Com- missioners offices, seeing that the Commissioners never built them, or expended a shilling in purchasing them, he thought they would be going beyond their moral right, dis- regarding the legal question, unless they took the ratepayers into their confidence, because the ratepayers took them for a different purpose, but had allowed the Commissioners the free use of them for 30 years. Mr. SHAW: May I ask what the original purpose was? Mr. HANDLE!: It was for the use of the Board of Sur- veyors, who were superseded by a special Act of Parliament being obtained. Mr. SHAW: That is drawing it very fine. Mr. HANDLEY said it was perfectly true. The Commis- sioners had never yet provided themselves offices, and the town could have used the present offices for the overseers as they were built for that purpose, but the overseers took another place simply for the convenience of the Commis- sioners and nothing else. The CHAIRMAN : How is it this question has never been raised? Mr. HANDLE!: 1 cannot tell you. It is not for me to say; but there is the fact. So far as I have been able to discover this building was never turned over to the Com- missioners. I don't know whether any title deeds were tamed over for it, but I do know that the title deeds of the town's yard were not. A 111331113 ER: I think this is a subject for the committee. Mr. HANDLEY said he was not afraid of it going to the public—not at all. Considering the circumstances he bad narrated, he thought on moral gtounds the Board ought not to part with the Commissioners' offices without taking the atepayers into their confidence. Then again' with regard to the Market Cottages, he thought they werebringinglin a revenue of about £3O a year, which helped the Board very much in maintaining the Market. The SURVEYOR remarkea that the cottages brought in £27 a year. Mr. HANDLEY (continuing) said in these matters the Board must certainly look ahead. If at any future time they wished to extend the Market they would have the ground if they retained the cottages, and they would be foolish if they told a piece of freehold land in the'centre af the town. The town's yard, too, was not acquired by the Commissioners, and its value would increase in the next 20 yews, and he thought they had much better not sell the property he had named; he would rather go in for selling 'Waterloo House, although there was no chance of at pre- sent gifting the amount expended upon it. He suggested that the matter be deferred for 12 months, and utilise the properties in the meantime, thinking very seriously over the ,question. Mr. SHAW remarked that the members had a duty they .were obliged to carry out—that was, they had to provide accommodation somewhere or other for the Public Library. It must be clear to everyone that the present habitation of the Library was a temporary one. It was utterly impossible to expect that the opening of the Library on only two nights a week was a state of things which could continue long, because if it did, it meant the early closing of the in- stitution, for while they had the facilities in one sense in the shape of books, they had not facilities for using then except on two evenings in each week. He did not know whether it had struck many members, but it had struck him that that place was unsuited for the library. So far as position went it was all that could be desired ; it was central; but any gentleman sitting at that Board ought to have found out before this that at times it was difficult to carry on business through the noise in the street. That was one great objection to that place being devoted for the purpose of the library, which oughtio be further from the main thoroughfare. The next serious objection was that the rooms were entirely unsuited, and never could be made suitable. All the work had to go on in one room. To him the principal reason why something-should be done with the properties of the Board was that they had to provide ac- commodation for the library. The ratepayers, too, were asking for more accommodation; what was the Board going to do? Mr. Handley had raisd some peculiar objections which really were not objections, and did not prevent the Board in any way from dealing with this property or any other property of the Board. It was all the ratepayers pro- perty, and as their representatives-they were perfectly at liberty to deal with it. It seemed to be the general opinion that the Board was forced to do something in the matter, and they had that-night to consider what was to be done. ,Under present circumstances they ought not to do anything rashly, or for the purpose merely of disposing of the pro- perty. The question of consolidating the various offices of the town, and the providieg of proper provision, there or elsewhere, for the library was a very proper one. In his opinion it would be wise to see if they could not dispose of these properties so that they might get a place that would • answer all the purposes they desired. He should certainly • 'vote for the resolution. The CHAIRMAN observed that Dr. Steele had intimated that. when this question was discussed he would propose that the resolution, passed at a ratepayers' meeting in March, asking for the full use of the Commissioners offices and Board-room for the Free Library be considered. He (Mr. Norman) of course could not tell what Dr. Steele would have hadto say on the subject. Mr. MRLDOWCROFT wished to know if the Board had decided to-leave those offices; if the yard at Delph Bridge was valneleas and useless; or could they End some building _more convenient for the purpose; and were they satisfied that Waterloo House was unsuited for the purpose of the 'Board. Otherwise there was no cause to advertise. They .ought to. consider how they were going to replace all the pro- perty which -was valued at nearly £5,000. Was it for a m.oment tabs.supposed that the ratepayers would sanction ao expenditure-of £5,000 to provide splendid offices for the Commissioners, when they already complaited of being hea,vily taxed. The chairman of the Finance Committee hadstated there were no spare funds, and the expense of ..advertiaing was of serious moment to him—(laughter)— and one he was anxious should be avoided. Mr. StitAw observed that the ratepayers were meet anxious Athat,the Board shou:d leave that place, and spend as much money as they thought proper. Mr. MF.A.uowcuovr said be should like to hear some areas= why all this property was to be sold, and what object *was to begaised, and where they would obtain the accom- es:lodation. Mr. ilinsw said he could tell where they iaould get good accommodation, bat he thought it would be very unwise to do so until they knew what sum they could get for this

property. Dr. .I.€l:lorcur.r., said he aympathised with the remarks of Mr. Shaw with respect to provision for the -Public Library. and he had stated the matter so plainly that it was not his (the speaker's) intention to go over that particular ground, but it seemed to him that there had been a disposi- 9.ion to put aside the observations of Mr. Handley without really answering them. There was no doubt that the rights in the building they were occupying bad never been con- veyed from the ratepayers to the Commissioners as tru Mr. SAW: If what you say is true, it would be fatal. The ratepayers save no authority to convey. Mr. MeDovoiL.T., I If Jam touching on dangerous ground, i 1 mention uot mention it.
[stem

Mr. Suave: Where are your titles? Dr. McDowell.: That is what I want to know. Mr. SHAW said the ratepayers never did convey anything to their representatives, and never could do. The thing was ridicalous. Dr. MCDOUGLLL: The question involves a much more serious principle than that. He went on to say that befote the Board could actually dispose of the property, it would be necessary, iii his opinion to take a vote of the ratepayers. The CHAIRMAN bserved that the Commissioners had already conveyed a portion of land belonging to that building. Mr. SHAW: And could convey it all to-morrow. Mr. LAKE inquired if there was a deed of trust. Mr. HANDLE : No, Itelieve not. (Laughter.) Mr. Snew : It was always in the hands of the ratepayers. Mr. HANDLEY: It was built for the purposes of the surveyors. _ Dr. AlcDougaet, said the Board ought not to confine their views to the legal aspect of the question ; they had a perfect right to look at it from all points of view, even the moral aspect. The ratepayers in public meeting assembled had passed a resolution asking for the use of the public offices, and it seemed to him that the Board could not ignore that resolution. Referring to Mill Brow, Dr. McDougall said that land, which was purchased for a small sum of money, was much more valuable now, and there was a time coming when the Commissioners would have to be not only their own .scavengers, but empty the ashpits as well, for if the population of the town increased in the same ratio during the next decade as it had the last, it would pay the Com- missioners to do the work themselves rather than transfer it to a contractor. He failed to see where the Commissioners were to get a suitable place for all the purposes they I re- quired. It must be apparent to everyone to what building Mr. Shaw was referring as suitable, but there was not a single room in that building equal to the room in which they were assembled ; and it was neither suitable for the purposes of the Board nor of the Library. Then there was the further point,7that if they concentrated all the depart- ments of the Board under one roof, With the nuisance pro- ducing peraphernalia, it would be rather an inconvn'lrl:t than otherwise. He tkought it would be infinitely better if the committee would come .f9fward and say they Would re- commend a new building to h,t erected suitable for the pul. pvra Of.. the .BOU, but from what Mr. Shaw said it •wae fitly lair to infer that the committee had a building in view which they could purchase. Mr. SHAW: Nay, doctor. Mr. LAKE remarked that the committee was in, laVour of erecting a new building. Dr. MCDOUGALL said if they went in ;or a new building he would vote for it. He hoped lake would withdraw eger brought forward at some the resolution, and have the lea future time with a sche 11.; fot erecting, with the £4,500 Mr. Lake had 7.-draateed the Board would get for the property, A new building worthy of the town, and wortby of the objects they bad in view. Mr. LAKE, as mover of the resolution, replied to the various arguments, and observed that the committee did not think Waterleo House quite the position for the public offices of the town. (Hear, hear,) The committee did not propose to spend any more money than was realised by the sale; but they could not bring forward a scheme, as they were only asked to report on the properties. He did not see his way to withdraw the resolution, which was given him to propose at that meeting, and he must leave it with the Board to deal with, 'and if they thought fit erect a new building. Dr. MCDOUGALL : t shall go in for that. The CHAIRMAN said that room was too small for the Library, and one of two things they must do—either erect a new build- ing or remove to Waterloo House,but the cost of altering that house would be very great. With reference to the town's- yard, he knew it cost the Board a great deal more for scav- enging, Sze. when they did it themselves—(Dr. McDougall: Query.)—than it had cost them since—(hear, hear)—and was never done so well. The cottages, too would never be of any use to the market as there was a public road between them, and at present they were doing the Board no good. There were always needing repair. Dr. McDorgem.: How much have they cost in repairs for the last few years, Mr. Barker? Mr. BARKER: Not much. (Laughter.) Mr. MEADOWCROFT: They are paying seven per cent. After a little further discussion Dr. McDougeit pro- posed an amendment that the recommendation be referred back to the Committee. Mr. BRISCOE seconded the motion, which was carried by five votes to four. Mr. Meadowcroft and Mr. Lake abstained from voting. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN PUBLIC LIBRARY.

The monthly meeting of the Committee was held at the Public Offices, the Rev. Canon Barclay presiding. There were also present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Frith, Briscoe, Handley, Riley, Brookes (secretary) and Jones (librarian). A. letter was read from Mr. Cowell, Chief Librarian of the Liverpool Free Public Library, stating that the committee of that isstitution having granted a copy of their catalogue to the Runcorn Library, he had great pleasure in notifying that the same had been forwarded. The following had also been received :—" Sandyknowe, Wavertree, Liverpool, July 21st, 1882. Dear sir,—l have instructed my publisher, Mr. Walmsley, to forward to yeur address a copy of my. Memorials of Liverpool' (2nd edition, 2 vols., 8vo.) for presentation to your Free Public Library, which I trust is proceeding satisfactorily. With kind remembrances to all friends, I remain y ours truly, J. A. PICTON. William Brookes, Esq." The secretary was instructed to acknowledge receipt of the communications, and to convey to the donors' the thanks of the committee. It was unanimously agreed that the thanks of the committee be given to Mr. John Simpson for having so cordially received and entertained Sir James Picton on the occasion of the recent demonstration. The Librarian reported that 372 persons had signed the necessary forms, and had become borrowers, of whom 40 were females. The number of volumes issued from July 11th to 25th was 753, an average. of 150 per day, and were classified as follows :—A. Theology, 24; B. Philosophy, ckc., 8; C. Science, 38; D. History, travel, ezc., 157; E. Poetry, 12; F. Fiction, 474; G. Miscellaneous, 40. He also reported cash received for borrower's tickets, £3 is. fid.; for catalogues, £2 18s. 6d.; total, £6.

div.head: ..----.11.1i..--.
div.p: PARE'S I B NKING COMPANY, LIMITED. HALF-YEARLY MEETING.

The half-yearly meeting was held at the Bank, yesterday, under the presidency of Mr. J. Fenton Greenall, deputy chairman. There were also present the following:— Directors: Lord Delamere, Sir G. Greenall, Sir Thomas G. Frost, Colonel Gamble, Messrs. P. Stubs, E. Greenall, T. P. Parr, N. Eckersley, J. Pearson, A. Hewlett, and John Thompson; shareholders: Messrs. Samuel Holden, H. B. Jackson, A. Mackie, W. Tipping, Jactes Marson, C. Broad- bent, W. Owen' jun., R. Pierpoint, Dr. Beaman, Dr. Lester, J. Dun -(general manager), J. Murray (secretary), Sze. Mr. Dux read the following report :

The directors have had before them the audited balance sheet of the Bank at the 30th June, 1882, and they beg to report that the profits of the half-year, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, hays been satisfactory. The directors recormnend that there be now declared for the half-year ending 30th June. 1882. an interim dividend at the rate of 215 perterft. per annum, free of income tax, amd payable on and after 4th August. After providing for this dividend there remains a con- siderable balance, which is carried forward to ncxt account. The position and prospects of the business continue to be in L every way satisfactory.

The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN, after apologising for the absence of Mr. Parr, the chairman, who he-stated was much better, observed that he was happy to be able to say in the words of the report, words which might be 'considered stereotyped, the position and prospects of the bank continued to be in every way satisfactory. 'Notwithstanding the depression in trade, notwithstanding the low rates of interest, the profits the directors had made this half year had been very satisfactory, and after providing for all bad and-doubt- ful debts, they had carried forward to next half year's account, a considerable balance. There was an inzrease in the money lodged in the bank, a considerable increase in the, number of accounts opened, an increase in the number of-shareholders, and the money which the directors had at call on notice they considered ample to meet any emergency. He was sorry not to be able to say that trade was better. He believe that every branch of business was more or lass in a depressed state. It had been -.so, as they were aware, for a long time past, and he very much feared the complications in Egypt would not mend matters. At the same time they could only hope-that the cloud of depression and anxiety which at present hung over us might soon give place to brighter c'ouds, and that peace, prosperity, and plenty might i succeed. He moved the adoption of the report. Sir GILBERT GREENALL seconded the motion, which was carried. LordiDELAMERE moved "that as recommended by the directors an interim dividend at the rate of 15 per cent, per annum, free of income tax, be now declared payable on and , after the ,Ith August at the bank, or any of its branches, or by Messrs. Glyn, Mills, Currie, and Co., London!' Mr. C. BROADBENT, in secotiding..said he •was,very sorry to hear the very discouraging account ,of the state of trade which the Chairman had given. At the same time they were aware that the manufacturing induotries were for the most part busy, that there was a good demand for ,labour, , that the accounts of pauperism of the,country showed that , there were fewer poor people receiving relief than ,usual, that generally there were indications that the workpeople of the country were very fully employed, and that the .ten- dency of wages was to rise, so that he hoped they need.not be discouraged as regarded the prospects of •trade. The motion was carried. Mr. Mariam; proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and

Mr. A. Ma.aaig, in seconding the proposition,.said he had no doubt, as Mr. Broadbent had said, that trade was in a better condition throughout the country than it had been for some time—to say the least it showed elements of recovery, and the great thing we now wanted was a pletszons harvest. (Hear, hear.) The proposition having been ogreel to, The DEPUTY-CHAIRMAN, in acknowledging tke ompli- malt, said he could only say that Le took means to gain the information which he hld given them respecting the state of trade, and he only hoped he had been misinformed. Th.a meeting then terminated.
The annual meeting of the Licensing Committee of the borongh, for the purpose of hearing and granting appli- cations for liceneee, will be held on the ;01 September.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 29, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 29, 1882.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.. • Mr. 7 Blackhurst presided at the fortnightly meeting on Wednesday. There were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Darbyshire, Burn Marsh, Cald- well, Longshaw, Brown, Greenall, Hunt, Burn, Taylor, Greening, Bonnell, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). Mr. Basil Caine Local Government Board inspector, was also present.
• FINANCIAL. The CLERK said he had recived Mr. Basil Caine's state-

ment of pauperism and expenditure during the past year. The Board would remember that a year ago he (the clerk) called attention to the extraordinary difference betneen the amount of the total cost of relief in the preTious year, and

that collected from the relatives of the persons who were re- lieved. He showed the Board that it was largely in excess of the total in the whole of Mr. Caine's district. He found the total cost of relief for Lancashire for the year ending Lady Day 1882 was £383,376, and the total sum collected from the relatives was £22,751, or a little over 5 per cent. On looking at he state of the Unions near them he found that in Liverpool the cost of relief was £45,887, of which £1,157 was collected, or 2i per cent.; West Derby, £39,701, collected £1,255, or 3.8 per cent.; Wigan, £l3 831, collected £438; and Warrington £8,468, collected £1,242, or 15 per cent. (Hear, hear.) If they took from the latter amount £5OO, the sum be collected, they would give Mr. Shearer credit for collecting 10 per cent. of indoor and outdoor relief within the year, as against 21- and 3 per cent. in other
Unions. Mr Fluowx said that showed the wisdom of appointing good officers. The CLERK: It shows that if a department and the clerk work together comfortably it must be for the good of the Union. _ _ _

Major CARTWRIGHT observed that no doubt it was a very flattering statement, but the system was in its infancy. These collections had been constantly insisted upon, and credit was due to the Board as well as to Mr. Shearer. , The CLERK: Credit is due all round. 'Major UARTUTstated ,tf.Tt the killCcefsS of their system had led other Unions to adopt it. THE STATE OF THE SCHOOLS. The Schools' Committee book contained the report, of Mr. H. Stevens sub-inspector, that he visite I the establ•sh- ment on the 14th inst. It was in good order, conside, inn s difficulties arising from the material fOrMIIV 1",:d yard' sur- face. The wa,ll house acCotrauod-tion was Very limited, but he presumed that these promises would not be occupied much longer. Tie was curry to learn that there had los•en a good deal of skin disease lattly among the child. en ; the apnearance of those at school was satisfactory.—lt was resolved that adver- tisements be inserted in the local new papers for tenders for 50 bedsteads according to sample at the Barracks already approved by the Board ; also that a committee be appointed to examine the furniture and goods at the Barracks, to consider what por- tion thereof were suitable for use at the new schools, and that such committee consist of Messrs. Brown, Caldwell, Darbyshire, and the Rev J. Yonge. The commit tee regretted to find that In opposttion to the practise pursued with regard to the washing of a portion of the larger aniclei from 1880, and to the direc tious of the Board of Guarditns thereon. such articles were still sentback to the Barracks and washed there. The com- mittee repeated their complaint, and again called attention to former molutions he -eon. On the proposition of Mr. BROWN, secolnded by Mr. GREENALL, the minutes were confirmed.

THE HOUSE COMMITTEE AND THEIR MINUTES-A " REFLECTION " UPON A MEMBER. On the minutes of the House Committee coming before the Chairman, he remarked that there was one minute which be thought ought not to be read, as it reflected upon _ _

a member of the Board. Mr. BROWN asked if Mr. Longshaw had received a copy of the minutes. Mr. LONGSHAW stated be had not, but had received a letter. Mr. BROWN therefore moved, and Mr. DARBYSHIRE seconded, that the minute be not read, the latter remarking that it was unusual to enter a minute about any member without that member had been informed of it, or furnished with a copy of it. Major CARTwRIGHT said he objected to that, and be should eertainly move an amendment, because the course suggested was one that had never been adopted since he had been a member of the Board. (Hear, hear.) The proper course to take, as the Clerk knew, if the minute was not passed, was to refer it back to the House Committee. It was very objectionable indeed to the chairman and the committee of that House, to have reflections made upon them and their management, because he always found that the reporters, who sat behind him, were very ready to report anything that was detrimental to the management of the House. He was very much surprised that they reported portion of a speech made at the last meeting by Mr. Langshaw, which he would read to show why the minutes ought to be read, and if the members liked to refer to the clerk after his remarks, he thought the clerk would advise them that it was only fair. Mr. LONGSIIAW : Will you be kind enough to read Mr. Greening's speech first? Major CARIWRIGHT : It is this: "Mr. Longshaw. The machinery and everything connected with this House is a perfect disgrace to the Rouse Committee, the Master, and everyone concerned." Well, now, that is very strong language, and it is language a gentleman ought to be cautions about using, more especially— Mr. LONGSHAW : Read Mr. Greening's speech before you read mine. Major CARTWRIGHT : I verily believe that gentleman has not visited this House, although he has been a member of the committee, and he is totally incapable of judging. Mr. Loalustaw : Will you allow me Major Canewnaum : I will allow you; in the meantime don't get excited. (Laughter.) You allow your temper to have power over you. It is so with all of us. Mr. Longshaw went on to say:" It is a perfect disgrace to the borough, and the sooner the House Committee do their own work properly, and say nothing about other people and shut their mouths the better." To the latter portion he had no objec- tion, but he bad a strong objectioa to the other remarks, because everybody did not know even the character of Mr. Longsbaw—how very irritable he was someti-,ues when he said things he was sorry for afterwards. These remarks went forth to the public, and one member said he had been stopped several times in the streets, and been asked whether the condition of things was as st tted. He thought it was only fair to the House Committee and officials connected with the House that such reports should not go the public without being contradicted. He would leave it to any disinterested person who would even read that minute privately, whether there was anything wrong in entering it on the book. He had given the Board the essence of the minute, and there- fore he called upon them, in fairness to him and the officials connected with that establishment, to pees the:minute, anti whatever remarks Mr. Longshaw might make in justifica- tion he would be very glad to hear. He did not want to place Mr. Longsh aw in an awkward position at all. Had he said anything at that Board reflecting upon any gentle- man he would have been the first to get up and "eat the leek," as it was commonly termed. He hoped the chairman, in fairness to the committee and everyone connected with the establ;shment, and for the honour of the Board, would read the minutes, becauee that was the first time in his experience a motion of that kind haa been proposed. Mr. BROWN said he made his motion upon the statement of the chairman, who said that upon the book there was a minute which reflected unfavourably or to the discredit of a member of that Board, and that he had not been officially advised of it. Upon that representation he had great pleasure in moving his resolution, and he thought it was only fair, honourable, courteous— Mr. BURN rose to a point of order, and said the reason why the matter came before the committee was because it sva)i reported in the newspapers. He thought under the circumstances they could not do other than read the minutes, and if Mr. Brown liked to move that the minute be referred back to the committee he could do so. He thought the chairman was bound in honour to read every minute of the committee to be disposed of as they thought best. Mr. BROWN said he based his proposition on the remarks of the chairman. Mr. WOOLFALL : The remarks were-uncalled for. The CHAIRMAN said there were so many gentlemen who knew better than be how to conduct the business that it would be better for them to come and take his place. It,sfas most unfortunate that, at every meeting they had they had these disputes 'occupying the attention of the Board, and gentlemen making use of language that they ought not to do. He did not see very much difference between Mr. Longshaw and other members of the Board. A letter was then handed to the chairman, and Major CARiIwRIGHT said they bad nothing whatever to do with any private letter any officer ef the Board might have written to an individual Guardian. He knew nothing of it beyond the fact that it had been written. The CLERK: Mr. Longshaw hands the letter in. He afterwards remarked that he had sat many years at that Board and never remembered any committee to pass censure upon a Guardian for having expressed an opinion, however objectionable that -opinion might be, in the course of the debate. Ma.jor CanTwutuarz : This is totally. uncalled for. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE never remembered sad_ a minute being put on the books befcre, and that was the .reason why he seconded the motion that it be not read. Mr. WOOLFALL : You don't know what theanintue is. Mr. DAREYSHIRE said he well remeinbered, the day when Mr. Longshaw made the remarks in question. Mr. Long- shasv asked the chairmanif he would be in order_in replying to Mr. Greening, and he hesitated whether he should reply or not; but he well remembered the Mayor saying-0 let the old fellow speak, he can't do much harm." Major CARTWRIGHT: I-totally object to that. .Lrise to a point of order. Mr. DARBYSHIRE: Wait a minute. Let me finish. Major CARTWRIGHT : He ...said I said so and so, end I never said it. Mr. DevaysurnE : I remember It perfectly well. Heasot only said it once but twice. He .said "Let the old fellcw speak." Major CAt.TwRIGHT : I did not,cali him an "old fellow:" fi called him an old gentleman. Mr. DAREWIRE said the Chairman allowed Mr. Long- shaw to make the remarks, and he thow,ht the Board should now support Mr. Longshaw even if he was wrong in his judgment that there was certain neglect. He had a right as a member of the ,Board to call attention to any neglect to hydrants. What M. Longshaw said was that the water pipes had been allowed to corrode, and were In such a state that they could not be used to put a fire out if necessary. and all he said was that it showed neglect that things were allowed to be in such z condition that nothing could be done in case of emergency. If a member of the Board was not to be protected when he said things in that House were being neglected, the business could not be carried in that efficient and business-like manner which it ought to be. .48 be bad never leen mintete put so OP House Committee's

books reflecting upon a member of the Board without that member being apprised of it, he seconded Mr. Brown's pro- position that it be not read. Mr. CAINE, on being appealed to, said it was a book that was directed to be kept by order of the Local Government Board. It was not to be supposed that those who had written nothing knew what was to come, and the entries in that book for the day ought to be read before the Board. There they would see an entry of the private opinion of individual Guardians that ought never to have been entered at all, but let it be read and then dealt with. He must say the book was never intended to contain 'minutes of that character, and if his jUdgment were asked he should dis- tinctly say that if any member had anything to say he ought not to put it in that book but to get up and say it before the Guardians. (Hear, hear.) The CLERK: Then on that advice I will read the
minutes? The CHAIRMAN: Yes. The CLERK then read the minutes which stated that Mrs.
Mackie reported that she was unable to do the washing of the Barracks at the House; also that the whole of the _ _

washing could be done with ease at the Barracks with their present staff. She added that it was not her duty accord- ing to her appointment to do their work. The Committee recommended that the question should be submitted to the Local Government Board for their decision to know whose duty it was. The

committee regretted exceedingly to refer to the reported speech of Mr. Longshaw, a member of the Board, They regarded it as an unwarrantable attack upon themselves, the master, matron, and other officers of the House. They were unanimously of opinion that Mr. Longshaw should be called upon to apologise or to substantiate the charges. Major CARTWRIGHT moved the confirmation of the minutes, and referring to the first minute said the Barracks Com- mittee appeared determined to insist upon the washing being done at the Workhouse, whether it could be done or not. He pointed out that for the last two or three weeks it had been satisfactorily done at the Barracks, and for aught he knew it could be done as easily there, with the present staff, with- out incucTing one farthing of expense. It was well known to the School Cc;rilnallte; tbat the Workhouse machinery was out of order, and that thcy I.lad hard work to get thlonrill the waott- g for tiA 111„emb"o... of the School Committee would or.ly visit the Laouse and see what there was to be done, they would never support such a resolution as had been passed. He did not agree with Mr. Caine's remarks. It was only his opinion. He was not a member of the House Committee, and therefore he did not feel anything respecting what was said and reported. There was nothing unusual or unfair in the second minute, and, as be had said laefore, Mr. Longshaw ought to have an opportunity of giv- ing his reason for using the expressions he did. Mr. WooLrara. seconded the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Bnowsr, in supporting the minutes, said he held that if they were to have proper discipline and proper respect paid by the officials of the Union the orders and directions of the Board should be supreme. If there were only two courses open, and the Board decided upon a certain course, he held it was only a right that that decision should be maintained. He was desirous they should have the matter settle'], as he was tired of these constant bickerings. Mr. DARBYSHIRE proceeded to review the state of affairs, and expressed a wish than an enquiry would be made. He concluded by moving that the House Committee's minutes be confirmed with the exception of that reflecting upon Mr. Longshaw. Mr. MARSH seconded the amendment. The CHAIRMAN said it was most unfortunate that this bone of contention should crop up just at the last moment. The small portion of washing from the Barracks had been done at the Workhouse without any complaint, but at the last moment there was all this confusion about the washing of the few articles. The only articles sent to the Workhouse were sheets and blankets which they had no convenience to wash at the Barracks. It had been stated by the House Committee that Mrs. Mackey bad not had time, but he was at a loss to understand how the matron could go to the Barracks for a whole day, and yet had not time to do the washing at the Workhouse. It appeared to him to be obstinate obstruction on the part of the House Committee, but, however, it remained entirely with the members whether they would allow the minutes of the Board, which had been passed more than once or twice to be over-ridden by the action of two or three members of the House Com- mittee. That was the point. (Hear, hear.) Were the Board to rule or two or three members of the House Com- mittee? (Cries of "the Board.") Mr. BURN supported the minutes bnause he thought it was quite time the matter was settled. He was sorry it had arisen, but it was the last straw that seemed to have broken the camel's back. They courted enquiry, and if there was no convenience for washing at the new schools it would settle the question. Mr. DARHYSHIRE said it was at first the intention of the Building Committee to have the washing of the heavy articles for the schools done at the Workhouse, but they had since sent plans of washhouses to the Local Government Board for approval. The CHAIRMAN then asked Mr. Caine whether the master was bound to obey the orders and resolutions of the Board or the orders of the House Committee when those orders clashed. Mr. CAINE remarked that there could be no difficulty in answering a general question of that kind. The whole Board were supreme, and were supreme over the committee themselves. (Hear, hear.) The committee could only make certain recommendations. The Board were not only supreme over the committee, but over all the officers of the Workhouse and schools; the business of the Union could not be conducted unless they were so. He expressed the hope that the new schools would soon be opened as it would be the means of obviating these misunderstandings—he was almost afraid he might say disagreements—which must be very unpleasant to the officers, some of whom did not know , who to look to and obey. Referring to the subject under discussion, he hoped it would terminate in that room that morning, and that they would start afresh when they got to the new establishment. Mr. Bosr.s.sra. said he would be very sorry if the matter went to the Local Government Board. The constant quib- bling had prevented the business of the ratepayers being carried on, and was kept up simply for the purpose of enabling members to make sensational speeches to go forth to the public. (Hcar, hear.) The amendment was then put to the vote, and 10 mem- bers voted in favour of it and 2 against. The amended minutes were afterwards adopted. The Clerk was directed to lay the whole of the circum- stances regarding the washing difficulty before the Local Government Board, and submit the letter to the Board at their next meeting. The CHAIRMAN : That will be a fortnight hence. The CLERK : It will; but the longer you put it off the better.
VAGRANTS' VERACITY.

The CHAIRMAN drew attention to the case of four tramps, who stated before the magistrates last week that they had been refused admission to the Workhouse. Mr. CURRY, the porter, was called before the Board, and he stated that on the night Of the 19th inst. he was stand- ing at the gate at a quarter past 10 o'clock when -four men came up. On receiving their tickets he looked at the time they were issued and saw it was nine o'clock. He questioned each of them as to where they had been since the tickets were issued, and three of them said they had been looking for a man to see if they could get the price of a night's lodging. The fourth man said he should come whenever he chose, and he told him he should not admit him and he might go about his business. The three others then said if the man did not go in they would not, and he told them to go to the magistrates and tell them he refused to admit them. They then went away. When befor the magistrates the men said that he tore up the tickets, but he went to Captain Litton's mill and took the tickets, which were not torn up. He showed Captain Litton his regula- tions, and after reading them the Captain said he was per- fectly satisfied be (the porter) had done his duty, and if he bad known that at the time he would have given the men seven days each for telling lies. The CHAIRM&N thought the explanation satisfactory, a remark in which the other members concurred.
CONCERTS AT THE wommor SE. The CLERE read the following letter which had been addressed to Chairman :

5, Museum-street, Warrington, 20th July, 1882.—Dear As you may be already aware the Warrington Kyrie Sm:ety has sat on foot A series of concerts at the Workhouse, which have been mirth appreciated by the inmates, and it is proposed to continue these concerts monthly. Up to the presenbthe society has hired a.planoforte for the use of the performers at 7s. 6d. a night, but the state of our finances will not permit,us to expend that amount on each concert. There is, in fact, only a nominal subscription to cover the expense of printing, Postage, and the like, and the members have other hims to pursue, though they are most anxious to keep up the performances at the Workhouse. Under these circura3tances, I beg to ioquire, on behalf of the society, whether the Board of Guardians would be disposed to,meet us by authorising, either directly or through their House Committee, the purchase of a rultaVe piano out of any avaliable fund, such instrument to be kept in the large rooria at the Workhouse, taivier the charge of the Master, and to he primarily for use at the society's conc&t. shall esteem it a favour if you will kindly bring this letter before the Board at their next meeting, .as our committee are pledged to give another concert in August, and hope that some arrangement may be come to such as I have ventured to sug- gest.—Yours faithfully WALTER D. THIIIRcAId, Hon. Secretary, Warrington Kyrie Society. The CLERK : We have no fupd you can apply for that purpose. The CITAIRMANT Raid he,knew nothing about the concerts, and did not know who had given permiseim for them to be held monthly.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.

Alderman Davies presided at a meeting of this Chamber, held at Bewsey Chambers, on Monday afternoon. There were also present—Messrs. Monks, Rigby, Edelsten, Jolly, Platt, Kean, Robinson, Carson, Morris, Woods, Owen, and A. Bennett (assistant secretary). THE LATE 'MR. ARTINGSTALL'S REPRESENTATIVES AND THE

div.head: CHAMBER.
div.p: CHAMBER.

The President read the following letter from the repre- sentatives of the late Mr. Artingstall, dated 11th inst. : "Dear Sir,—We are duly in receipt of yours of yesterday, handing to us copy of resolution passed at your meeting with reference to the death of Mr. Artingstall, for which we are obliged. We thank you for your kind invitation to be- come members of your Council, but at present we feel we should not have the time at our disposal to attend to it. We note your remark respecting the portrait, and will see what can be done when we get matters something like straight.—Yours truly, for G. Artingstall and Company, J. WARBURTON.

div.head: WIRE GAUGE.
div.p: THE WIRE GAUGE.

The PRESIDENT said on reference to the minutes it would be found that the Board of Trade invited the Chamber to inspect and consider the standard wire gauge which they were about to adopt, unless they heard something to con- trovert it, and the result bad been that the proposed standard of the Bard of Trade not meeting with the wishes of the Warrington manufacturers, they were invited to appoint a committee with a view to clearly representing to the Board of Trade what they considered would be a desirable wire gauge. He dared say Mr. Monks, as chairman of that committee, would be able to make a report to them on the matter. Mr. MONKS said the committee at their last meeting but one it was thought better to defer the matter until the master wire-drawers bad fairly considered it. Mr. Carson and Mr. Morris reported that day that the masters had finally aiopted a wire gauge as expressed in decimals of an inch in the table which had been handed to the secretary, and the sub-committee had considered and adopted it, recommending that the Warrington chamtp3r 9! Commerce §bould submit it to the noardof Trade as the standard in lieu of tht BOard of Trade gauge. There was a variation id many of the sizes of the latter gauge, but the master wire drawers' gauge would, he thought, very fairly meet the difficulty. Mr. JOLLEY remarked that this seemed to be a simple matter, but it was really a very serious one. If the standard were changed there would be a vast amount of property in the shape of gauges rendered useless, but he presumed that was only a secondary consideration if they could obtain an universal standard, the want of which had been long felt. Mr. MONKS said at present there were a dozen different gauges, and what they required was an universal one, and he thought the Board of Trade in their decision would fully consider the various trades.

div.head: MANCHESTER TIDAL NAVIGATION SCHEME.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER TIDAL NAVIGATION SCHEME.

The PRESIDENT said the members were aware that at the last meeting they memorialised the Board of Trade not to allow the Vyrnwy aqueduct pipes to be laid under the Mersey without giving the chamber, as representing War- rington commercial interests, notice, and asking them to let the pipes be laid at such a depth as would not interfere with any proposed improved navigation of the river. The reply, which was very satisfactory, was as follows:- 18th July, 1880.—The Liverpool Corporation Water Works Act, 1880.—Sir,—In reply to the memorial addressed to the President, dated the 10th instant, and slinea by you on behalf of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, I am directed by the Board of Trade to acquaint you that whenever any application is received by them to prescribe, in pursuance of section 16 of the above Act, the depth at which the aqueduct referred to in that section shall be laid under the bed of the river Mersey, the Board of trade will consider the representations of the Warring- ton Chamber of Commerce, and, if necessary, give them an opportunity of further stating their view upon the subject. No such application has been yet received at this office.—l am, Ac., C. Osom TREVOR. There was nothing more except that he thought he might report to the Chamber that the progress of the scheme in Manchester was very satisfactory. Every meeting that he had had the pleasure to attend had been stronger than any previous meeting. Mr, Momts : In what respect? The PRESIDENT replied that it was stronger both pecu- niarily and representatively. Since the last meeting of the Chamber two very able men had bzen fully instructed to report as to the feasibility of the scheme, and the provisonal committee would be prepared to move in the matter from a common _sense point of view on receiving the report of these engineers as to the feasibility or unfeasibility of the scheme. The mem- bers would observe that the communication they bad received from the Board of Trade invited their personal appearance whenever the application for the laying of the aqueduct was discussed, and Ist asked the Chamber to authorise a deputa- tion to wait upon the Board of Trade at the proper time to represent the interests of that Chamber and Warrington generally as to the interference of the navigation by the Tyrnwy aqueduct. Mr. KEAN then moved, Mr. JOLLEY seconded. and it was agreed, that the president, vice-president (Mr. Broadbent), Mr. Bleckly, Mr. Monks, and Mr. Carson be appointed a deputation to wait upon the Board of Trade when called upon. Mr. RO/3INSON asked if there were any plans of the pro- posed scheme. The PRESIDENT stated that there were none, but observed that one of the engineers let fall the remark that if the scheme were carried out, Warrington would become the finest sight for ship-building in the world. Mr. JOLLEY : There have been some fine ships built in the river at Warrington.

THE ASSOCIATED CHAMBERS. On the proposition of Mr. Kean seconded by Mr. PLATT, the president, vice-president, Mr:Meekly, Mr. Rigby, and Mr. Monks were appointed delegates to attend the autumnal meeting of the Associated Chambers of Commerce. This was all the business.

EXTRA_ORDINARY ACCIDENT WITH A FIRE ENGINE AT NEWTON. A VALUABLE HORSE KILLED AND A MAN INJURED. One of the most extraordinary accidents that has occurred in this district for many years past happened about eleven olcloek on Friday night last at Newton, when a very valu- able and favourite horse belonging to Colonel McCorquodale, High Sheriff of the County, was killed, and an under gardener, named J. Ball, in the employ of the same gentle- man, received somewhat severe injuries. It appears that in connection with the firm of Messrs. George McCorquodale and Co., whose works are near to Newton Bridge railway station, is a trained fire brigade composed of the hands, and in addition to possessing complete stationary apparatus, and a steam fire engine, there is also a splendid manual engine kept in a buildidg specially erected for the purpose. A watchman (whose name is Wm. Hall) is kept on the pre- mises all night, and his duty in case of an alarm of fire is to call up the brigade by the ringing of the "fire bell," and to keep all gates and doors locked until at least four of the firemen arrive to take charge. The brigade is the only one In the district for miles round, and whenever a fire occurs, which fortunately is very seldom, their services are gener- ally called upon. On the night in question an alarming and destructive fire occurred at the cotton mill of Mr. Edmundson, Chowbent, about eight or nine miles away. Owing to the fierceness of the flames the reflection from them was observable in the neighbourhood of Newton, and several persons brought news of the conflagration to the watchman on the premises of Messrs. McCorquodale. As it was thought advisable to call up the fire brigade, because their services might be re- quired, the "fire bell" was rung, and a number of the firemen were quickly at the works. When they arrived, however, they were bonsiderably surprised to find that a number of men, apparently entire strangers, had opened the gates, brought the engine out of the shed through the yard, and it was standing outside the gates on the brow leading to the station. Everything was upset and in estate of turmoil, the firemen for a long time being unable to find any lights or lamps, owing to the manner in which the " strangers " had gone about their work. Within a short period a horse was heard approaching at full speed, and as it neared the gates warning cries were shouted to the man on its back to beware of the engine. Apparently unheeding these, however, the horse, with the man on its back, dashed rapidly forward, and at full speed ran against the engine. The poor animal was literally transfixed to one of the iron couplings of the pumping handle of the engine, the iron rod measuring 14 inches long by three inches in width piercing I its breast to the full length up to the very cord of the engine. A fearful gash was made just below the neck, anA blood flowed almost in a torrent from the wound. When the horse was released it was found that the injuries were of a fatal character, and the animal expired immediately. The man on its back, who turned out to be James Ball, under I gardener, who was attracted by the ringing of the fire bell I and was bringing one of the horses from the stables of Mr. McCorquodale, a short distance away, was thrown into the ; street and alighted on his head. Both his eyes were ;discoloured, and in addition he received a wound .on his nose. This occurrence added much to the excitement that prevailed. It was not at first known where ,or what the fire was, but by means eta private telegram sent from the railway station it was ascertained that it was at,Chowbent. As the firemen had received no order to I attend, nor had their services or help been requested, the fire engine was put back into the yard. the dead carcase of the , horse was removed, and the blood-stained pavement was "swilled" with water poured thereon by means of the steam.fire engine kept at the weeks. Considerable mystery still surrounds the occurrence, and enquiries are being inetituted with the view of accertaining how andly what means the men gained admission into the yard and shed and were allowed to bring out the engine. It is stated that the watchman denies having unlocked the doors and gate, but on the contrary it is said that when the firemen arrived they found a number of men "buslying " themselves about the place' and they found the fire engine outside on the " brow" of. the road. If all had gone on right, the duty of the firemen who turned up (P. Percival, S. Rimmer, A. Chisholme' J. Egan, J. Jarding, and A. Craughton) would simply have been to get every thing in readiness for proceeding to the fire, but not move out of the yard until a message requesting their help was received. The engine was, however, moved into the road, with the result that has been described. The drirer of the horse states that he lost entire control of it, and that it took fright. He was entirely unaware of the engine being outside the gates, and as he was approaching thereto some one shone a lamp directly at them, coin- Plefely blinding him and the horse until the atnident had happened,

div.p: THE STATE .07 THE! HOUSE.

The MASTER reported on the 14th inst., that he had admitted 8 boys and 1 girl, and 7 boys on the 15th from the Barracks to the Hospital with skin disease, making 55 children (nearly one-third) from the school at the Barracks —rather a large number to be away from instruction. There were only 2 children on the sick list from the school at the Workhouse, where all the younger and more deli- cate children were. This was a matter the House Committee had reason to eongrattitate themselves upon. ,Oct the 23rd inst. the Rev. S. Wilkinson and a number,of his cosgregation, together with the Sunday school teachers and schslars, went through tie veins of the institution, and sang for the inmates, after which they presented each with a bouquet. The scene was an interesting one, and the visitors expressed themselves very pleased at the cleanli- ness, Ice., of the place, and the good order that prevailed everywhere. There were 485 inmates, as ageing 481 in the corresponding week of last year. Daring the week 176 vagrants (125 men, 30 w4u3en, and 21 children) were relieved. It was resolved that a vote of thanks be tendered to Ur. Wilkinson, This was All the 1A28410114

The horse which met with so sudden and shocking a death was an old favourite of Col. McCorquodale's, and was a very valuable one. He had had it in his possession for a great many years, and rode it at all the military reviews, kc., at which he was present. It was well known in the district, and was debarred from taking prizes in connection with the competition of horses of the Lancashire Hussars.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. The anniversary services in connection with the Earles- town Primitive Methodist Sabbath School, were held on Sunday last, and were of a very successful and encouraging character. The preacher for the day was the Rev. John Shephard, of Bradley Green, whose well-known ability and soul-stirring eloquence gained for him a hearty welcome, and the large congregations assembled to hear him testified to his popularity in the district. Notwithstanding the unfavourable weather in the forenoon there was a numerous attendance, and in the evening the chapel was croavded to excess, the congregation on each occasion being an attentive and interested one. In the afternoon the same rev, gentleman gave an excellent address to parents, teachers, scholars, and friends, to a large audience. At each of the services a collection was made in aid of the school funds and towards the expenses to be incurred in securing improved accommodation fer the scholars and congregation. The total sum realised was £l9 is. 9d., a sum in excess of that collected last year. As will be seen from a statement (given below) read by the Rev. John Shephard at the close of the evening service, the schools are in a flourishing condition, and a fair balance remains in hand after a year's working. Preaching in the morning Mr. Shepherd selected as his text the words, "And .His kingdom ruleth over all" (Psalm c. iii., 9th v.) He observed that the more correct rendering Of the text ought to be "And His government ruleth over all," for government was A Very extensive word with a varied and comprehensive meaning. Government meant not only a political organisation appertaining to particular subjects but it meant all things, naval and military, local and imperial, and everythijig associated with the people and I I their regular government in every respect. It was in that wide and extenaive sense he wished them to understand the word in his text. They called it God's providence, for God in providence was always nil ing and interfering in matters when they acted contrary to His will, and thus regulating all affairs in life. They were taught that God was in every thing and in every place and worked everything for good, that everything was governed and controlled by Him. There was a special providence watching ever God's church, and 'even as regarded their own denomination there was no one who could consider its beginning, rise, and position at the present time without seeing that God in His providence had been watching over them. Anyone who could read ecclesiastical history, the history of the Waldenses. the Hugenots, the Pilgrim Fathers, Nonconformity, Methodism, or the history of their own church, would see God's provi- dence for His church, and that He had nourished it, kept it, and blessed it. The preacher pointed out that there had been times in the history of the church when it had been in a low, languishing condition, and to all human appearance it seemed as though it were really going to die out, but God had been taking care of it, and had watched over it in his providence. He next alluded to the defeat of the Spanish Armada, remarking that though Popery with its ecclesias- tical and political powers united its forces to crush the Protes- tantism of England, yet pur forefather's, headed by their maiden queen, arose to meet their enemies, and by the help of God they defeated them.saving the Bible and the Protestan- tism in our land, which was now spreading and increasing all around. Thus God had been with His children. and had taken care of it in moments of danger, and he believed He was taking care of it to-day. Providence was sometimes mysterious and dark to us, and he was not going to say that everything was clear and explainable. There was a great deal of truth in the o4t-repeated words— . God moves in a mysterious way, His wonders to perform; He plants His footsteps in the sea, And rides upon the storm." He could not understand everything, but providence was not the only thing in which there was mystery. If an infidel came up and said there should be no mystery about it, he would tell him that there was no truth in what he called his creed because there was mystery in it. That secret power by which God is ever controlling the sun, moon, and stars was a mystery that the finest astronomical scientist could not understand, and thus they could not understand all things that an all-wise and gracious God gave them. He knew that providence was a mysterious work, but it was not a finished work, and when a thing was not finished they could not understand it very well. It was commenced about 8,000 years ago' and it might take as many more for what he knew to finish it. In concluding, the preacher beseeched his hearers to trust in the Lord and believe on Him, hoping in His government, and be guided by His laws, and He would afterwards receive them unto glory. The rev, gentleman selected as his text in the evening Genesis xxii., 2nd verse: "And He said, take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah ; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains, which I will tell thee of." The preacher delivered an eloquent discourse. In appealing for liberality at the collection, Mr. Shephard remarked that in the forenoon the amount received was rather less than last year, but they must keep up the collections. He hoped they would strain a point that night and do their best not to let the collections go down. He afterwards read a statement from which it appeared that the teachers in the school numbered 27 males and 7 females, total 34. Thirty-two of these were members of society—Christian persons. Scholars, males 90, females 33; total 184. Twenty-five of these scholars were members of the church; 38 besides were members of the Catechumen class. The Band of ,Hope numbered 120 members, the library contained 172 vols. and was well patronised by teachers and scholars, providing very healthy reading. The balance now in hand was £2l Ds. Eh., which was invested in the building society for the purpose of enlargement or improvement of the premises. They hoped that day would come when they wonld have two good school-rooms and a beautiful chapel. Their teachers and friends were doing a very worthy thing for the young and should have their sympathy and countenance. He was sure the position of the school and its finances were only due to them for the liberality and the interest they had taken in the place. It must be gratifying and it was highly creditable to the teachers. The object they had in hand was that of seeking better accommodation for the scholars and extending their premises, and he was sure their friends would give them their hearty support. Their work was such a noble one, and he was certain they had some claim upon their practical sympathy. Mr. Shepherd subsequently announced that the amount collected was £l9 is. 91, and he was deaired to return hearty and sincere thanks. The committee thought it a very handsome sum, and he was happy to say it was in advance of that of last year.

div.head: ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. P. E. Thompson, judge. CLAIM AGAINST A WIDNES HOTEL KEEPER.—Hugh Brown, landlord of the Albion Hotel, Widnes, was sued by John Holland, of Widnes, for £8 16s. id, for work done.— The plaintiff said deftendant kept a large hotel in Widnes, half way up the Waterloo-road.—ln answer to Mr. Riley, who appeared on behalf of the defendant, plaintiff said he was not aware that the defendant had reqently lost two of his children. The hotel defendant lived in was not so large as the Railway or Grosvenor hotels, but was a roadside inn. —MrAßiley said he had only been instructed by letter. In that letter the defendant stated his circumstances, and said he could not pay more than.Ll per month, which was the utmost he could do.—The plaintiff expressed his willingness to accept this offer, and an order was made accordingly. A LONG-STANDING Dien.—John Liversage was sued by Jane Oldfield, for the sum of £lO 19s. for goods delivered. Mr. Riley appeared for the plaintiff. It appeared that the. plaintiff had carried on business as a grocer and baker in Traviss-street, Parr. Defendant lived in a private Iwuse in the same street, but used the front room as a small shop. Previous to 1872 the plaintiff supplied the defendant with bread, dic., to sell in their shop, and it was for these goods the amount stated was claimed. Books were handed in to prove the claim, and Mr. Swift, who represented the defen- dant, said it certainly seemed from the books that the amount was due, but it Ni4s strange that greater exertion had not been made to recover the debt before the present time.—The defendant said he was at present a labourer and sometimes made £2 per week. An order for ss. per month was made. A HEATY CLAIM. —An application for a commit- ment order was made en behalf of the Mersey Loan Company, against Charles Taylor, for £42 9s. Bd. Mr. McCray represented the plaintiffs, and Mr. Riley, solicitor, the defendant—Mr. Riley said the sum was a very large one and his client only received 255. a week wages. He bad a wife to maintain, and had also to partly maintain his mother. He said he could only pay 10s. a month.—Defen• dant said he was employed by Mr. Scott, Manchester, who had a shop at St. Helens. He himself lived at Cropper's Hill, St. Helens.—His Honour: What was the amount for? —Mr. Riley: It was a loan, sir.—Mr. McCray said he thought the defendant had more than 255. per week, and he would ask that the case be adjourned to allow of his em- ployer being subpcened.—This application was granted. A Too YOUTHFUL BONDSMAN.—A young man, named William Barston, was sued on behalf of the Mersey Loan Company for the sum of £2 17s. 9d, the balance of a loan by John Roughley, Barston, step-father to the defendant.— Mr. R. W. H. Thomas, solicitor, appeared for the defemiant, and said his client had stood surety for his father-in-law, but at the time the loan was contracted he was only 17 year of age, antliving at home, and besides he had had no inti- mation of those proceedings. The notice had been served on defendant's step-father or mother, and they had pur- posely withheld it, as the step-father had promised that no .claim should be made on defendant for that amount.—Mr. McCray (who represented the plaintiffs) : Did you know .that you were acting a fraud in signing that note ?—Defen- dant: No, I did not know; I am no scholar.—ln answer to further questions, defendant said he was now married, and had recently removed several times.—His Honour said de- fendant had evidently had no intimation of the proceedings, and he would not make way order.—Mr. Thomas: Will you allow the defendant's costs, eir.—His Honour: Oh, no.
